docs.title: Welcome to Circulatory Autogen
docs.text:
Circulatory Autogen automates combining CellML modules into a system model, then calibrating the model to experimental or clinical data.

Common use cases include coupled biochemical cell models, neuron–cardiomyocyte models, and patient-specific 0D blood flow networks.

docs.title: Why Circulatory Autogen
docs.text:
Circulatory Autogen provides the following benefits.

  • Allows module reusability in system models:

    This software allows reusability and easy coupling of CellML modules. A wide range of openly available modules can be accessed and easily coupled to whatever modules you want to develop. Therefore, instead of having one huge model that will rarely be reused, you can easily integrate modules to create a system model and the modules can be used by others.

  • Provides the ability to calibrate model parameters to clinical or experimental data:

    This software supports parameter identification algorithms which you can use to calibrate the model parameters to clinical or experimental data.

  • Code generation

    By generating models in CellML, the user can then re-generate their model in whatever language they want (C++, Fortran, Matlab) with libcellml. This allows for easy coupling with other types of models (PDE), C generation for embedded systems, and much more.

  • Open Source

    Circulatory Autogen is completely open source. Unlike Software like Simulink, you will never need to pay to use Circulatory Autogen and you can continue using it outside of academia. This further promotes reproducible science by encouraging anyone to use and check the modules or models that are created.

docs.title: What Circulatory Autogen can do
docs.text:
Circulatory Autogen provides the following two main functionalities.

  1. Model Autogeneration

    This generates a system model by combining CellML modules in a user-defined network/arrangement. For more information, refer section Model Generation and Simulation.

  2. Parameter Identification

    This allows calibrating model parameters to data. See section Parameter Identification for more information.

You do not have to bring a CellML model. If you already have a solver of your own — a finite-element code, a compiled library, a hand-written scheme — Circulatory Autogen can drive it through the same pipelines. See External Python Solvers.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
If you are new to the project, follow these in order:

  1. Getting Started: install prerequisites and Python dependencies from pyproject.toml (virtual environment recommended).
  2. Designing a model: define your modules and configuration files.
  3. Model Generation and Simulation: generate a model and run it in OpenCOR or Python.
  4. External Python Solvers: or plug in a solver of your own that does its own time-stepping.
  5. Parameter Identification: calibrate parameters to data.
  6. Sensitivity Analysis and Identifiability Analysis: evaluate parameter influence and uncertainty.

If you are running on HPC, also read Running on HPC.

docs.title: Designing a model
docs.text:
This section describes how to design a model to be run in Circulatory Autogen. There are two sub sections included in this guide as follows.

  1. Creating a new model

  2. Converting an existing CellML model to run in Circulatory Autogen

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Familiarity with your CellML module structure.
  • A place to store user modules and configs (module_config_user/ or an external modules directory).

docs.title: Creating a new model
docs.text:
This software is designed so the user can easily make their own modules and couple them with existing modules. The steps are as follows.

  1. Either choose an existing [module_category]_modules.cellml file to write your module, or if it is a new category of module, create a [module_category]_modules.cellml file in [project_dir]/module_config_user/.

  2. Put your cellml model into the [module_category]_modules.cellml file.

  3. Create a corresponding module configuration entry in a JSON file within [project_dir]/module_config_user/. The code loads all *.json files in module_config_user (and in src/libcuflynx/generators/resources), so you can name it with your category (e.g. [module_category]_modules_config.json). These module declarations detail the variables that can be accessed, the constants that must be defined, and the available ports of the module.

  4. When possible, use units defined in [project_dir]/src/libcuflynx/generators/resources/units.cellml. If you need to define new units, define them in [project_dir]/module_config_user/user_units.cellml (or in an external modules directory; see below).

  5. Include your new module into a [CA_user_dir]/[file_prefix]_module_array.csv file.

    Note

    Modules that are connected as each others inputs and outputs will be coupled together with any ports with corresponding name.

    For an example, if VesselOne has an exit_port 'vessel_port' and VesselTwo has an entrance_port 'vessel_port', they will be coupled with the variables declared in their corresponding 'vessel_port'. You must be careful when making a new module, that the modules it couples to only has matching port types for the ones that are necessary for coupling.

    Additionally, if a module has a general_port [port_name], it will couple to any entrance, exit, or general port in a connected vessel with the port name [port_name].

    Standard usage: entrance and exit ports are used for spatial connections (e.g. exit to entrance of a parent and daughter vessel), whereas general ports are used for non-spatial connections (e.g a port for a material property of a whole vessel)

  6. Define model constants in a [CA_user_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters.json file. OR run the autogeneration, which will call an error and create a [CA_user_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters_unfinished.json. See model generation and simulation

The following sections include more details on creating the above required files.

docs.title: Creating module_array and parameter files
docs.text:
This section discusses creating a module_array and parameters files to build a new desired model.

One standard module array file contains five important columns, described below. The names are PhLynx's (#163).

  • name is the name of the module instance, often a common organ or part of the cardiovascular system.
  • module_type is the module, which exists in the [project_dir]/src/libcuflynx/generators/resources/*_modules_config.json files, one of the [project_dir]/module_config_user/*_config.json files, or a module library.
  • module_subtype is its variant: for a vessel, the type of the boundary condition at its input and output.
  • inp_instances are the instances feeding this one.
  • out_instances are the instances this one feeds.

The order of these lists matters for a module with more than one port of a type: its inputs take its entrance ports of each port_type in the order inp_instances lists them, and its outputs its exit ports in out_instances order (an instance with no port of that type is skipped). A monolithic heart's three vessel_port entrances are v_ivc, v_svc and v_pvn, so its vessel inputs are listed inferior vena cava, superior vena cava, pulmonary vein; its two exits are the aorta and the pulmonary artery. The rows' order in the array does not matter. A port left unconnected is a boundary condition, which needs a value in the parameters file; to leave an earlier port out while connecting a later one, list a module that sets it in its place, e.g. a zero_flow instance (module_type zero_flow, module_subtype nn) first among a heart's vessel inputs for a heart with one vena cava.

Some examples of possible inputs

Column name Possible inputs name User defined, but it is better to use common names like 'heart', 'pvn', 'par', etc. module_subtype 'vv', 'vp', 'pv', 'pp', 'pp_wCont', 'pp_wLocal', 'nn' (linked to module_subtype in the modules config JSON files) module_type 'heart', 'arterial', 'arterial_simple', 'venous', 'terminal', 'gas_transport_simple', 'pulomonary_GE', 'baroreceptor', 'chemoreceptor' (linked to module_type in the modules config JSON files) inp_instances name of the input instances, one (or more) of the names in the other rows out_instances name of the output instances, one (or more) of the names in the other rows

A module array with the columns BC_type, vessel_type, inp_vessels or out_vessels is refused; convert it once with cuflynx-upgrade module-array [file].

docs.title: JSON module arrays
docs.text:
The module array can also be a JSON file, [file_prefix]_module_array.json: a list of records, one per module instance.

[
 {"name": "src", "module_type": "flow_src", "module_subtype": "nn", "inp_instances": [], "out_instances": ["coll"]},
 {"name": "coll", "module_type": "collector", "module_subtype": "nn", "inp_instances": ["src"], "out_instances": []}
]

A record uses these keys. name and the type and subtype are required. The input and output lists are optional JSON lists; a space-separated string is accepted too. A record may also name the parameterisation whose parameters it uses, "parameterisation": "[name]" (see Module versions and parameterisations). Other keys are allowed, and keys holding plain values become extra columns, as extra CSV columns do.

A CSV module array is read by converting each row to this record first, so a CSV and its JSON conversion generate byte-identical models. The generator looks for the module array in this order: [file_prefix]_module_array.json, then [file_prefix]_module_array.csv. A [file_prefix]_vessel_array.json or .csv is refused; cuflynx-upgrade module-array [file] renames and converts it.

To convert CSV arrays, run

python -m libcuflynx.utilities.config_schemas to-json resources/my_model_module_array.csv [more.csv ...]

This writes my_model_module_array.json next to each CSV, one record per line. From Python, use libcuflynx.utilities.config_schemas.module_array_to_json(csv_path, json_path=None), and read_module_array_records(path) to read either a CSV or a JSON array as records.

JSON Schemas for the module array, for module config files and for the top level of obs_data files ship with the package, in libcuflynx/schemas/: module_array.schema.json, module_config.schema.json and obs_data.schema.json. libcuflynx checks every file against its schema when it reads it, so a file that an editor or PhLynx validates against the schema is one libcuflynx accepts. Errors name the file, the record (with its name) and the key, and say what the key is for.

Below figure is an example of a module_array file.

Every row of the module array file represents a specific part or module in the defined system. Therefore, each module needs several parameters for modeling and generating a CellML file.

These parameters go in the model's parameters file, [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters.json, beside the module array. It is JSON nested by instance, sub-instance and variable (schema libcuflynx/schemas/parameters.schema.json):

{"schema_version": 1,
 "global": {"R": {"value": 8.314, "units": "J_per_mol_K", "data_reference": "..."}},
 "aortic_root": {"C": {"value": 1.2e-8, "units": "m3_per_Pa", "data_reference": "Liang2009"}},
 "heart": {"lv": {"E_A": {"value": 366575000, "units": "J_per_m6", "data_reference": "Liang_2009_Table_2"}}}}
  • A parameter is an object with value (a number, or text such as EMPTY_MUST_BE_FILLED), units (as in CellML's units file) and data_reference (where the value comes from, typically [last_name][date][first_word_of_paper]). An optional origin says what set the value (measured, inherited, set_by_hand, derived or calibrated), and reason says why, which set_by_hand requires; a value a derivation calculates names it in derivation and has origin derived (see parameter-derivations.md), and a calibrated value is written with origin calibrated and no derivation; generation carries both into its parameters file for a calibration workflow's provenance diagram. Any other string key, such as a library's sourced, is kept and not read.
  • Every other object is an instance (a module-array record) or a sub-instance of a supermodule instance. global holds the global constants.
  • global, value and schema_version are reserved: no module-array record, submodule or variable may have those names.
  • Numbers keep the text they are written with (1.2e-8 stays 1.2e-8 in the generated model).

A parameters CSV (variable_name,units,value,data_reference) is refused. Convert one once with cuflynx-upgrade parameters [file], which writes the .json beside it, and name the .json file in input_param_file.

Note

If you forget to add or insert any needed parameter in the file when you run the code, it shows you this message at the end:

At this time, you should open [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters_unfinished.json, which holds every parameter the model needs, with EMPTY_MUST_BE_FILLED value and data_reference for those your file does not set. Fill them in, then remove _unfinished from the file's name (overwriting the original) and rerun the code.

docs.title: Naming parameters
docs.text:
A parameter's path in the parameters file is how it is written everywhere else, with a / between the levels, as obs_data operands and params_for_id targets do:

Written Meaning Name in the generated model aortic_root/C C of the vessel aortic_root C_aortic_root heart/lv/E E of the submodule lv of the supermodule instance heart E_heart__lv R or global/R the global constant R R

The generated model uses [variable_name]_[vessel_name], because a CellML name cannot contain /. A parameter is checked: one under a vessel that is not in the module array, a variable its module does not have, a global constant under a vessel, or a global (C_aortic_root under global) no module declares, is an error that lists every such parameter.

A parameters CSV written in the older [variable_name]_[vessel_name] form is converted in two steps, after the model's module configs and module array: cuflynx-upgrade parameter-names --module-array [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_module_array.csv (add --module-library-dir for modules from a library), which rewrites a name only when exactly one reading of it is a variable of that vessel's module and reports the rest, then cuflynx-upgrade parameters [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters.csv.

docs.title: Modules and definition of a new module
docs.text:
In the [CA_dir]/src/libcuflynx/generators/resources directory, there are several CellML files which contain the modules that can be coupled together in your model. Each module file has a corresponding *_modules_config.json file that defines connection ports and variables. Additionally, CellML and JSON files in module_config_user contain extra modules you define locally.

If you want to create a new module, create or add to a module_config_user/[module_category]_modules.cellml file and a matching JSON config file (e.g. module_config_user/[module_category]_modules_config.json). You can also keep these files outside the repo by setting external_modules_dir in your user_inputs.yaml to a directory containing *_modules.cellml, *_modules_config.json, and optionally any *units.cellml files (e.g. user_units.cellml).

To use a module library laid out one module per directory (for example circulatory-autogen-modules), set module_library_dirs to one or more directories. Each one is searched recursively for *_modules.cellml, *_modules_config.json (or *_module_config.json) and *units.cellml files; other JSON files, such as parameter or obs_data files kept next to a module, are ignored. Set use_builtin_modules: false to use only external modules. The built-in and module_config_user modules are then not loaded. Units defined identically in several files are written once; a unit defined differently in two files is an error.

A (module_type, module_subtype) defined in more than one source comes from the most specific source: external_modules_dir first, then module_library_dirs in the order you list them, then module_config_user, then the built-in modules. The other definitions' config entries and CellML components are left out of the model. Because one module silently replacing another is easy to miss, a ModuleShadowWarning lists every type defined more than once and which source won. For a library that replaces the built-in modules, set use_builtin_modules: false to avoid the warning. A type defined twice within one source (two files of one library, say) is an error.

module_library_dirs:
  - /path/to/circulatory-autogen-modules/modules
use_builtin_modules: false

As shown in the below figure, there are three different parts for each module: the primary specification (module_type, module_subtype, component_file, component_type), then the ports and their types, and finally, variables and constants.

Following is one of the modules in the BG_modules file. The main body of a specific module contains variables declaration, constitutive parameters, and state variables. Then, the constitutive relations and eventually, ODE equations.

docs.title: Example of creating a new module
docs.text:
This section shows a simple example to create a new module

We want to define a new module type with the name of "arterial" with the subtype (boundary condition type) "vp". Additionally, we want to use the "vp_type" module, whose cellml code is shown in the above figure. Also, the module is located in the BG_modules.cellml file.

module_type, module_subtype, module_format, component_file, component_type and other related information are added to the modules config JSON file, as shown below (the figure uses older key names: vessel_type, BC_type, module_file and module_type for the component). We can now use this module_type in the module_array file in [resources_dir] to add the module with specified inputs, outputs and parameters. In the ports, you should add the "vessel_port" type for connecting to the other parts. Additionally, each CellML component can be used by many module types.

The entries in the module config JSON file are detailed as follows.

The keys are PhLynx's. An entry with the older keys vessel_type, BC_type or module_file, or with default_instance, is refused; convert the file once with cuflynx-upgrade module-config [file]. An entry missing one of its four keys stops the generation with an error.

  • module_type: This will be the "module_type" entry in the module_array file
  • module_subtype: This will be the "module_subtype" entry in the module_array file
  • module_format: cellml for a CellML module. external_api marks an entry that is not CellML but describes, in an api block, how the generated model talks to another model (see below).
  • component_file: The file within [CA_dir]/src/libcuflynx/generators/resources/, [CA_dir]/module_config_user/, or your external_modules_dir that contains the CellML module this config entry links to.
  • component_type: The name of the module/computational_environment within the module cellml file.
  • entrance_ports: Specification of the port types that this module can take if it is connected as an output instance (in the other's out_instances) of another module. If a port_type matches to the port_type of a exit_port in a module coupled as an input, then the port_types variables, e.g. [v_in, u] get mapped to the variables in the coupled modules exit port e.g. [v, u_out].
  • exit_ports: Specification of the port types that this module can take if it is connected as an input instance (in the other's inp_instances) of another module.

  • general_ports: Specification of the port types that this module can take if it is connected as any type of connection to another module. Port entries are:

    • port_types: The name of the type of port. If two vessels are connected vessel_a to vessel_b, and vessel_a has an exit_port with the same port_type as an entrance_port of vessel_b, then a connection will be made.
    • variables: These are the variables within the module that will be connected to the variables in the corresponding port of the connected vessel/module.

    Note

    If you want a port variable to be able to couple to multiple other modules, set "multi_port": "True" in the entrance, exit, or general port. "multi_port": "sum" is used for variables that take in multiple port variables and sum them to equal this variable.

    • multi_port (optional): lets one port connect to several modules. Its values are case-insensitive: "sum", "Sum" and "SUM" are the same. It is either a string that applies to the whole port, or a list with one entry per port variable (below). The string forms are:
      • "True": this module's port variables are mapped to the corresponding variables of every connected module.
      • "sum": each of the port's variables is the sum, over every module connected through the port, of the neighbour's corresponding variable. This is the same as the list form with "sum" for every variable, described below, and it means the same on every port_type. It is what PhLynx's "Sum" means. For example, a volume_sum module has an entrance volume_port [q] with "sum", so q is the total volume of every module connected to it through that port. For example, the module library's microvasculature_network Nout modules have an exit flow_port [v_out_sum] with "Sum", so v_out_sum is the sum of the downstream modules' inflows. As in the list form, the sum is positive on both entrance and exit ports, and only one side of a connection may sum.
      • "Multiply": the port must have exactly one variable. Whichever end of a connection it is on, each connected module's corresponding variable is set to multiply_factor times this module's variable. The generated component that does this is multiport_multiply_[neighbour_name]_[neighbour_variable]. If the neighbour's port is a "sum", the scaled value is added as one term of its sum instead. A connection cannot be Multiply on both ends. This matches PhLynx.
      • Leave multi_port out, or set it to null or false, for a one-to-one port. The string "False" is refused; cuflynx-upgrade module-config [file] drops it.
    • multiply_factor (optional, default 1): the factor of a port's Multiply variables, e.g. {"port_type": "gain_port", "variables": ["x"], "multi_port": "Multiply", "multiply_factor": 2.5}. For a list-form port it may instead be a list aligned with variables, a number for each "multiply" entry and null for the others: {"variables": ["v", "u"], "multi_port": ["multiply", "True"], "multiply_factor": [4, null]}. A PhLynx export without a multiply_factor keeps the factor in PhLynx's user interface, not in the config file; add it to the config by hand. It is an error on a port with no Multiply variable.

    • multi_port as a list with one entry per port variable, aligned with variables, when some variables must be summed over the connected modules and others shared with them:

      {"port_type": "vessel_port", "variables": ["v_in", "u"], "multi_port": ["sum", "True"]}
      • "sum": this module's variable (an input of the module) equals the sum, over every module connected through this port, of that module's corresponding port variable, i.e. the variable at the same position in its matching port, which a plain one-to-one mapping would have paired it with. The sum is computed in a generated algebraic component, multiport_sum_[vessel_name]_[variable_name], declared in the units of this module's variable. A neighbour variable in different but compatible units (e.g. mm3_per_s summed into m3_per_s) is scaled; incompatible units stop the generation with an error. A connected "sum" variable may be of any parameter type (below). If no module is connected through the port, it must be a boundary_condition: it is then a constant like any other unconnected boundary condition, its value [vessel_name]/[variable_name] must be set in the parameters file, and no sum component is written for it. A "sum" variable of another parameter type with nothing connected stops the generation with an error. A neighbour that reaches a "sum" through two connections (it is listed twice in out_instances, or it or the summing module has two ports of the matching port_type that both connect it) would be counted twice, so generation stops with an error naming both modules.
      • "True": this module's variable is mapped to the corresponding variable of every connected module. It is normally an output of this module (one source, many sinks).
      • "multiply": as a whole-port "Multiply", for this variable only: each connected module's corresponding variable is set to this variable times its factor (multiply_factor, above), or gets it as one term of its "sum". Only one end of a variable pair may be "multiply".

      A list-form port works as an entrance port (many upstream modules), an exit port (many downstream modules) or a general port. With one connected module it behaves exactly like a plain port. For example, a flow_merge node (many inflows, one outflow) has the entrance port above, [v_in, u] with ["sum", "True"], and a plain exit port [v_out, u_d], with v_out = v_in and u = u_d: the node's inflow is the sum of the upstream flows, and every upstream module reads the node pressure. A flow_split node (one inflow, many outflows) puts the list on its exit port instead, [v_out, u_d] with ["sum", "True"]. Only one side of a connection may mark a variable "sum". A variable may be "sum" on several of a module's ports: it is then the sum over the neighbours of all of them, in one multiport_sum_[vessel_name]_[variable_name] component. When coupling a C++ model to a 1D model (couple_to_1d), the port of a module that faces a 1D vessel cannot be "sum", "Multiply" or list-form if 0D modules also connect to it: the coupler sets that port's variables, so generation raises NotImplementedError. Such a port is allowed when the 1D vessel is its only neighbour (the sum then has no terms and stays the boundary condition the coupler sets), and such ports elsewhere in the module and the 0D model, such as a volume sum, are allowed. - variables_and_units: This specifies all of the constants and the accesible variables of the cellml module. The entries are: - [0] variable name: corresponding to the name in the cellml file - [1] variable unit: corresponsing to the unit specification in units.cellml - [2] access or no_access: whether the variable can be accessed within the cellml simulation. This should always be "access" for accessibility, unless you want to decrease memory usage. - [3] parameter type: can be constant, global_constant, variable, or boundary_condition. - If parameter_type is boundary_condition it will be set to a variable accesses from another module if the corresponding port is connected. However, if the corresponding port is not connected, the boundary_condition will be set to a constant, and required to be set in the [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters.json file

    Note

    All constants are required to be entered in the [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters.json file, under their vessel: [vessel_name]/[variable_name] (see Naming parameters).

    All global_constants are required to be entered in the [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_parameters.json file under global.

docs.title: Connecting vessels at a node
docs.text:
A node is a point where vessel_port ends meet: the outlet of a vessel, the inlets of the vessels it feeds through that port, the outlets of anything else feeding those inlets, and so on. A vessel's subtype letters say what each of its ends does at a node: v (compliant, it sets the pressure there and takes the flows) or p (it takes that pressure and gives its flow).

A node of two ends is a plain pair: a v end meets a p end. At a node of three or more ends, one side of the node (the upstream outlets, or the downstream inlets) has a single end, and that end must be compliant: a vessel end with letter v, or, for a module that is not a vessel, a port whose multi_port has a "sum" entry (a whole-port "sum", or a list containing "sum", such as a heart chamber's [v_in, u] port with ["sum", "True"]). It owns the node: its flow is the sum of the flows of the ends on the other side, all of them its direct neighbours, and they all read its pressure.

"Compliant" means the same for every module: the end that takes the sum and shares the pressure. A "Multiply" port broadcasts one scaled value and a plain "True" port maps one value to every neighbour; neither sums anything, so neither can own a node of three or more ends, and such a node is refused. Either still connects to a single neighbour (a two-ended node).

  • A split: the parent's outlet is v and the daughters' inlets are p, e.g. a Nout_junction pv feeding pv and pp vessels.
  • A merge: the child's inlet is v and the merging outlets are p, e.g. vp vessels into a venous vp.

Generation refuses a node that breaks this, naming the node's ends and the end that must be compliant. Fix it by swapping subtypes so the end alone on its side is v and the others are p (for a split, parent pp -> pv and a compliant daughter vv -> pv, with a module type whose port there takes several connections), for a module that is not a vessel by giving that port a "sum" entry, or by putting a lumped vv vessel between the lone end and the others, which then owns the node. A node with several ends on both sides cannot be owned by one end and is refused: join those vessels through a vv vessel they merge into and split from, whose inlet and outlet then each own a node. Nodes with a 1D (FV1D_vessel) end are coupled by the 1D coupler and are not checked. See issue #616. resources/generic_junction_test_open_loop_module_array.csv follows the rule at every split; generic_junction_test2_open_loop is the same network with four of its splits mixed, and is refused.

Models made with the junction module types. The module library had junction module types (Min_junction, Nout_junction, MinNout_junction, split_junction, merge_junction, 2in2out_junction, their _simple and venous_ variants, the microvasculature's <vessel>_Min/_Nout/_Minlet/_Noutlet/_MinNout, flow_merge and flow_split): vessels with a fixed number of numbered ports, or a summed port named v_in_sum/v_out_sum. It replaced them by the ordinary vessels, whose compliant end sums its node as above. Convert a model once, after cuflynx-upgrade module-names, with cuflynx-upgrade junctions [resources_dir]/[file_prefix]_module_array.json --module-library-dir [library]/modules. It retypes each junction to the version the library's renames.json names (the equations are the same), splits an inlet_flow constant_2 into two constant sources, removes a flow_merge or flow_split and joins its neighbours, and renames what changed in [file_prefix]_parameters.json, [file_prefix]_obs_data*.json and [file_prefix]_params_for_id*.json: v_in_sum and v_out_sum become v_in and v_out, and a numbered port flow (J/v_out_1) becomes the inflow of the neighbour on that port (s1/v). It lists values the new version has no variable for, which it drops, and any name it could not map.

docs.title: Coupling to other models: the api block
docs.text:
A module config entry with "module_format": "external_api" and an api block is a module that is not CellML: another model the generated C++ (model_type: cpp) runs with. It is a row of the module array, connected to CellML modules through its ports like any module, and values it sets become libCellML external variables of the generated code. Three kinds exist:

  • a Python model, such as a FEniCS PDE (role: provider, transport: python), run with cuflynx-couple;
  • the FV 1D solver (FV1D_vessel / FV1D_solver: named_pipe consumers and a process), run through the coupler;
  • a C++ program driving a generated class (role: provider, transport: cpp_class).

Coupling to external models describes all three. The blocks are validated when the module configs load (libcuflynx/generators/cpp/api.py).

docs.title: Supermodules
docs.text:
A supermodule is a named group of modules that a module array uses like one module. Its version is an entry in a *_modules_config.json file, in a directory listed in module_library_dirs (or in external_modules_dir), naming the module versions it is built from:

{"module_type": "heart", "module_subtype": "supermodule", "module_format": "supermodule",
 "description": "four chambers, four valves and a cardiac clock",
 "submodule_versions": [
   {"module_type": "cardiac_clock", "module_subtype": "nn"},
   {"module_type": "chamber", "module_subtype": "vv"}
 ],
 "default_parameterisation": "adult"}

Its instances and their connections are a module array of their own, [module_type]_[module_subtype]_module_array.json beside the config (heart_supermodule_module_array.json):

[{"name": "clock", "module_type": "cardiac_clock", "module_subtype": "nn", "out_instances": ["ra", "rv", "la", "lv"]},
 {"name": "ra", "module_type": "chamber", "module_subtype": "vv", "inp_instances": ["clock"], "out_instances": ["trv"]}]
  • module_type / module_subtype: the type that instances name in a module array.
  • module_format: "supermodule". A supermodule has no component_file/component_type; it is never a component module, and its type may not also be a component module's type.
  • submodule_versions: the versions its module array's records use. Each record uses one of them, and each is used.
  • The module array's names are local to the supermodule, and their input and output lists name other submodules only. A record names no "parameterisation".
  • default_parameterisation (optional): the parameterisation used when a module-array record names none. It is the template of a new instance's values.
  • An inline submodules list or a default_parameters CSV is refused. cuflynx-upgrade module-config [file] --module-library-dir [library] converts them: the submodule records to the module array file, submodule_versions into the entry, each instance's values into the default parameterisation, and a default_parameters CSV to the parameterisation parameterisations/default/.
  • description (optional).

A supermodule's parameterisation, parameterisations/[name]/[name]_parameters.json, is nested by its instances, with its globals under global:

{"schema_version": 1,
 "global": {"T": {"value": 1, "units": "second", "data_reference": "Liang_2009_Table_2"}},
 "ra": {"E_A": {"value": 7998000, "units": "J_per_m6", "data_reference": "Liang_2009_Table_2"}},
 "lv": {"E_A": {"value": 366575000, "units": "J_per_m6", "data_reference": "Liang_2009_Table_2"}},
 "soma": {"i_M": {"g_M": {"value": 1.0, "units": "dimensionless", "data_reference": "..."}}}}

An instance that is itself a supermodule nests a level further (soma above), over its own version's default parameterisation. A supermodule version's directory has no other parameters file; a [module_type]_[module_subtype]_parameters.json beside its module array is refused, and cuflynx-upgrade parameters [its config] folds it into the default parameterisation.

docs.title: A model's supermodule instances
docs.text:
A supermodule instance's values are in the model's parameters file, under its name, like any instance's: heart/lv/E_A is {"heart": {"lv": {"E_A": ...}}} in resources/3compartment_parameters.json.

  • They are copied once, when the instance is made, from its version's template: the version's default parameterisation, or the one the record names in its place, and the templates of the supermodules nested in it under them:
cuflynx-upgrade supermodule-instances resources/3compartment_module_array.json --module-library-dir [library]

(with --external-modules-dir and --no-builtin-modules as the model is generated with, and --parameters [file] for a parameters file that is not [prefix]_parameters.json beside the array). It writes the values of each supermodule instance the file has no entry for, and leaves the others; --instance [name] picks instances and --replace writes theirs again from the version, over the model's values. - A named supermodule parameterisation replaces the default, so it sets every instance value the default sets; an instance made from one that lacks some is refused, naming them. (Its globals are read from it at generation; a global it lacks comes from the submodule version's default.) - After that the model's file holds the instance's values, so editing or calibrating one model changes no other. Generation refuses a supermodule instance the file has no entry for, naming that command. - Of the supermodule's parameterisation, generation reads only the globals. A value the model's file does not set comes from the submodule version's default_parameterisation. - A calibration of the model (a calibration workflow, or a selection of a nested instance) writes its values to the model's file. In a module library, calibrate apply of a submodule version writes every instance of it, in the supermodule versions' default parameterisations and in every system model's parameters file. - A model made with the per-instance files [prefix]_supermodule_parameters/[instance].json beside its module array is converted by cuflynx-upgrade parameters [prefix]_parameters.csv (or the .json), which moves each file in under its instance; the model's own values win.

An instance in a module array names the supermodule's type and links its hosts, the modules outside it, to individual submodules:

{"name": "heart", "module_type": "heart", "module_subtype": "supermodule",
 "per_submodule_inputs": {"ra": ["venous_svc"], "la": ["pvn"]},
 "per_submodule_outputs": {"aov": ["aortic_root"], "puv": ["par"]}}

per_submodule_inputs lists, for a submodule, the hosts that feed it; each of those hosts lists the instance (heart) in its outputs. per_submodule_outputs lists the hosts a submodule feeds; each of those lists the instance in its inputs. Either may also be written as a list of one-key objects, [{"ra": ["venous_svc"]}, {"la": ["pvn"]}].

Before anything else reads the module array, each instance is replaced, at its position, by one record per submodule:

  • submodule ra becomes heart__ra (the levels of a path are joined with __), and its links to other submodules are prefixed the same way;
  • the hosts in per_submodule_inputs["ra"] come first in heart__ra's inputs, and the hosts in per_submodule_outputs["ra"] last in its outputs;
  • in a host, the instance name is replaced, in place, by every heart__[submodule] that the instance links it to.

So the model's parameters and outputs are named after the expanded modules, e.g. E_heart__lv, heart__lv/q. In your own files, write the path instead: heart/lv/E in a parameters file and heart/lv/q in obs_data operands, or SN/soma/membrane/V two levels down. The flat heart__lv/q is accepted too. A path that is not a submodule is an error. A supermodule parameterisation CSV row in the older [variable]_[submodule] form can only be split by guessing (g_leak_Na is g of leak_Na or g_leak of Na); cuflynx-upgrade parameter-names --supermodule-config [config] --module-library-dir [library] rewrites such rows once, checking each against the submodules' variables, before cuflynx-upgrade parameters. The supermodule parameterisation's globals are used for every global that [file_prefix]_parameters.json does not set, so values in your parameters file always win. A global used by several parameterisations is added once. The supermodule's globals win over those of its submodules' own parameterisations.

A submodule can itself be a supermodule instance, with its own per_submodule_inputs/per_submodule_outputs naming its siblings; it is expanded in turn. A supermodule that contains itself, directly or through others, is an error.

docs.title: Naming a submodule by its path
docs.text:
A host can also name a submodule directly, by its path, in its own inp_instances/out_instances: "out_instances": ["heart/ra"], or "neuron/soma/membrane" two levels down. The reference becomes heart__ra where it stands, so each host keeps its own order (with per_submodule_*, every host gets the submodules in that object's order), and the submodule takes the host as it would from per_submodule_*. A per_submodule_* key may be a path too, {"soma/membrane": ["axon"]}: it is passed down to the nested instance soma. Paths are allowed only in a host's lists and in per_submodule_* keys, not in the instance's own lists or in a supermodule's submodule records, and a path that names nothing once everything is expanded is an error.

Because the levels are joined with __, a module-array or submodule name may not contain __ nor begin or end with _: then heart__ra splits back into heart/ra one way only (with a single _, a + b_c and a_b + c would both be a_b_c). Nested levels joined with a single _ (heart_ra/q in an obs_data operand or a params_for_id row, E_heart_ra in a parameters CSV) are refused; cuflynx-upgrade parameter-names rewrites them in a parameters CSV.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
A supermodule entry may declare an ordered interface:

"interface": [{"name": "venous_return", "submodule": "ra", "port_type": "vessel_port", "label": "RA inflow"},
              {"name": "aortic_outflow", "submodule": "aov", "port_type": "vessel_port", "label": "aorta"}]

Each entry names a submodule (a path for a nested one) and a port type; names are unique and every path must exist. A host that lists the instance with no per_submodule_* entry for it is linked to the first entry whose port_type is one of its own ports facing the instance (its exit and general ports when it feeds the instance, its entrance and general ports when the instance feeds it). Keys starting phlynx_ (PhLynx's layout and interface metadata) are read and ignored, on records and on config entries.

Expansion stops with an error that names the file, the instance and the key when a per_submodule_* names a submodule that does not exist, or a host that does not exist or does not list the instance back; when a module lists the instance but no per_submodule_* entry (or interface entry) links them; or when no supermodule of the instance's type was found. An instance named heart is not treated as the legacy heart module: after expansion there is no module called heart.

docs.title: Module versions and parameterisations
docs.text:
A module library (such as circulatory-autogen-modules) lays out each version of a module with its parameterisations, named parameter sets:

modules/<category>/<module_type>/versions/<version>/
    <module_type>_<version>_modules.cellml
    <module_type>_<version>_modules_config.json      one entry; module_subtype is <version>
    <module_type>_<version>_units.cellml
    parameterisations/<name>/
        <name>_parameters.json                      nested parameter values, rooted at the module
        <name>_obs_data.json                        optional; "obs_data_name": "<name>"
        <name>_params_for_id.json                   optional

Note

A version with an instances/ directory and no parameterisations/ is refused: rename the directory to parameterisations/. A parameterisation with only a [name]_parameters.csv is refused: convert it with cuflynx-upgrade parameters [file], or a whole library with cuflynx-upgrade parameters [modules directory]. A module-array record names its parameterisation with "parameterisation": "instance" there is an error, since an instance is the record itself.

A parameterisation changes only parameters, never the equations. Its parameters file has the model file's form rooted at the module: the module's own variables at the top, with no vessel, and the global_constant variables it sets under global:

{"schema_version": 1,
 "global": {"rho": {"value": 1050, "units": "Js2_per_m5", "data_reference": "known", "sourced": "yes"}},
 "C": {"value": 1.2e-8, "units": "m3_per_Pa", "data_reference": "Liang2009", "sourced": "yes"}}

A global constant of the module at the top, or a variable under global that is not one of its global constants, is an error.

The config entry names the parameterisation used by default:

{"module_type": "chamber", "module_subtype": "v1", "component_file": "chamber_v1_modules.cellml",
 "component_type": "chamber_type", "default_parameterisation": "adult", ...}

A module-array record chooses a parameterisation with "parameterisation":

{"name": "lv", "module_type": "chamber", "module_subtype": "v1", "parameterisation": "neonate",
 "inp_instances": ["mv"], "out_instances": ["aov"]}

When the model is generated, the parameterisation's parameters file is looked for next to the config file the record's (module_type, module_subtype) came from: [config directory]/parameterisations/[name]/[name]_parameters.json. Each of its variables [variable] becomes [variable]_[record name] (C_lv); a global keeps its plain name. A record without "parameterisation" uses the entry's default_parameterisation, if the entry has one and that file exists. Otherwise no parameterisation parameters are loaded.

Parameterisation parameters are defaults. A parameter that [file_prefix]_parameters.json sets keeps the value from that file. The order of precedence is:

  1. your [file_prefix]_parameters.json, which holds a supermodule instance's values too;
  2. a supermodule's parameterisation (its globals);
  3. the parameterisation of an ordinary module: the one its record names, or its version's default_parameterisation (for a submodule, always the default).

Within one level, the first record in the (expanded) module array wins, so a global set by several parameterisations is added once. A global is one value for the whole model, so if parameterisations set it to different values you get a ConflictingGlobalWarning naming each value, its units and the record that set it: the modules after the first run at a value their parameterisation did not choose. Set the global in [file_prefix]_parameters.json to choose it, which also silences the warning. A supermodule parameterisation overriding the parameterisations inside it is not warned about. If the units differ too, the modules most likely mean different quantities by one name, and one of them needs renaming.

A parameterisation that does not exist is an error. The error names the version directory and lists the parameterisations it has. Naming a parameterisation of a module whose config has no parameterisations/ directory next to it is an error too.

An obs_data file may carry a top-level "obs_data_name", a string naming the data set. A parameterisation's [name]_obs_data.json sets it to the parameterisation's name. If a file in parameterisations/[name]/ has a different or missing obs_data_name, a warning is raised when the file is read. Files without the key are read without a warning. The parsed obs_data carries the name as obs_data_name, or None when the file has none.

docs.title: Converting an existing CellML model to run in Circulatory Autogen
docs.text:
Circulatory Autogen provides a script to convert an existing CellML model (with parameters hardcoded in the modules) to a format that can be used with Circulatory_Autogen. This format defines parameters in a separate file so they can be used for calibration and specifies modules in a config file with ports for easy coupling. You can find the script "generate_modules_files.py" at [CA_dir]/src/libcuflynx/scripts.

Update the script to change the input_model variable to the path of your CellML model and output_dir variable to the directory where you need to create the resources files and the new [file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml file.

This script generates [file_prefix]_modules.cellml and [file_prefix]_module_config.json in the module_config_user directory. [file_prefix]_parameters.json and [file_prefix]_module_array.csv files are created in [output_dir]/resources and [file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml is created in [output_dir].

You only need to update the user_inputs.yaml file at the user_run_files directory to set user_inputs_path_override: to [output_dir]/[file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml to run model autogeneration.

Note

You can update the file_prefix, vessel_name and the data_reference variables in the generate_modules_files.py at the src/libcuflynx/scripts directory before running the script, so it will generate files with the defined variables.

Warning

You need to specify the variable name of time as the time_variable.

Variable component_name should be the name of the component for which you want to generate files.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
You should have:

  • A *_modules.cellml file and a matching modules config JSON.
  • Updated *_module_array.csv and *_parameters.json files referencing your modules.
  • A user_inputs.yaml file that points to your resources directory.

docs.title: Emulators
docs.text:
An emulator is one kind of surrogate: a fast statistical stand-in for your model. Circulatory Autogen fits one that maps the parameters in your params_for_id.json to the scalar features of your obs_data.json data items — the same numbers the cost function is computed from. Once it is trained, calibration, sensitivity analysis, UQ/MCMC and identifiability analysis can all evaluate the emulator instead of running the solver.

The training runs are paid up front

Training costs num_train_samples simulations. That is only worth it when the downstream use is much larger:

  • Sobol sensitivity analysis — num_samples × (2M + 2) model evaluations. Worth it.
  • MCMC / UQ — tens of thousands of evaluations. Worth it.
  • Identifiability analysis — a Hessian's worth per parameter pair. Usually worth it.
  • A single genetic-algorithm calibration — often cheaper run directly. Not worth it.

Scope: scalar features, not waveforms

The emulator predicts each data item's value after its operation (max, mean, max_minus_min, …). It does not produce simulated traces, so data_type: series and frequency observables, prediction traces and output plots are not available in emulator mode — CA refuses them explicitly rather than returning something that looks plausible. Emulating full time series is a planned follow-up. Prediction items that reduce to a scalar can be emulated: see Prediction features.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The emulator backend is autoemulate, an optional dependency (it pulls in torch, gpytorch and lightgbm — about 750 MB — and needs Python ≥3.10, <3.13):

pip install "libcuflynx[emulation]"

Everything else in CA works without it; only do_emulation / use_emulator need it. CA never imports autoemulate unless one of those flags is set — it checks whether the package exists without loading it, so a normal run does not pay torch's import time.

Two installation gotchas

Pin a CPU torch. Left alone, pip installs the CUDA build and its ~2.5 GB of nvidia-* wheels. On a machine without a GPU:

pip install torch==2.12.1+cpu --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install "autoemulate>=2.1,<3" --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

autoemulate 2.1.2 cannot sit alongside torch ≥ 2.13. Its harmonic dependency pins setuptools==68.0.0 while torch 2.13 requires setuptools>=77.0.3, so pip reports ResolutionImpossible. Pinning torch to 2.12.x (as above) resolves it. Without a pin, pip silently backtracks through several 500 MB torch wheels looking for a combination that works.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Two independent flags, because emulation has two steps:

do_emulation: false   # train an emulator against the solver named by `solver`
use_emulator: false   # make the analyses evaluate the trained emulator

solver: keeps meaning the truth solver — the one the emulator is trained against, and the one you compare it with. That is deliberate: switching to an emulator should not lose track of what it is approximating.

emulator_settings:
  # emulator_dir:            # default <param_id_output_dir>/emulators/<file_prefix>_<obs_prefix>
  models: default            # 'default', 'all', or a comma-separated list of emulator names
  num_train_samples: 128     # simulations run to build the training set
  reuse_samples: false       # refit the samples a previous run saved, instead of simulating
  sample_type: sobol         # sobol | latin_hypercube | random
  log_scale_params: false    # space the design logarithmically (needs every min > 0)
  random_seed: 0
  test_fraction: 0.2         # held out and never trained on -- what R2/RMSE are measured on
  n_splits: 5                # autoemulate cross-validation folds
  n_iter: 10                 # hyper-parameter settings sampled per emulator
  min_r2: 0.9                # refuse to USE an emulator worse than this
  out_of_bounds: error       # error | warn | clip
  fd_rel_step: 1.0e-3        # step for the finite-difference gradient over the emulator
  include_prediction_items: false  # also emulate prediction items that have an operation

The available models names come from the installed autoemulate and are discoverable in code:

from libcuflynx.emulators.emulator_trainer import emulator_model_names
print(emulator_model_names())   # GaussianProcessRBF, RadialBasisFunctions, LightGBM, ...

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
cd user_run_files
./run_emulator_training.sh 8      # 8 MPI processes

The design points are spread across MPI ranks, each runs the real solver, and rank 0 fits and saves the emulator. The script prints the held-out R² per observable:

[emulator] training on 64 samples across 8 rank(s)
[emulator] saved to .../emulators/Simple_ODE_Benchmark_Simple_ODE_Benchmark_obs_data
    held-out R2   1.0000   x_{SS} (steady_state_avg benchmark/x)
    held-out R2   1.0000   y_{SS} (steady_state_avg benchmark/y)

Read those numbers before using it. They are the only thing standing between you and a set of Sobol indices for a model you did not simulate.

How good an emulator you can get depends on the parameter box

Difficulty grows with the width of the params_for_id ranges, the number of parameters and how rough the feature is. Two worked examples from this repo, at opposite ends:

  • Simple_ODE_Benchmark — steady states of dx/dt = -x + p, dy/dt = -3y + q, i.e. a smooth monotone response. 64 Sobol samples give held-out R² of 0.99999 and 0.99997. This is what a well-posed emulation problem looks like.
  • Lotka_Volterra — max of each state over the full declared ranges (alpha 0.1–7, gamma 0.1–10, the response spanning 20–3900). A 128-sample Gaussian process manages only about 0.2 and 0.5, and 256 samples does not reliably improve it: max of an oscillation whose period shifts sharply with the parameters is close to discontinuous.

If your R² is poor, the useful moves are, in order: narrow the parameter ranges to the region you actually care about; add samples; set log_scale_params: true when a bound spans decades; try models: all; and consider whether the feature is a smooth function of the parameters at all. What you should not do is lower min_r2 to make the run proceed.

The saved directory contains:

File What it is emulator.joblib the fitted emulator emulator_metadata.json per-feature R², RMSE, MAE, bias, max abs error and nRMSE; the training box; the design; provenance training_data.npz the design and its simulated targets, so it can be refitted or extended without re-simulating emulator_validation.npz the held-out points: theta, the simulator's y_true and the emulator's y_pred, in real units

docs.title: Trying another emulator without re-running the simulations
docs.text:
Training is two costs: the num_train_samples runs of your model — minutes to hours, and the whole reason emulators exist — and the fit, which takes seconds. training_data.npz above is what makes the second one repeatable on its own:

emulator_settings:
  reuse_samples: true        # refit what emulator_dir already holds; run no new simulations
  models: all                # ... with a different emulator,
  test_fraction: 0.3         # ... or a different split, n_iter, n_splits, min_r2, random_seed

./run_emulator_training.sh 1    # one rank is enough: there is nothing left to parallelise

The result is an ordinary emulator bundle, written over the same directory, and its metadata records design.reused_samples: true so the provenance never claims simulations that run did not perform.

What it does not do

  • It runs no simulations, so num_train_samples, sample_type and log_scale_params are ignored — the saved design is what gets fitted, however many points it holds. If your num_train_samples disagrees with what was saved, CA prints the number it is really using rather than letting the requested one stand.
  • It needs a previous training run in emulator_dir. The first run has to have reuse_samples: false; that is the run that pays for the simulations.
  • random_seed still applies — it seeds the fit and the train/test split — so re-fitting with a different seed is a meaningful thing to do.
  • Samples belong to one problem. If the parameter bounds, obs_data.json, protocol or the model file have changed since they were simulated, CA refuses rather than refitting them: retrain with reuse_samples: false instead. Reusing them would produce an emulator that is confidently wrong about a study it was never trained for.

docs.title: Analysing the error
docs.text:
The statistics say how wrong the emulator is on average; the held-out points say where, which is what decides whether the region you care about is one of the good ones. Both are read through the bundle:

from libcuflynx.emulators.emulator_bundle import EmulatorBundle
bundle = EmulatorBundle.load(emulator_dir)

for row in bundle.error_stats():
    print(row['label'], row['r2'], row['bias'], row['nrmse'])

points = bundle.error_points()      # None if the bundle predates this
# points['y_pred'] vs points['y_true']  -> parity plot
# points['residual'] vs points['theta'] -> where in the space it goes wrong

residual is prediction minus truth, fixed here so every consumer agrees on the sign: positive means the emulator reads high. Why more than R²:

  • bias — a feature can score a good R² and still read systematically high, which shifts every downstream cost rather than just adding noise to it.
  • nrmse — RMSE in one feature's units says nothing against another's, so it is the only one of these that can rank features against each other.
  • max_abs_error — an emulator that is good almost everywhere still misleads a calibration that walks through the one place it is not.

These points are free: training already paid to simulate them and then deliberately did not fit to them.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Set use_emulator: true and run any of the usual scripts unchanged:

./run_param_id.sh 4
./run_sensitivity_analysis.sh 4
./run_identifiability_analysis.sh

Nothing else in the configuration changes. To sanity-check a result, run the same analysis with use_emulator: false and compare — that is what keeping solver: meaningful is for.

docs.title: Prediction features
docs.text:
With include_prediction_items: true, the emulator is also trained on the prediction_items that have an operation (see Prediction items as scalar features). This is for a sensitivity analysis with sa_options.include_prediction_items: true on the emulator.

  • Only scalar prediction items with an operation are included: data_type: constant, or no data and a reducing operation such as max. Series items are never included. The others are skipped, with a warning that names them. An operation that returns more than one number is an error.
  • They are the last emulator outputs, after the data_item features, named by data_item_name. The bundle lists them in emulator_metadata.json as prediction_feature_labels, and EmulatorBundle.prediction_feature_labels / data_feature_labels split feature_labels.
  • The fingerprint gains a separate prediction_sha256 covering them. inputs_sha256 does not change, so an emulator trained without the option has the same fingerprint as before.
  • A calibration (or UQ, or IA) on this emulator still fits only the data_item features. It does not check the prediction features, so editing a prediction item does not make the emulator stale for calibration, and a poorly emulated prediction feature does not stop it.
  • An SA with include_prediction_items: true checks both: the same prediction items as at training (otherwise stale), and their held-out R² against min_r2. On an emulator trained without the option it stops, saying to retrain with emulator_settings.include_prediction_items: true.

docs.title: When CA refuses
docs.text:
An unvalidated emulator does not fail loudly; it returns plausible wrong numbers, and every downstream index, cost and posterior inherits the error with nothing to show for it. So CA refuses rather than proceeding quietly:

Situation What happens Worst held-out R² below min_r2 refused at setup, naming the observable and its R² A parameter outside the training box refused (or warns/clips, per out_of_bounds) Parameter bounds, observables, operations, protocol or the model file changed since training refused as stale — retrain A series or frequency data item refused: the emulator predicts scalars only sa_options.include_prediction_items on an emulator trained without include_prediction_items, or for other prediction items refused — retrain with emulator_settings.include_prediction_items: true reuse_samples: true with no previous emulator, or one saved without its samples refused, naming the directory it looked in — train once without the setting first reuse_samples: true after the bounds, obs_data, protocol or model changed refused as stale — retrain with reuse_samples: false autoemulate not installed refused, naming the install command

An emulator is an interpolant. Outside the box it was trained in it is an extrapolation with no error estimate at all, which is why out_of_bounds: error is the default.

docs.title: If saving fails: model_serialiser
docs.text:
Training pays for every simulation before it writes anything, so a model that cannot be pickled costs the whole run rather than just the save. Some fitted emulators hold an uninitialised C-extension descriptor that pickle cannot take apart, and the run ends with:

TypeError: cannot pickle '_abc._abc_data' object

emulator_settings.model_serialiser decides which container is used:

Value Behaviour auto (default) joblib, then cloudpickle, then dill, until one works — with a warning saying which joblib joblib only — fail rather than switch container cloudpickle cloudpickle only dill dill only

None of the three is a superset of the others, which is why auto falls back in order rather than simply preferring the most capable one. Measured against autoemulate 2.1.2:

an object pickle cannot name a torch-backed emulator joblib fails works cloudpickle works works dill works fails (a PyCapsule it recurses on)

So joblib stays first — it is what autoemulate itself writes and reads — and switching to dill outright would break the common case to fix the rare one.

Which container wrote a bundle is recorded in emulator_metadata.json as model_serialiser, so it reads back without the setting having to be repeated; a bundle written before the setting existed still loads, because all three are tried. Note that a bundle saved with a fallback needs that library present wherever it is loaded.

If a training run dies while saving, leave this at auto and make sure the fallbacks are installed (pip install "libcuflynx[emulation]" brings them), or name one outright.

docs.title: One failure no container can fix
docs.text:
PicklingError: Can't pickle sentinel: it's not the same object as typing_extensions.sentinel

This one is not about the container, and changing model_serialiser will not help — joblib, cloudpickle and dill all fail identically. A PEP 661 sentinel pickles by name: its __reduce__ returns a string, and pickle stores it as a global, checking on the way back in that the name still refers to the same object. typing_extensions 4.16.0 ships one where that check cannot pass:

_marker = sentinel("sentinel")     # named "sentinel", bound to _marker

typing_extensions.sentinel is the class, so the identity check fails for any object holding _marker. CA handles it by reducing sentinels to where they actually live rather than to what they call themselves, so nothing needs configuring — but if you meet this outside CA, the workaround is pip install "typing_extensions!=4.16.0" (4.15.0 is unaffected).

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
Over an emulator the only gradient source is finite differences on the emulator itself. The analytic arms (CasADi AD, Myokit CVODES FSA, AADC) all differentiate the real model, which is not the function an emulator run is evaluating — using one would mean the optimiser descends a different function than the cost it reports.

This costs 2M emulator evaluations per gradient, which is a matrix multiply apiece rather than 2M simulations, so gradient-based calibration (sp_minimize, multi_start_sp_minimize) and the Laplace identifiability analysis work normally. do_ad is turned off automatically, with a message, when use_emulator is set.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from libcuflynx.emulators.emulator_trainer import EmulatorTrainer
from libcuflynx.param_id.paramID import CVS0DParamID

inp["do_emulation"] = True
inp["emulator_settings"] = {"num_train_samples": 200, "models": "GaussianProcessRBF"}
bundle = EmulatorTrainer.init_from_dict(inp).train()
print(dict(zip(bundle.feature_labels, bundle.meta["feature_r2"])))

inp["use_emulator"] = True
pid = CVS0DParamID.init_from_dict(inp)   # calibrates against the emulator

EmulatorTrainer.init_from_dict always builds its engine with use_emulator forced off, so training runs the real solver even when the config asks for an emulator elsewhere.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The training targets are computed through the same code path as the cost (libcuflynx.param_id.fd_backend.observable_features), so the emulator approximates exactly what your calibration is fitting rather than a second implementation of it.
  • Parameters are mapped to the unit box and features are standardised before fitting. CA parameters routinely span a compliance near 1e-9 and a resistance near 1e8, and autoemulate works in float32; the transforms are stored in the bundle and inverted on prediction.
  • Modifier and grouped parameters are supported: the emulator is trained on θ — one value per params_for_id entry — not on the expanded per-parameter values.
  • params_to_change from your protocol are held at the values they had during training. Change the protocol and the emulator is refused as stale.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Python environment with libcuflynx installed (see Getting Started).
  • The example resource files in resources/.

A schematic view of this model is shown above with details of boundary conditions, parts' names, vein connection, and direction of blood flow through. The heart is modeled as a simple valve module in this example. According to this schematic, the vessel and parameters files are designed as shown in below figures.

In the module_array file, there are five columns: name, module_subtype, module_type, inp_instances, and out_instances

name is the user-chosen module's name, for example "heart" or "aortic_root".

module_subtype is the boundary condition type for circulatory system vessels. The BC of vessel modules should be one of the "vv", "vp", "pv", and "pp" types. The first letter defines input pressure (p) or flow (v) boundary condition, the second letter defines output pressure (p) or flow (v) boundary condition. For example the pulmonary vein (pvn) in the above example has a vp BC type, meaning it has input flow and output pressure boundary conditions.

Info

A vessel with "output flow" BC must be connected to a vessel with "input pressure" BC and vice versa. E.g. a "vp" can only have either a "vv" or "vp" vessel as ouputs. This is checked in the software, and will throw an error if there are incorrect BC connections.

The module_type and module_subtype must match a module with the same module_type and module_subtype in the modules config JSON files defined at [CA_dir]/src/libcuflynx/generators/resources/.

These files define the variables of each module and the connection ports that allow linking between modules; each module links to a CellML module. For more information, refer to Designing a model.

inp_instances and out_instances are the inputs and outputs of each module, respectively. Some modules have multiple inputs and outputs, like split_type vessels that split from one to two vessels.

Note

A module's inputs take its entrance ports of one port type in the order inp_instances lists them, and its outputs its exit ports in out_instances order. The heart module's vessel ports are, in order:

inp_instances:

  1. inferior vena cava
  2. superior vena cava
  3. pulmonary vein

out_instances:

  1. aorta
  2. pulmonary artery

This model has no inferior vena cava, so its heart lists a zero_flow instance first, which sets the first port's flow to zero. Nothing is added for the heart: every module it connects to is in the module array. A port left unconnected is a boundary condition, which needs a value in the parameters file.

Tip

Currently, the terminal vessels should only have a module_subtype starting with "pp".

Results:

In the below figure, three different variables are plotted versus time. The step size was adjusted to 0.01 seconds. These variables are the "Aortic_root flow rate", "pvn flow rate", and the "volume of the heart", respectively.

This is the model before doing model calibration. See section Parameter Identification for info on the parameter identification.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text: You should be able to generate and simulate the 3-compartment model and reproduce the example outputs.

docs.title: External Python Solvers
docs.text:
Circulatory Autogen can calibrate, sweep and emulate a model it did not generate and does not integrate. You write a Python class that owns its own time-stepping — a finite-element solver, a compiled library behind a ctypes wrapper, a hand-rolled scheme, anything — drop it in a file, and CA drives it through the same calibration, sensitivity-analysis and emulator pipelines it uses for CellML models.

This is model_type: external_python with solver: external.

Running alongside a generated model instead?

This page is for a model CA runs on its own, for calibration, sweeps and emulators. To run your model together with a generated C++ 0D model, exchanging values every step (a FEniCS tissue fed by 0D capillaries, say), see Coupling to External Models.

docs.title: Which backend do I want?
docs.text:
There is one way to bring your own Python, and this is it. The choice is only between letting CA build the model for you and writing it yourself:

You provide CA does the time-stepping Use when cellml CellML modules and a module array yes (Myokit / libOpenCOR CVODE) the model is a network of reusable CellML components python the same, emitted as Python yes (scipy.solve_ivp) you want CA's generated model in Python external_python a solver class with its own run() no — you do the model is code you already have, or an ODE you would rather write directly

The distinction that matters

CA hands over the record grid, asks for a run, and reads named traces back. Everything in between is yours. That is the shape a real solver needs — a PDE code has a mesh to build, forms to compile, an operator to assemble and a factorisation to reuse, and none of it survives being squeezed through a per-step RHS callback — and it costs an ODE almost nothing, because "integrate this" is one solve_ivp call inside your run().

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Put a class in a Python file and name it SIM_HELPER at module level. CA loads the file by path and instantiates the class once.

import numpy as np


class MyModel:
    # --- self-description (required) ---------------------------------------------
    parameters = {"heat/k": 0.05, "heat/u_D": 0.25}        # name -> default
    output_names = ["heat/T_p1", "heat/T_p2", "heat/T_p3"]

    # --- required methods --------------------------------------------------------
    def init_solver(self, config):
        """Called once. Do the expensive setup here: mesh, assembly, JIT."""

    def update_times(self, dt, start_time, sim_time, pre_time):
        """Set the record grid. Must be cheap — no re-assembly."""

    def set_param_vals(self, param_dict):
        """A subset of `parameters`. Must not require a re-init."""

    def run(self):
        """Solve the whole grid from the initial condition. Returns True/False."""

    def get_results(self):
        """{output_name: 1D np.ndarray}, on the grid, pre_time samples included."""

    # --- optional ----------------------------------------------------------------
    def get_init_param_vals(self, names): ...
    def reset(self): ...
    def extra_plots(self): ...      # -> list[matplotlib.figure.Figure]
    def close(self): ...


SIM_HELPER = MyModel

docs.title: parameters and output_names — literals, not expressions
docs.text:
Both are read by parsing the file, without importing it, so that a tool (or a machine with none of your solver's dependencies installed) can list a model's parameters and outputs. Keep them plain dict and list literals.

parameters = {"heat/k": 1.0}                    # ✅ readable without importing
parameters = {f"heat/{name}": 1.0 for ...}      # ❌ invisible to the parser
parameters = dict(DEFAULTS)                     # ❌ likewise

Names use CA's canonical component/variable form, so they line up with the targets of params_for_id.json and with the operands in obs_data.json without any translation.

docs.title: init_solver(config)
docs.text:
Called once, before anything else. This is where the cost goes: build the mesh, compile the forms, factorise what can be factorised, locate your probes.

config carries:

key meaning dt output sampling step sim_time logged simulation duration pre_time unlogged spin-up duration start_time time of the first sample solver_info the solver_info block from user_inputs.yaml

solver_info.get('user_config') is a free-form dict, untouched by CA, that carries whatever your solver needs — a mesh resolution, a tolerance, a path to a data file.

def init_solver(self, config):
    user_config = (config.get('solver_info') or {}).get('user_config') or {}
    nx = int(user_config.get('nx', 16))
    ...

docs.title: update_times(dt, start_time, sim_time, pre_time)
docs.text:
Sets the record grid, and nothing else. CA may call it many times over a run, so it must be cheap — no re-meshing, no re-assembly, no recompilation.

After it, run() must produce samples at start_time + i*dt for i in 0..N, where

N = int(pre_time/dt) + int(sim_time/dt)

Compute N with that exact arithmetic rather than with rounding or np.arange, so your length and CA's agree exactly instead of approximately.

Tip

If a quantity like dt appears inside a compiled expression (a UFL form, a generated kernel), store it as a mutable constant that the expression already references. Then update_times is one array write instead of a round trip through the compiler.

docs.title: set_param_vals(param_dict)
docs.text:
Receives a subset of parameters — whatever the calibration is currently varying — and must not require a re-init. A calibration calls this thousands of times on one instance; if each call had to rebuild the model, the run would be dominated by setup.

Reject unknown names loudly. A typo in params_for_id.json that is silently ignored produces a calibration that reports success and has fitted nothing.

docs.title: run()
docs.text:
Solves the whole grid from the initial condition, and is repeatable: two calls with the same parameters must give the same trace. This is the rule most often broken by accident — a solver that carries its final state into the next call makes sample 500's cost depend on sample 499's parameters, which shows up as a calibration that "almost works" and never converges.

Return True on success and False if the solve diverged or produced non-finite values. False is not an error: CA drops that sample and carries on, which is exactly what you want when an optimiser wanders into a corner of parameter space where your scheme is unstable.

docs.title: get_results()
docs.text: Returns {output_name: 1D np.ndarray} — one array per name in output_names, each of length N + 1, on the record grid. Include the pre_time samples; CA discards the leading int(pre_time/dt) of them itself.

docs.title: The optional four
docs.text:
• get_init_param_vals(names) — the defaults for the named parameters. CA falls back to the parameters dict when you do not implement it.
  • reset() — return to the initial state. Useful to call from your own run().
  • extra_plots() — a list of matplotlib.figure.Figure objects: fields, meshes, convergence histories, anything CA cannot know how to draw. CA collects them alongside its own plots, and the CUFLynx GUI surfaces them as extra tabs on the run. Build them with matplotlib.figure.Figure directly rather than pyplot — no global state, no backend to configure, safe on a headless node.
  • close() — release whatever needs releasing. Called when CA is done with the instance.

docs.title: user_inputs.yaml
docs.text:
file_prefix: my_model
model_type: external_python
solver: external

# Defaults to funcs_user/{file_prefix}_model.py, so this is only needed when the file
# lives elsewhere. Absolute, or relative to the yaml.
external_model_path: /path/to/my_model.py

pre_time: 0.0
sim_time: 2.0
dt: 0.02

# Anything under user_config reaches init_solver untouched, as
# config['solver_info']['user_config'].
solver_info:
  user_config:
    nx: 16
    tolerance: 1e-8

Everything else — params_for_id, obs_data.json, param_id_method, resources_dir — works exactly as it does for a CellML model. See Parameter Identification.

docs.title: Starting from other values: external_parameters_file
docs.text:
external_parameters_file names a parameters file, in the nested form of a model's <prefix>_parameters.json, whose values replace the class defaults:

# Absolute, or relative as external_model_path is
external_parameters_file: /path/to/heat1d_calibrated_parameters.json

{"schema_version": 1,
 "heat": {"k": {"value": 0.25, "units": "", "data_reference": "..."},
          "u_D": {"value": 0.1, "units": "", "data_reference": "..."}}}

The values are set on your class right after init_solver, and they are the defaults that a reset returns to. A name your class does not declare in parameters is refused. Calibration workflows use this file to run each step with its values, and write their result in this form.

docs.title: Calibration workflows
docs.text:
A calibration workflow can run an external model. Name it with {"external_model_path": ...}, relative to the workflow file, as the workflow's target and as the model of every step that runs one:

{"workflow_name": "heat1d",
 "target": {"external_model_path": "heat1d_model.py"},
 "settings": {"dt": 0.005, "param_id_method": "CMA-ES"},
 "steps": [
   {"id": "boundary", "kind": "set",
    "set": [{"parameter": "heat/u_D", "value": 0.1, "reason": "boundary temperature is measured"}]},
   {"id": "fit-k", "model": {"external_model_path": "heat1d_model.py"},
    "obs_data": "heat1d_obs_data.json", "params_for_id": "heat1d_k_params_for_id.json",
    "fixed_from": ["boundary"]}]}
  • The model is never generated. Each step runs your .py with its values in <step>/model/generated_models/<step>/<step>_parameters.json: your class defaults, with the values the step is given (fixed_from, result_from) over them. CA passes that file as the step's external_parameters_file.
  • The model is also the target. Every step that names a model names the same file. A module_map, submodule, module or select is refused.
