  • Parameters keep your names. In a params_for_id, a set step or a sweep, a parameter is component/variable, as your parameters declares it. A name your class does not declare is refused before anything runs.
  • model_type and solver are always external_python and external. solver_info's user_config still reaches init_solver.
  • Every step kind works: calibrations (with store_distribution and priors_from), sensitivity, reduction, emulation, identifiability, set and sweeps (also on_target).
  • --write-calibrated writes the merged values as <prefix>_calibrated_parameters.json beside the .py. The prefix is the file name without _model.py, so heat1d_model.py gives heat1d_calibrated_parameters.json. Run the model from it with external_parameters_file.
  • --pack copies the .py with every file beside it, since a model may read data there.

The shipped example funcs_user/example_model_external/heat1d_calibration_workflow.json:

  1. sets u_D by hand;
  2. fits k with u_D held, and samples k's posterior by MCMC;
  3. refines u_D, with k's posterior as its prior.
cuflynx-calibration-workflow funcs_user/example_model_external/heat1d_calibration_workflow.json \
    --output-dir heat1d_run --write-calibrated

It recovers k ≈ 0.25 and u_D ≈ 0.1 in under a minute. refine takes from fit-k, which takes from boundary, so its u_D and k replace theirs. tests/test_workflow_external_python.py runs every step kind on this model.

docs.title: The simple case first: an ODE with scipy
docs.text:
funcs_user/example_model_scipy/ is the smallest thing this contract can be. A damped oscillator x'' + c·x' + k·x = 0, integrated by scipy.integrate.solve_ivp inside the class's own run():

def run(self):
    solution = solve_ivp(self._rhs, (self.t_eval[0], self.t_eval[-1]),
                         y0=_INITIAL_STATE, t_eval=self.t_eval,
                         method=self.method, rtol=self.rtol, atol=self.atol)
    if not solution.success or not np.all(np.isfinite(solution.y)):
        return False
    self._solution = solution
    return True

That is the entire cost of owning the time loop for an ODE — the grid is built once in update_times, and get_results() slices the trajectory into {name: array}. Read this one first, and copy it.

funcs_user/example_model_external/ is the next step up: the same contract on a 1D heat equation with an explicit finite-difference scheme it wrote itself, NumPy only, no external dependencies.

docs.title: Walkthrough: a FEniCSx heat solver
docs.text:
funcs_user/heat_fenics/ is the real one — a FEniCSx (dolfinx) finite-element solver for

u_t = k Δu    on the unit square

u(x, 0) = 1                    a uniformly hot plate
u = u_D  on the left edge      calibratable
u = 0    on the other three    fixed

backward Euler in time, P1 Lagrange in space, and three point probes read out every step as heat/T_p1, heat/T_p2, heat/T_p3. Two parameters are exposed for calibration: the diffusivity heat/k and the driven-edge value heat/u_D.

Driving one edge and fixing the other three is what makes the three probes independent: p1 is nearest the driven edge and answers mostly to u_D, p3 is furthest and answers mostly to k. (u_D defaults to 0.25 rather than 0 for the same reason — at u_D = 0 every edge is identical and the structure disappears.)

It is small on purpose — a 16×16 mesh and 100 steps, milliseconds per run once the forms are compiled — because it is a teaching artefact, not a convergence study.

docs.title: 1. Install FEniCSx
docs.text:
dolfinx is a conda-forge package. It is not on PyPI, and it is not the legacy dolfin.

conda create -n fenicsx -c conda-forge fenics-dolfinx python=3.11
conda activate fenicsx

docs.title: 2. Install CA into the same environment
docs.text:
cd /path/to/circulatory_autogen
pip install -e ".[dev,emulation]"

[dev] brings pytest, [emulation] brings autoemulate — needed only if you want to train a surrogate of the model (see Emulators). Drop it otherwise.

docs.title: 3. Check it runs
docs.text:
python funcs_user/heat_fenics/heat_fenics_model.py

The example has a __main__ block that drives the class directly, with no CA involved, and prints the sample count and the two observable values. A few seconds, including the one-off form compilation.

Tested against dolfinx 0.8.x and 0.9.x

The calls most prone to move between dolfinx releases — the function-space constructor, the bounding-box tree, the PETSc assembly helpers — are looked up through a small _resolve helper in the example, which raises a message naming the tested versions instead of an AttributeError from three frames down. If you are on a newer dolfinx and something raises, that message tells you which call moved.

docs.title: 4. Point user_inputs.yaml at it
docs.text:
file_prefix: heat_fenics
model_type: external_python
solver: external
external_model_path: <CA_dir>/funcs_user/heat_fenics/heat_fenics_model.py
resources_dir: <CA_dir>/funcs_user/heat_fenics
param_id_obs_path: <CA_dir>/funcs_user/heat_fenics/heat_fenics_obs_data.json

# No pre_time/sim_time: the run window comes from the obs_data's protocol_info
# (pre_times: [0.0], sim_times: [[2.0]]). dt is still a yaml setting.
dt: 0.02

param_id_method: genetic_algorithm

solver_info:
  user_config:
    nx: 16

resources_dir is where CA looks for heat_fenics_params_for_id.json, which defines the calibration box:

{
 "version": 1,
 "params": [
  {"targets": ["heat/k"], "min": 0.001, "max": 0.2, "param_type": "const", "name_for_plotting": "k"},
  {"targets": ["heat/u_D"], "min": -0.5, "max": 0.5, "param_type": "const", "name_for_plotting": "u_{D}"}
 ]
}

and heat_fenics_obs_data.json holds the run window and six scalar targets — the mean and the min of each of the three probes, so every probe is scored rather than just the centre one. The window is its protocol_info (pre_times: [0.0], sim_times: [[2.0]]), which is where it belongs: the six values are what that window produces, so the two cannot drift apart, and the CUFLynx GUI reads the window from there rather than from the yaml.

docs.title: 5. Calibrate and sweep it
docs.text:
Nothing about the entry points is special-cased for an external model:

./run_param_id.sh 4               # calibration on 4 MPI ranks
./run_sensitivity_analysis.sh 4   # Sobol indices for k and u_D

And a surrogate, if you are heading for MCMC or a large Sobol design:

do_emulation: true
emulator_settings:
  num_train_samples: 64
  sample_type: sobol
  models: RadialBasisFunctions

docs.title: Gotchas worth knowing before you write yours
docs.text:
Build your mesh on MPI.COMM_SELF, not COMM_WORLD

CA parallelises over independent simulations — each MPI rank runs its own parameter sample. A solver that builds a distributed mesh on COMM_WORLD is instead splitting one problem across the ranks, and it will deadlock the moment two ranks ask for different parameters. Each rank must own a complete serial problem.

run() must restart from the initial condition

See above. Test it: run at parameters A, run at B, run at A again, and assert the first and third traces are identical. tests/test_heat_fenics_example.py does exactly that.

Pick observables that actually vary

The heat example deliberately does not use max(heat/T_p2): the centre probe's maximum is its initial value, which is 1 for every parameter set. A constant feature contributes nothing to the cost and scores NaN R² as an emulator target. min (the relaxed final value) and mean both move with the parameters, so that pair is well conditioned.

Give yourself a free correctness check

In the heat example, p1 sits nearer the driven left edge than p3, so with u_D above the fixed edge temperature p1 must run warmer — on any mesh, at any step size. One assertion covers the probe locating, the assembly and the boundary split at once. Look for an inequality your physics guarantees rather than a value your discretisation happens to produce.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• funcs_user/example_model_scipy/README.md — the ODE example in detail.
  • funcs_user/heat_fenics/README.md — the FEniCSx example in detail, including how to regenerate its obs_data.json values for your own build.
  • funcs_user/example_model_external/ — the dependency-free NumPy version of the same contract.
  • tests/test_scipy_ode_example.py and tests/test_heat_fenics_example.py — smoke, physics-sanity, plotting and emulator round-trip tests you can copy for your own model.
  • Parameter Identification and Sensitivity Analysis — the pipelines this backend plugs into.
  • Emulators — when a surrogate of your solver is worth training.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer (pyproject.toml declares requires-python = ">=3.10"). Use the same interpreter for the whole project.
  • Git, to clone the repository.
  • pip (usually bundled with Python).
  • MPI (optional): needed only if you run parameter identification or sensitivity analysis with multiple processes. See MPI and system libraries below.
  • Compiler / SUNDIALS (optional on Linux): the default solver, Myokit’s CVODE, compiles each model when it is first run, so it needs a C compiler, the Python development headers and SUNDIALS: build-essential, python3-dev (or pythonX.Y-dev for the Python you use) and libsundials-dev, or your OS equivalent.

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text:
The repository is called circulatory_autogen; the package it installs is called libcuflynx. Both names refer to the same project — papers and the repository use the first, PyPI and every import uses the second.

pip install libcuflynx

That is all that is needed to import the library, run the console commands (cuflynx-generate, cuflynx-param-id, …) and work from any directory — no checkout, and no import path to set up. Optional capabilities are extras, because they are large; see the size table in the README:

pip install "libcuflynx[mpi]"        # multi-rank runs under mpiexec (needs a system MPI)
pip install "libcuflynx[casadi]"     # model_type: casadi_python, symbolic AD gradients
pip install "libcuflynx[uq]"         # the pyMC sampler
pip install "libcuflynx[emulation]"  # surrogate models (pulls in torch; big)

Import from the libcuflynx namespace

The flat imports (from param_id.paramID import CVS0DParamID) were removed in 0.6.0 and raise ModuleNotFoundError. Use from libcuflynx.param_id.paramID import CVS0DParamID.

docs.title: Where an installed libcuflynx reads and writes: CUFLYNX_USER_DIR
docs.text:
Every stage needs a user directory — the one holding user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml and, unless the config overrides them, resources/, module_config_user/, funcs_user/, generated_models/ and param_id_output/. It is chosen in this order:

  1. $CUFLYNX_USER_DIR, if set — an absolute path (~ is expanded).
  2. the circulatory_autogen checkout this libcuflynx is being run from, if it is one (including pip install -e .), so the developer workflow needs no configuration;
  3. otherwise the current working directory.

After a plain pip install libcuflynx there is no checkout, so rule 2 never fires: either run from your working directory, or point the variable at it, which is the only way to run from anywhere else without editing a config.

export CUFLYNX_USER_DIR=/path/to/my_study     # holds user_run_files/, resources/, …
cuflynx-generate False

The package ships no user_inputs.yaml of its own. cuflynx-init writes a starter study to begin from: user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml and the 3compartment model's resources (module array, parameters, params_for_id and obs_data), then prints what to run next. It never overwrites a file unless given --force.

mkdir my_study && cd my_study
cuflynx-init                    # or: cuflynx-init /path/to/my_study
cuflynx-generate
mpiexec -n 2 cuflynx-param-id

Nothing is ever written inside the installed package — that was issue #431. Individual directories can still be overridden per-run with resources_dir, generated_models_dir, param_id_output_dir and external_modules_dir in user_inputs.yaml; CUFLYNX_USER_DIR is what the defaults hang off when the config names none.

The rest of this page sets up a checkout, which is what the tutorial's shell-script workflow (user_run_files/*.sh, resources/, module_config_user/) and any development work need. If you only want to drive the library from Python, the pip install above is enough — skip to Model Generation and Simulation.

docs.title: Clone the repository
docs.text:
Clone the Circulatory Autogen project from the GitHub repository.

Note

If you have not used Git before: install Git, open a terminal, go to the folder where you want the code, then run:

  • git clone https://github.com/physiomelinks/circulatory_autogen

To contribute via a fork:

  • git clone https://github.com/<YourUsername>/circulatory_autogen

  • git remote add upstream https://github.com/physiomelinks/circulatory_autogen

docs.title: Directory layout
docs.text:
[project_dir] is the folder where the repository was cloned, for example:

[project_dir]: ~/Documents/git_projects/circulatory_autogen

The rest of this page assumes commands are run from a terminal and that [project_dir] is your current directory when installing.

docs.title: Install Python libraries from pyproject.toml
docs.text:
Use the same Python you will use to run scripts and tests (check with python --version or python3 --version).

1. Create a virtual environment (recommended)

Linux / macOSWindows (cmd)Windows (PowerShell) 
cd [project_dir]
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

cd [project_dir]
py -3 -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate.bat

cd [project_dir]
py -3 -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

If you prefer not to use a venv, skip the steps above and use python -m pip / python3 -m pip for the installs below.

2. Upgrade pip (recommended)

python -m pip install --upgrade pip

3. Install the project and dependencies

Dependencies are listed in pyproject.toml. Installing the package in editable mode pulls them in automatically.

  • Runtime only (autogeneration, parameter ID, solvers such as Myokit, etc.):

    cd [project_dir]
python -m pip install -e .

    When you choose solver: CVODE for CellML models, the project defaults that to the CVODE_myokit backend. To run CellML models with libOpenCOR instead, see Optional: the libOpenCOR solver.

  • With development tools (pytest, formatters, linters):

    cd [project_dir]
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"

The authoritative lists are [project.dependencies] and [project.optional-dependencies] in pyproject.toml. Highlights:

  • Autogeneration: pandas, pyyaml, rdflib, libcellml, pint, etc.

    libCellML 0.7.2 or later

    The requirement is libcellml>=0.7.2, installed from PyPI. 0.7.1 drops an imported unit's exponent, so models such as SN_simple fail with a units mismatch under it. If libCellML came from conda or a system package rather than pip, an older version there can make the resolver fail with a version conflict; installing into a fresh virtual environment avoids that.

    • Parameter identification: mpi4py, nevergrad (CMA-ES), emcee, numdifftools, and related scientific stack.
    • Sensitivity analysis: SALib, seaborn.
    • Development: the dev extra (e.g. pytest, pytest-mpi).

4. Activate the venv before using the shell helpers

The shell scripts under user_run_files/ (run_param_id.sh, run_autogeneration.sh, …) run the console commands (cuflynx-param-id, cuflynx-generate, …) found on your PATH, so activate the venv in the shell you run them from (source venv/bin/activate). To use an interpreter without activating its environment, set CUFLYNX_PYTHON:

CUFLYNX_PYTHON=[project_dir]/venv/bin/python ./run_param_id.sh 4

Note

user_run_files/python_path.sh only names the interpreter run_pytest.sh runs the tests with. Its default is venv/bin/python, relative to the repository root, so a venv named venv needs no edit.

5. Run scripts

With the project installed, the console commands are on your PATH and can be run from any directory: cuflynx-generate, cuflynx-param-id, cuflynx-sensitivity, cuflynx-identifiability, cuflynx-train-emulator and cuflynx-plot. Every one of them reads user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml and takes --help. cuflynx-calibration-workflow instead takes a calibration_workflow.json (see Calibration workflows).

The other scripts that ship in the package are run as modules, for example:

python -m libcuflynx.scripts.<script_name>

or use the shell helper for the same stage, e.g. cd user_run_files && ./run_autogeneration.sh (each helper invokes the matching console command, so the editable install above is a prerequisite for them).

For a notebook-oriented walkthrough, see tutorial/interactive/generation_and_calibration.ipynb (generation, simulation, and calibration as a workflow) or, for the calibration workflow alone in a few minutes, tutorial/interactive/workflow_quickstart.ipynb.

6. Run the tests (optional, but do this after any change)

cd [project_dir]
./run_pytest.sh

run_pytest.sh runs pytest under mpiexec using the python_path named in user_run_files/python_path.sh.

  • ./run_pytest.sh -n 4 — -n N is the MPI rank count, not pytest-xdist (xdist is force-disabled, because its workers conflict with MPI ranks).
  • ./run_pytest.sh -m "not slow" — skip the expensive tests. -k <expr> and any other arguments pass straight through to pytest.
  • The CVODE_libopencor tests are marked need_libopencor and skip unless libOpenCOR is installed (see below).

  • Equivalent without the script (handy if python_path.sh is set for someone else’s machine):

    mpiexec -n 1 venv/bin/python -m pytest -p no:xdist

docs.title: Optional third-party backends (not part of Circulatory Autogen)
docs.text:
Circulatory Autogen itself is fully open source (Apache License 2.0) and everything described in this documentation works without installing anything below.

This section describes optional, third-party software that is not part of Circulatory Autogen. It is not bundled with it, not installed by pip install -e ., not required by any feature, and not distributed under Circulatory Autogen's license. It is developed and licensed by other parties, on their terms. Circulatory Autogen merely provides an optional adapter so that users who already have a licence for such a product can plug it in. If you install one, you are entering a licensing relationship with that third party, not with this project.

docs.title: AADC (Matlogica) — proprietary, optional, not included
docs.text:
AADC is third-party proprietary software and is NOT part of Circulatory Autogen

  • Not included, not required. AADC is not shipped with Circulatory Autogen and no feature of Circulatory Autogen depends on it. The project is fully functional, and fully open source, without it. Nothing installs it unless you ask for the [aadc] extra below, which is in neither [all] nor [dev].
  • Not open source. AADC is a commercial product of Matlogica, distributed under Matlogica's own proprietary licence — not under Circulatory Autogen's Apache-2.0 licence, and not under any open-source licence. Its terms restrict it to academic / non-commercial use.
  • You must obtain your own licence. The Circulatory Autogen maintainers do not supply, sublicense, or broker AADC licences, and cannot support licensing issues. Read and accept Matlogica's licence terms yourself, directly with Matlogica, before installing or using it.
  • Its gradients are licence-gated at runtime. Forward simulation may run with a bare pip install aadc, but anything that records a tape — the automatic-differentiation gradients, and the on-tape damping in semi_implicit — raises RuntimeError: AADC License check failed without a valid licence.
  • Use CasADi if you want a fully open-source pipeline. CasADi (LGPL) is the default and supported AD backend and requires no proprietary licence — see model_type: casadi_python in Parameter Identification. AADC is only an optional alternative for licensed academic users; you never need it.

If, and only if, you hold a Matlogica licence and accept their terms, the optional adapter is enabled by installing the aadc extra:

python -m pip install "libcuflynx[aadc]"

(Into the same venv you installed the project into. From a checkout, python -m pip install -e ".[aadc]".)

The extra installs two packages from PyPI:

  • aadc>=2.12,<3 — Matlogica's AADC, under the Matlogica EULA: non-commercial / academic use only, published as binary wheels only (no source), for Python >= 3.10.
  • aadc-ode — ODE integration on top of AADC. The gradient_strategy: kernel gradient of method: semi_implicit_signed replays its recorded kernel through it. Without it that strategy warns and falls back to gradient_strategy: tape, which integrates the same scheme with a slower gradient.

and then selecting it in your user_inputs.yaml:

model_type: aadc_python
solver: aadc_semi_implicit
solver_info:
  method: adaptive_rk45   # non-stiff forward solve; see the gradient caveat below

Available solver_info.method values for the AADC adapter are adaptive_rk45 (adaptive, so accurate for a forward solve but untapeable — its step sequence depends on the parameters, so it cannot produce an AD gradient), and the fixed-step implicit_euler_ift, semi_implicit, and rk4 (the only methods that can be recorded on a tape for an AD gradient).

method: bdf was removed from the AADC adapter

AADC previously offered a bdf method. It ran the solve inside scipy.solve_ivp with AADC supplying only the RHS and its Jacobian, so the trajectory never reached the tape — and the AD tape had no bdf branch, so do_ad: true silently recorded rk4 instead, making the cost and the gradient different functions. Its RHS kernel was also taped once at t=0 with the integrator discarding t, so a time-dependent model would have been integrated with its t=0 right-hand side throughout. Setting method: bdf on an aadc_python model now raises. Use semi_implicit for stiff models — subject to the accuracy warning below — or model_type: casadi_python with method: bdf for a differentiable symbolic BDF.

AADC gradients do not work on stiff models

Only the fixed-step methods can be taped, and fixed-step schemes are inaccurate or unstable on stiff models: on the 3compartment cardiovascular model semi_implicit deviates from the CVODE reference by ~35% and implicit_euler_ift by orders of magnitude. Reducing dt does not help — semi_implicit diverges under step refinement (~35% at dt=1e-3 rising to ~280% at dt=1e-4), because its damping factor 1/(1+dt*lam) tends to 1 as dt shrinks and the scheme degenerates into explicit forward Euler on a very stiff system. The AADC backend probes the first second of dynamics and warns loudly when it detects a stiff model. For gradient-based calibration of a stiff model, use CasADi cvodes (CasADi AD by CVODES forward sensitivities), CasADi bdf, or Myokit CVODES forward sensitivity instead — see Parameter Identification. AADC's tape gradient is appropriate only for non-stiff, state-observable, single-experiment problems.

docs.title: MPI and system libraries
docs.text:
Warning

mpi4py needs an MPI implementation on the machine. On Linux you may need:

sudo apt install libopenmpi-dev openmpi-bin

On macOS, for example: brew install openmpi. On Windows, install MS MPI and the SDK, and ensure the MPI bin paths are on your PATH (see Microsoft’s documentation).

Myokit (CVODE) on Linux needs a compiler, the Python development headers (Python.h; pythonX.Y-dev for a Python other than the system one) and SUNDIALS headers, for example:

sudo apt install build-essential python3-dev libsundials-dev

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
You should now have:

  • A clone of the repository at [project_dir].
  • A Python environment (venv or global) with dependencies installed from pyproject.toml via pip install -e . or pip install -e ".[dev]".
  • The ability to run python and import the project after cd [project_dir] with your chosen interpreter.

docs.title: Optional: the libOpenCOR solver
docs.text:
libOpenCOR is OpenCOR's simulation engine as a Python library. It runs CellML models as the CVODE_libopencor solver, an alternative to the default CVODE_myokit:

python -m pip install -e ".[libopencor]"

solver: CVODE_libopencor
solver_info:
  MaximumStep: 0.001
  MaximumNumberOfSteps: 5000
  rtol: 1.0e-8
  atol: 1.0e-8
  • libOpenCOR's wheels need Python 3.12 or later (Linux, macOS, Windows). On older Pythons the extra installs nothing and the solver says how to get it.
  • It compiles the model once and is several times faster per run than CVODE_myokit on the models in benchmarks/solver_comparison.py; calibrations use finite-difference gradients with it.
  • It has no time-varying inputs (protocol_traces / protocol_shapes) and no forward sensitivities (FSA): use CVODE_myokit for those.
  • The OpenCOR desktop application is still a good way to open and run a generated model by hand (see Model generation and simulation). CA does not run inside OpenCOR's bundled Python: the solver name CVODE_opencor is an alias for CVODE_libopencor.

docs.title: Identifiability Analysis
docs.text: Identifiability Analysis (IA) ensures that identified parameters can be trusted, i.e. have a small uncertainty.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A completed parameter identification run (best-fit parameters computed).
  • param_id_output directory available for the model and dataset.

docs.title: The Laplace Approximation
docs.text: The Laplace approximation makes an approximation of your parameter posterior distribution, assuming it is gaussian. This uses the Hessian of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameters.

docs.title: Profile Likelihood Analysis
docs.text:
Profile likelihood analysis assesses parameter identifiability by holding each parameter at a sweep of values around its best fit and re-calibrating all the other parameters at each one. For each parameter it:

  1. holds the parameter at num_points values, within range_factor of its [min, max] range either side of the best fit (clipped to [min, max]);
  2. re-calibrates the other parameters at each held value with your param_id_method, starting from the optimum at the neighbouring held value (the sweep runs outwards from the best fit; the genetic algorithm and bayesian methods draw their own starting points instead);
  3. records the cost at each re-calibrated optimum, and plots cost against the held value.

A grouped params_for_id entry (several targets sharing one value) is held as a whole, and a modifier entry is held at its theta and applied through its modifier function, as in calibration.

The resulting profiles reveal:

  • Identifiable parameters: clear minima with steep cost increases.
  • Non-identifiable parameters: flat profiles, where other parameter combinations compensate.

The 95% interval. Profile likelihood runs on @is_MLE costs (such as gaussian_MLE), so the cost is a scaled negative log-likelihood: -ln L = cost * N, where N is the number of weighted observable values (the same relation MCMC uses). The 95% profile-likelihood interval for one parameter is where -ln L stays within chi2(0.95, 1 dof) / 2 = 1.92 of its minimum, so in cost units the threshold is min cost + 1.92 / N. It is drawn on the plots and written to each parameter's JSON as ci_95 (lower/upper are null where the sweep never rises above the threshold, i.e. the interval is open on that side within the sweep).

Costs. As for Laplace, an observable whose cost is not @is_MLE but has an MLE form is switched to that form for the profile (the best fit it is measured from and every re-fit), with a warning naming the observable: MSE becomes gaussian_MLE, which has the same minimum. Your calibration's own costs are put back when the profile finishes. A cost with no MLE form (such as AE, or a custom cost without @is_MLE) is an error naming the observable.

Each profile point is a full calibration, so the run costs about num_points x num_parameters calibrations; use optimiser_options to give the profile points a smaller budget. With use_emulator the re-fits run on the emulator.

docs.title: IA in Circulatory_Autogen
docs.text: IA is run following a parameter identification run.

docs.title: Configuration for user_inputs.yaml
docs.text:
To run IA, you need to set 

do_ia: True

and add a specific ia_options block to your user_inputs.yaml configuration file:

docs.title: For the Laplace approximation
docs.text:
ia_options:
    method: 'Laplace'

docs.title: For profile likelihood
docs.text:
ia_options:
  method: 'profile_likelihood'
  num_points: 50              # held values per parameter (>= 2)
  range_factor: 0.2           # sweep half-width, as a fraction of the parameter's [min, max] range
  optimiser_options:          # optional: merged over optimiser_options for each re-calibration
    num_calls_to_function: 200

Results go to <param_id_output_dir>/profile_likelihood/: one JSON and one PDF per parameter, profile_likelihood_plots.pdf with every profile, and summary.json. The re-fits' optimisers write no files of their own (no best_cost.npy or history CSVs), so the calibration's best_param_vals.npy and other outputs are left as they were.

Each parameter's JSON holds:

  • param_name, best_val, best_cost: the profiled entry and the best fit;
  • param_values, costs: the held values and the cost at each re-calibrated optimum;
  • other_param_names and optima: the re-calibrated entries, in order, and one row per held value with their values at that point's optimum (null where the point's cost is not finite), in the same name form as param_name;
  • nll_per_cost and ci_95: the cost-to--ln L factor and the 95% interval.
{
  "param_values": [0.6, 0.8, 1.0],
  "costs": [3.1, 2.9, 3.4],
  "param_name": ["oscillator/c"],
  "best_val": 0.8,
  "other_param_names": [["oscillator/k"]],
  "optima": [[5.1], [5.4], [5.7]],
  ...
}

docs.title: Running identifiability analysis
docs.text:
You can run IA as part of parameter identification by setting do_ia: True and running:

./run_param_id.sh <NUM_CORES>

Or run it separately after parameter identification completes:

./run_identifiability_analysis.sh

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text: Laplace approximation results are saved in your param_id_output directory alongside parameter identification outputs; profile likelihood results in its profile_likelihood/ subdirectory.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: • If IA fails with missing files, confirm that parameter identification finished successfully and produced best_param_vals.npy and related outputs.

docs.title: Writing up a model and its calibration
docs.text:
Two commands turn a model and its calibration into the methods section of a paper:

  1. cuflynx-variable-mapping lists every variable and parameter of the model with the LaTeX symbol it is written as;
  2. cuflynx-methods-latex writes a methods section in LaTeX. It has four parts:
    • the model's equations, one subsection per module;
    • a table of every parameter with its value and source, citing your references;
    • a flow chart of the calibration;
    • what was done in each step of the flow chart.

To see one without setting anything up, run the workflow example in Calibration workflows → Try it.

docs.title: The variable mapping
docs.text:
cuflynx-variable-mapping generated_models/<prefix>/<prefix>_flat.cellml
cuflynx-variable-mapping --workflow workflow.json

Each command writes <prefix>_variable_mapping.csv beside the model. For a calibration workflow, the file goes beside the target's parameters file instead, as <name>_variable_mapping.csv (<name> is the target module array's prefix, or its parameterisation).

Column What it holds variable_name component/variable, with _module dropped from the component (mod_C/z, parameters/p_mod_A). These are the names obs_data operands and CUFLynx use. latex The symbol, without $. Edit these. kind state, parameter, constant, algebraic or time. component, units Where the variable is defined, and its units. any other Kept as it is. A CellDL editor or bgtool --variable-mapping adds bondgraph, each variable's bond graph name.

The file's structure is defined by src/libcuflynx/schemas/variable_mapping.schema.json, the JSON form a CSV is converted to when it is read (variable_mapping_document). Only variable_name and latex are required. An empty kind or units is filled in from the model when the file is refreshed. Reading or writing a file the schema refuses raises an error that gives each problem and where it is: the row's index among the non-blank rows, counting from 0, and the column (variables[1].kind).

The default symbols follow a simple rule, meant to be edited:

  • Subscripts: a name is split on _. The first part is the symbol and the rest are its subscripts: g_leak_Na → $g_{\mathrm{leak},\mathrm{Na}}$.
  • Greek letters: the name of a Greek letter becomes that letter: rho_M → $\rho_{M}$, Delta_C → $\Delta_{C}$.
  • Upright text: one-character parts stay italic, and longer ones are set upright: Nai → $\mathrm{Nai}$.
  • Module subscript: the module a variable belongs to is added as a last subscript. A generated parameter <var>_<vessel> is split into its variable and its vessel. In a model generated alone (vessel mod), the mod_ prefix is dropped: p_mod_A → $p_{A}$.

Running the command again keeps every symbol already in the file, and every column beyond these. It adds new variables with the default rule and drops variables the model no longer has. The command also warns when two variables share a symbol, because they could not be told apart in the equations. CUFLynx edits the same file from its Variables panel.

docs.title: The methods section
docs.text:
# a calibration workflow (see Parameter Identification -> Calibration workflows)
cuflynx-methods-latex --workflow workflow.json --run-dir workflow_output/<name> -o methods.tex --pdf

# one calibration
cuflynx-methods-latex --model <prefix>_flat.cellml --obs-data <obs>.json \
    --params-for-id <params>.json --settings user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml \
    --run-dir param_id_output/<method>_<prefix>_<obs> -o methods.tex

The document has four parts.

  1. Model. Each module gets a subsection with:

    • its ODEs and algebraic equations, as written by Myokit's LaTeX writer in the mapping's symbols, with conditionals set as cases;
    • its initial values;
    • a table of the parameters it uses (symbol, value, units, name in the model).

    For a workflow, the model is the target, and each module is labelled with its module type, version and parameterisation, from the target's module array or supermodule config. 2. Parameters and sources. One table of every parameter of the model: symbol, value, units and source (see Citations). A parameter that was calibrated names the step that calibrated it, with a link to that step's subsection. 3. Flow chart. This is a TikZ figure. - For a workflow: one box per step (its model, how many parameters and observables, the method). Arrows run from each step to the steps after it: solid for values passed on as fixed values, dashed for priors. A last box shows the merge into the target. - For one calibration: the model, observables and parameters feed the optimisation, followed by MCMC and identifiability when they were run. 4. One subsection per step. Each covers: - which model the step calibrates and against which observations; - the values it was given by earlier steps, and the priors it was given; - the protocol (experiments, pre-times, segment durations, inputs set per segment); - the observables (feature, observed value ± standard deviation, weight, experiment and segment); - the calibrated parameters with their ranges and priors; - the method, from CA's own description of it, with its settings, the solver, and the cost function as a formula; - MCMC settings when the step stored its posterior; - with --run-dir, the calibrated values and the best cost. A step that used priors reports its posterior medians.

docs.title: Citations
docs.text:
A parameter's source is its data_reference in the generated model's parameters file, the <prefix>_parameters.json beside it (the workflow's target, or the calibrated model). By convention it starts with the BibTeX key of the source, followed by a note: martin2023modelling; Methods (p. 16): w_inf k = 10 mV. Every word in it that is a key of the bibliography becomes \cite{key}; other words, such as definitional or user_defined, stay as text. An obs_data item's data_reference is cited the same way in the step's Sources line.

  • For a workflow, the bibliography is the *_references.bib (and *_references_proposed.bib) of every module version in the target, as the module library keeps them. Pass --bib to use other files instead.
  • For one calibration, pass the .bib files with --bib (repeatable). The parameters are the <prefix>_parameters.json that generation writes beside the generated model, or --parameters; when that file does not exist the command stops with an error naming it.

The command writes the cited entries to a .bib beside the .tex (methods.bib for -o methods.tex), and the document ends with \bibliography{methods}. --pdf compiles it with latexmk, which runs BibTeX.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Meaning --workflow a calibration_workflow.json; with --module-library-dir for libraries the file does not list --model, --obs-data, --params-for-id one calibration instead of a workflow --settings the user_inputs.yaml of that calibration (method, optimiser options, solver, UQ) --run-dir a workflow's output directory, or a param_id run directory: adds the results --mapping the variable mapping CSV (default: the one cuflynx-variable-mapping writes) --parameters the generated model's parameters file, <prefix>_parameters.json (one calibration) --bib a .bib file the sources cite (repeatable) -o the .tex to write --title the document title --body-only the sections without a preamble, to \input into a paper; the packages it needs are listed in its first line --flowchart-only just the figure --pdf also compile it with latexmk

cuflynx-variable-mapping writes beside the model by default, or where -o says.

The full document needs amsmath, amssymb, booktabs, longtable, graphicx and tikz. Compile it with latexmk (--pdf does this), or run pdflatex, BibTeX and pdflatex twice, so the references and the figure resolve.

From Python:

from libcuflynx.reporting import workflow_methods_latex, calibration_methods_latex, update_variable_mapping_file
update_variable_mapping_file(model_path, mapping_path)
text = workflow_methods_latex(workflow_path, run_dir=run_dir, mapping=mapping_path)

Note

The output is a starting point for the paper's methods, not the paper. Check the symbols, and reword the text to suit. A very long single equation can run past the margin: LaTeX cannot break an align line by itself.

docs.title: Importing other model formats
docs.text:
A study's model is CellML. Two other formats are read into CellML on the way in, so everything downstream -- the generators, the solvers, params_for_id's component/variable naming, the calibration and sensitivity pipelines -- keeps seeing the CellML it already expects, and no solver or model_type has to know these formats exist.

Format Extension Reader Myokit .mmt libcuflynx.parsers.MyokitParsers EasyML (openCARP) .model libcuflynx.parsers.EasyMLParsers

docs.title: Myokit (.mmt)
docs.text:
from libcuflynx.parsers.MyokitParsers import cellml_from_myokit, protocol_info_from_mmt
from libcuflynx.utilities.obs_data_helpers import fill_protocol_info

cellml, saved = cellml_from_myokit(data, filename="lr-1991.mmt", out_dir=outputs)
info, notes = protocol_info_from_mmt(data, filename="lr-1991.mmt")
obs_data = fill_protocol_info(obs_data, info)   # obs_data's own vocabulary

The two halves of a .mmt are read separately and deliberately. The [[model]] section becomes CellML without its protocol: baking Myokit's stimulus into the exported model would give it two sources of pacing that disagree, since the protocol belongs in obs_data. The [[protocol]] section becomes a one-experiment protocol_info whose events are Myokit's own five fields -- level, start, length, period, multiplier -- which are the same five protocol_shapes uses, so they copy across unchanged.

A periodic Myokit protocol usually runs forever (multiplier = 0) while an experiment here has a finite length, so an indefinite protocol is cut to beats (default 2) and the cut is reported in notes.

docs.title: EasyML (.model)
docs.text:
from libcuflynx.parsers.EasyMLParsers import import_easyml

read = import_easyml(data, filename="Courtemanche.model", out_dir=outputs)
read["cellml"]           # bytes
read["warnings"]         # what the reader had to decide -- show these
read["parameters"]       # the .param() group
read["protocol_info"]    # a default stimulus, offered not applied

EasyML is the language openCARP's published ionic models are written in. This is an independent reader of the file format: no openCARP code is used or vendored, because openCARP is distributed under the openCARP Academic Public License, which is neither OSI-approved nor compatible with this package's Apache-2.0 licence.

Three things are implicit in EasyML, supplied by openCARP's own translator and so supplied here too:

Gating variables have no equation. A Hodgkin-Huxley gate is written by giving either alpha_X/beta_X (or the short a_X/b_X) or tau_X/X_inf; writing diff_X as well is an error in EasyML. The state equation is reconstructed from whichever pair is present.

X_init is generated when absent, at the steady state the pair implies. A gate started at zero instead is a different simulation for the first few beats.

There is no membrane equation. A published model declares V; .nodal(); .external(Vm); and Iion; .nodal(); .external(); -- in openCARP the tissue solver owns V. Read as written, such a model has no dV/dt at all, so one is synthesised:

dot(V) = -(Iion + i_stim)

with no capacitance term, because EasyML's currents are in A/F, V is in mV and time is in ms, and A/F is mV/ms. The sign is openCARP's: an inward (negative) current depolarises, so a depolarising i_stim is negative. i_stim is an ordinary variable, not a state, so a protocol_info can drive it.

docs.title: .method() groups are read, not executed
docs.text:
An EasyML file says how openCARP would step each state -- rush_larsen for gates, markov_be for Markov chains, cvode for the rest. Those are discretisation choices for a fixed-step tissue solver, where per-cell CVODE is unaffordable across millions of cells and forward Euler is unstable for fast gates. The ODE system is the same either way, and here it is integrated as one system, which for single-cell work is at least as accurate -- it is the reference the Rush-Larsen scheme approximates.

Dropping that silently would be the wrong kind of quiet, so every non-CVODE group comes back in warnings, naming the states it covered.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: EasyML records none. Its conventions are V in mV, time in ms, currents in A/F and concentrations in mM. Variables are left dimensionless rather than annotated from a guess: a partial annotation makes every equation mixing an annotated and an unannotated term inconsistent, and libCellML reports those. The convention is recorded in the model's metadata instead.

docs.title: Names
docs.text: EasyML is flat. The reader puts everything in one component named after the model (from the file's name: header, else its filename), so a variable addresses as Decker2009/GNa -- the component/variable form params_for_id and obs operands require.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Python environment with libcuflynx installed (see Getting Started); OpenCOR, to open the generated model by hand.
  • A user_inputs.yaml file configured with file_prefix, resources_dir, and generated_models_dir.
  • *_module_array.json (or .csv) and *_parameters.json files in your resources directory.

docs.title: Software Outline
docs.text:
The Circulatory_Autogen project ([project_dir]) contains five folders as presented below:

  • resources: Contains example files that define models ([file_prefix]_module_array.csv), parameter values ([file_prefix]_parameters.json), parameters to calibrate ([file_prefix]_params_for_id.json), and ground truth data to calibrate towards ([file_prefix]_obs_data.json) for generating and calibrating models.
  • src: Containts the source code for autogeneration, parameter id, and other utilities.
  • user_run_files: Includes bash run files for the user and the user_inputs.yaml file, which is the main config file for the run settings.
  • funcs_user: Where you put your own functions for calculating output features from model outputs (operations), your own cost functions, and your own modifier functions. Name the file in user_inputs.yaml with operation_funcs_external_path / cost_funcs_external_path / modifier_funcs_external_path; copy one of the *_funcs_example.py templates to start, and see funcs_user/README.md. The built-in operations and costs ship inside the package, at [project_dir]/src/libcuflynx/param_id/operation_funcs.py and [project_dir]/src/libcuflynx/funcs/.
  • module_config_user: Contains user defined units, CellML modules, and configuration files for those modules. This allows the user to create their own modules and specify how they can be coupled with other modules. The corresponding source directory, which contains all built-in modules and configs, is [project_dir]/src/libcuflynx/generators/resources/ in a checkout, and ships inside the installed package as libcuflynx/generators/resources/.

Note

For recommended use, the user should create a separate [CA_user_dir] for the specific model they are creating. In this dir there should be the following:

  • [file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml
  • resources: Contains the files that define the model connection network ([file_prefix]_module_array.csv) and parameter values ([file_prefix]_parameters.json) that will be generated and config files to prescribe the parameters to calibrate ([file_prefix]_params_for_id.json) and the ground truth to calibrate towards ([file_prefix]_obs_data.json).

Note

Set external_modules_dir to a directory where you store additional *_modules.cellml and *_modules_config.json files if you want modules external to the repo. This path can be relative to your user_inputs.yaml location. To load a whole module library (one module per subdirectory), use module_library_dirs, and set use_builtin_modules: false to use it instead of the built-in modules; see Designing a model.

The following folders will be generated in [CA_user_dir] (or [project_dir] if user_inputs_path_override isn't defined) after running model autogeneration and parameter identification.

  • generated_models: Includes the generated code for the models that have been automatically generated. It also contains the generated models with parameters that have been fit with the parameter identification code. These models can be opened and run in OpenCOR, or simulated from Python with libcuflynx.
  • param_id_output: Includes all outputs from parameter identification runs, including predicted parameter values, minimum costs, standard deviations of parameters (if doing MCMC), and plots of the fitting results and parameter distributions.

docs.title: Model Generation
docs.text:
This section shows how to generate your desired model. There are several examples to show the generality of the circulatory_autogen software.

The following are the steps for model autogeneration.

  1. Create the module_array and parameters files for the intended model. Standard names are [model name]_module_array.csv and [model name]_parameters.json (nested JSON; see Designing a model), respectively. The module array may also be a JSON file, [model name]_module_array.json (see Designing a model).

    Those files should be added to your resources directory which is set with resources_dir in your [CA_user_dir]/[file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml (or [project_dir]/user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml if user_inputs_path_override isn't defined).

Note

The standard location for the resources dir is [CA_user_dir]/resources.

Info

If the name of your model is 3compartment, the user files needed for generation are:

  • 3compartment_module_array.csv
  • 3compartment_parameters.json

Note

You can refer to the section Designing a new model for more details on creating module_array and parameters files.

  1. Go to the [CA_user_dir] and open the [file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml to edit. You can use your editor of choice. file_prefix should be the name of your model, and input_param_file should be [file_prefix]_parameters.json. If you keep the default user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml, set user_inputs_path_override to point to your [CA_user_dir]/[file_prefix]_user_inputs.yaml. Set model_type to cellml (default), python, or cpp depending on the output you want. In place of file_prefix and resources_dir you can name the module array file itself, module_array_path: resources/[file_prefix]_module_array.json, and in place of input_param_file a parameters file anywhere, parameters_path: path/to/[file_prefix]_parameters.json. A key libcuflynx does not read is refused, with the key you probably meant.

  2. To run autogeneration, navigate to the user_run_files directory and run:

    ./run_autogeneration.sh

    As shown below, this will create CellML files for the generated model and test that the simulation runs. Consequently, If there are no errors, it shows the "Model generation has been successful." message at the end.

    Note

    Alternatively, use an IDE, set the Python interpreter to your venv's (see Getting Started), and run python -m libcuflynx.scripts.script_generate_with_new_architecture (the module lives at [project_dir]/src/libcuflynx/scripts/ in a checkout).

  3. Generated files are located in [generated_models_dir]/[file_prefix]. (generated_models_dir defaults to [project_dir]/generated_models unless you set it in user_inputs.yaml.)

    For model_type: cellml, five CellML files and a JSON file are generated: the main model [file_prefix].cellml, the modules, parameters and units/constants files it imports, [file_prefix]_flat.cellml (the same model in one file) and [file_prefix]_parameters.json with the model's parameter values (see the note below).

    For model_type: python, a Python module is also generated alongside the CellML files. For model_type: cpp, the model equations are generated by libCellML as C code (model0d_core.c/.h) and wrapped by a C++ Model0d class, a main0d driver and a CMakeLists.txt. These files are written to cpp_generated_models_dir, or to the model folder when that is not set. Build them with cmake -S <dir> -B <dir>/build && cmake --build <dir>/build, adding -DSUNDIALS_DIR=<prefix> for the CVODE solver if CMake can't find SUNDIALS (versions 5-7 are supported). The solvers are CVODE and the fixed-step RK4, Heun, midpoint and explEul. A cpp model needs solver_info.dt_solver, the step of the generated solver (for CVODE, the interval at which it returns), in user_inputs.yaml; generation stops with a message naming the key when it is missing. PETSC is not supported by the current generator. The generated C names every index, e.g. rates[S_heart_module_q_lv] and variables[V_parameters_r_pvn]. The names match the generated Python's (var.parameters_r_pvn), and model0d_core.h lists them with their units.

    Info

    The generated [file_prefix]_parameters.json, beside the generated model, holds every value the model uses, in the form of a model's parameters file (aortic_root/C, heart/lv/E_A, globals under global), each with its units and data_reference: the values from your [file_prefix]_parameters.json in the resources directory and the parameterisations. A model generated with identified parameters has the identified values there. It is the only parameters file generation writes beside the model; the generated model itself names a parameter C_aortic_root (<variable>_<vessel>, a nested vessel's levels joined with __: E_A_heart__lv).

    A value your [file_prefix]_parameters.json does not set (a supermodule instance written "heart": {}, or a module's default parameterisation) names where it came from at the start of its data_reference, from <module_type>/<module_subtype> parameterisation <name>: <its own data_reference>:

    "heart": {
 "lv": {
  "E_A": {"value": 366636512, "units": "J_per_m6", "data_reference": "from chamber/Liang2009NoVisco_v02 parameterisation lv: liang2009multi; Table 2 (p. 748), ..."}
 }
}

    It is the run's complete record: generating again with it as the model's parameters file, and the same module array, gives the same model (a data_reference already starting from is not prefixed again), without needing the module library's parameterisations to say the same.

Note

There is a test for the autogeneration running. To run the test, navigate to user_run_files and run the below command.

./run_test_autogeneration.sh

docs.title: Model Simulation
docs.text:
Once you have generated the models, open OpenCOR and open the generated [file_prefix].cellml, which is the main CellML file. This file automatically incorporates the [file_prefix]_modules.cellml, [file_prefix]_parameters.cellml and [file_prefix]_units.cellml files.

When it is opened, click on the Simulation tab (highlighted with a yellow box in the below image). If there is no error, OpenCOR shows you a new page where models can be simulated. (If there is an error specific to the cellml code then it will be shown here.)

Several individual parts on this page are:

  • Simulation settings
  • ODE solver settings
  • Parameters and variables
  • Run control
  • Run diagnostics
  • Graphs and results

You should set the simulation's starting, ending, and data output step size. Also, if you have a stiff problem you may need to set the maximum_time_step to a small value.

ODE solver settings contains many settings related to the solver such as maximum step size, iteration method, absolute and relative tolerance, name of solver, etc. (shown in the blue box in the above image.)

The parameters and variables section shows all constant and variable parameters that are used in the model (see Designing a model for more information on setting up parameters). You can plot variables by right-clicking each parameter you want for the y-axis and then choosing the x-axis variable (e.g., time).

The run control is on the top left section, as shown in the purple color box in the image. Click on the triangle button to run. For further control, see the OpenCOR Tutorial.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
You should have a generated model in [generated_models_dir]/[file_prefix] and be able to run it in OpenCOR or via Python.

The results will be shown after running the model. These results include run-time, settings, and other related parameters, as shown in the yellow box at the bottom of the image.

docs.title: Other Useful Scripts
docs.text: These scripts ship inside the package, as libcuflynx.scripts.* (in a checkout, src/libcuflynx/scripts/). Most are examples or utilities and may need adjustments for your specific model. Run one with python -m libcuflynx.scripts.<script_name>, or copy it out of the package and edit your copy.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• pip install libcuflynx (or an editable install of a checkout).
  • A configured user_inputs.yaml and relevant resource files.

docs.title: generate_modules_files.py
docs.text:
Converts a generic CellML file into the modular format used by Circulatory_Autogen.

  • Currently works for models made from a single module.
  • Generates [file_prefix]_modules.cellml and [file_prefix]_module_config.json in module_config_user/.

docs.title: generate_obs_json.py
docs.text:
Example script for automating creation of an obs_data.json file from input data.

  • Use this as a template if you do not want to hand-edit JSON.
  • Note: it uses legacy fields such as sample_rate; update to obs_dt for series entries.
  • For a more structured helper, see example_format_obs_data_json_file.py.

docs.title: example_format_obs_data_json_file.py
docs.text: Example script showing how to build an obs_data.json using the helper class libcuflynx.utilities.obs_data_helpers.ObsDataCreator. Copy it and change it for your own task.

docs.title: read_and_insert_parameters.py
docs.text: Sets every parameter of one parameters file (nested JSON) in another, in place: read_and_insert_parameters.py parameters_to_add.json updates the file input_param_file names, and read_and_insert_parameters.py parameters.json parameters_to_add.json the one given.

docs.title: convert_0d_to_1d.py
docs.text: Utility for converting a 0D module array into a 1D representation (useful when preparing 1D-0D coupled models).

docs.title: run_multiple_param_id.py
docs.text: Runs multiple parameter identification experiments over a list of observation files.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text: You should be able to locate and run auxiliary scripts for module conversion, data preparation, and batch workflows.

docs.title: Deriving parameters from experimental data
docs.text:
Many parameters are calculated from measurements rather than measured: a bed's resistance from the mean arterial and central venous pressures and its flow, a compliance from stroke volume and pulse pressure. A derivations file records each calculation: its inputs, with their values, uncertainties and sources, the equation, and the parameters it sets. cuflynx-derive evaluates it, checks the values cached in the parameters file, and with --write updates them.

Derivations are for data only. They never run inside a simulation; a parameter you calibrate stays a model parameter in params_for_id, and a derived value can be its starting value.

docs.title: The inputs: input_items in obs_data
docs.text:
A number a derivation reads that is not a calibration target goes in the obs_data's input_items, beside data_items and prediction_items. Input items are never scored, plotted or validated against.

"input_items": [
  {"data_item_name": "CVP_Smith2001", "value": 5.0, "std": 1.0, "unit": "mmHg",
   "data_reference": "Smith2001", "comment": "Table 2, supine adults"},
  {"data_item_name": "CO_Rowell1986", "value": 1e-4, "std": 1e-5, "unit": "m3_per_s",
   "data_reference": "Rowell1986", "comment": "6 L/min"}
]
Key data_item_name Required. Unique across the file's data, prediction and input items. value, unit Required. One number and its unit (a CellML unit name). std Its standard deviation. data_reference Where it comes from (a citation key, DOI or reference); carried into each derivation's inputs. An input item does not take source: one with it is refused, naming data_reference (a data item's source is still read as its data_reference, with a warning). comment, species, location Free text; not read. prob_dist_params The number as a distribution; not read yet.

A derivation may also read a data_item with a constant value, when the same number is a calibration target and an input (mean arterial pressure, say): then the target and the input are one number.

docs.title: The derivations file
docs.text:
<name>_derivations.json sits beside the <name>_parameters.json it sets, with its CellML and Python files next to it or below it. Paths in it are relative to it.

{"derivations": [
  {"name": "R_T0",
   "inputs": {"MAP": {"data_item": "MAP"},
              "CVP": {"input_item": "CVP_Smith2001"},
              "Q":   {"parameter": "Systemic_T/Q_T0"}},
   "outputs": {"R": "Systemic_T/R_T0"},
   "cellml": "derivations/systemic_resistance.cellml",
   "comment": "the bed's resistance from its pressure drop and flow"},
  {"name": "Q_T0",
   "inputs": {"CO": {"input_item": "CO_Rowell1986"},
              "frac": {"parameter": "Systemic_T/frac"}},
   "outputs": {"Q": "Systemic_T/Q_T0"},
   "python": "derivations/derivation_funcs.py:flow_share"}]}
  • inputs map each symbol to exactly one source: parameter (a path in the parameters file, as in params_for_id: instance/variable, heart/lv/E_A, global/R), input_item or data_item. Its units are the source's.
  • outputs map each symbol to the parameter it sets. The parameter must be in the parameters file, with its units. Each parameter is set by one derivation at most.
  • Chains: an input may be another derivation's output (above, R_T0 reads Q_T0). Derivations run in the order their inputs need, whatever their order in the file; a loop is an error.
  • Method: exactly one of cellml or python.
  • fixed_constants (cellml only): constants of the CellML model that keep their initial value from the CellML file, such as the gas constant. See below.

The structure is defined by src/libcuflynx/schemas/derivations.schema.json.

docs.title: A CellML derivation model (preferred)
docs.text:
The equation is a CellML 2.0 model. Its inputs are constants named as the input symbols (their initial values are placeholders); its outputs are computed constants named as the output symbols. Every constant of the model must be an input or a fixed constant: one the derivation leaves out is an error, not its placeholder. The model may import units or components from other CellML files beside it or below it.

A constant whose initial value is its value, such as a physical constant, is listed in the derivation's fixed_constants instead of its inputs:

{"name": "E_K",
 "inputs": {"T": {"input_item": "T_body"}, "K_o": {"input_item": "K_o"},
            "K_i": {"input_item": "K_i"}},
 "outputs": {"E": "membrane/E_K"},
 "cellml": "derivations/nernst.cellml",
 "fixed_constants": ["R", "F"]}

R and F keep the values and units the CellML file gives them. Every other constant must still be an input, so a forgotten input is still an error. Naming a fixed constant that is not a constant of the model (a computed constant, or no variable at all), or that is also an input, is an error. Each derivation's result records its fixed constants with their values and units (fixed_constants of the result: {"R": {"value": 8.314, "units": "J_per_K_per_mol"}}), and cuflynx-derive prints them:

E_K (cellml)
  fixed constant R = 8.314 J_per_K_per_mol (from the CellML file)
  fixed constant F = 96485.0 C_per_mol (from the CellML file)
  membrane/E_K: cached -0.0897, derived -0.0897 V

A fixed constant may say what set its value, as {"name": "R", "origin": "measured", "data_reference": "[CODATA][2018][gas_constant]"} (origin: measured, inherited or set_by_hand; set_by_hand needs a reason). cuflynx-derive --write records each derived parameter's fixed constants, with value, units and origin, in its fixed_constants key, and a calibration workflow's provenance diagram draws them in a "Fixed constants of derivations" box in the row above the derived values. A constant given as a bare name has no origin and is drawn unclassified.

A number written in the equation itself (<cn>) needs no listing, but a named fixed constant shows its value and units where the derivation is reviewed.

<component name="derivation">
  <variable name="MAP" units="Pa" initial_value="0"/>
  <variable name="CVP" units="Pa" initial_value="0"/>
  <variable name="Q" units="m3_per_s" initial_value="1"/>
  <variable name="R" units="J_s_per_m6"/>
  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
    <apply><eq/><ci>R</ci>
      <apply><divide/><apply><minus/><ci>MAP</ci><ci>CVP</ci></apply><ci>Q</ci></apply>
    </apply>
  </math>
</component>

libCellML validates and analyses the model, and generates its Python code, which is evaluated once. Any issue is an error, including units that do not balance in an equation. An input whose units differ from its variable's but have the same dimension is converted (MAP in mmHg into Pa above, if the model defines mmHg); so is an output whose parameter is in other units of the same dimension. Units of different dimensions are an error. Implicit equations are refused: use a Python function for those. An output that is not a finite number (a division by zero flow, say) is an error.

You can write the model in CellML Text and convert it with physiomelinks' cellml-text-editor, or edit it in PhLynx's Instance Editor (the CellML Text and Math Editor tabs) and export the component.

docs.title: A Python function
docs.text:
For a calculation CellML cannot state (an implicit equation, a network solve), name a function as file.py:function:

def flow_share(inputs, units):
    """The flow through a bed: its share of the cardiac output."""
    return {'Q': inputs['CO'] * inputs['frac']}

It is called with inputs ({symbol: value}, in each source's units) and units ({symbol: units} for the inputs and outputs), and returns {output symbol: value} in the output parameters' units: it converts units itself. A template is in funcs_user/derivation_funcs_example.py.

docs.title: The parameters file
docs.text:
A derived parameter keeps its value, as a cache every reader of the parameters file uses as it is, names its derivation, and has origin derived (a leaf with derivation and another origin, or none, is refused):

"R_T0": {"value": 146654199.99999994, "units": "J_s_per_m6",
         "data_reference": "derived; derivation R_T0", "origin": "derived", "derivation": "R_T0"}

The provenance diagram of a calibration workflow marks such a value derived.

docs.title: When a derived parameter is calibrated
docs.text:
A derived value is only a calibration's start value. When a calibration fits the parameter, the calibrated leaf has origin calibrated and no derivation: write_calibrated_parameters (a workflow's <name>_calibrated_parameters.json) and generation with fit parameters (cuflynx-generate True) both write it so. cuflynx-derive prints a calibrated parameter's derived value but neither checks nor writes it, so --write can never overwrite a calibrated value.

The derived value is not lost:

  • the parameters file the calibration started from still has it, with its derivation: a workflow writes only the calibrated file;
  • the derivations file still calculates it: cuflynx-derive prints it beside the calibrated value;
  • each workflow step's generated parameters file (generated.parameters_path in its result) holds it as the value that step started from.

docs.title: cuflynx-derive
docs.text:
cuflynx-derive BVC_derivations.json --obs BVC_obs_data.json
cuflynx-derive BVC_derivations.json --obs BVC_obs_data.json --write

The first evaluates every derivation and prints each parameter's cached and derived value. It exits 0 when every cached value matches within a relative tolerance of 1e-9 and 1 otherwise, so a test or CI job can run it. A parameter that names a derivation that does not set it is reported too. --write writes the derived values into the parameters file, and adds derivation and origin derived to each output parameter; every other key and parameter is kept, and a calibrated parameter (origin calibrated) is left as it is. It exits 1 when a parameter still names a derivation that does not set it, which --write cannot fix: remove that derivation key. A file or derivation that cannot be read or evaluated is an error message and exit 2.

--obs may be given several times; --parameters names the parameters file when it is not <name>_parameters.json beside the derivations file. From Python:

from libcuflynx.derivations import (check_derivations, evaluate_derivations, load_derivations,
                                    read_parameters)
doc = read_parameters('BVC_parameters.json')
results = evaluate_derivations(load_derivations('BVC_derivations.json'), doc, ['BVC_obs_data.json'])
print(check_derivations(results, doc))   # [] when the cache is current

Each result carries its inputs with their values, units, standard deviations and sources, and its fixed constants with their values and units, for a review page or a table.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text:
pack_workflow (and cuflynx-calibration-workflow --pack) copies the derivations file beside each parameters file it packs, with the CellML and Python files it reads at the same paths relative to it, so they go into the OMEX archive CUFLynx makes from the pack. A CellML derivation model brings the CellML files it imports. A derivation's files must be in the derivations file's directory or below it. A module version from a library is packed whole, with its derivations.

A study's working dir does the same: when the parameters file is copied into inputs/system/<date>/, its derivations file and the files it reads are copied beside it, and an edit to any of them makes a new dated copy.

docs.title: Parameter Identification
docs.text:
The parameter identification part of Circulatory_Autogen is designed to allow calibration of a model to experimental or clinical data. It implements an optimisation method to find the best fit parameters that give a minimal (local minima) error difference between the model output and the ground truth observables (experimental or clinical data or user specified). The creation of below two configuration files is necessary:

  • params_for_id
  • param id observables

Those files should be added to the [CA_dir]/resources directory (or your custom resources_dir). Proper names of the files are [file_prefix]_params_for_id.json and [file_prefix]_obs_data.json, respectively. You can also set params_for_id_file in user_inputs.yaml if you want to use a non-standard filename.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A generated model (see Model Generation and Simulation).
  • param_id_obs_path and params_for_id files in your resources directory.
  • A Python environment with libcuflynx installed, and the mpi extra if running in parallel.

docs.title: Creating params_for_id file
docs.text:
This file defines which parameters (constants and initial_states) within your model that you will vary in the parameter id process and their allowed ranges (prior distribution). It is JSON, a flat list of entries, one per calibrated value:

{
 "version": 1,
 "params": [
  {"targets": ["global/q_lv_init"], "min": 200e-6, "max": 1500e-6, "param_type": "const", "name_for_plotting": "q_{sbv}"},
  {"targets": ["aortic_root/C"], "min": 1e-9, "max": 5e-8, "param_type": "const", "name_for_plotting": "C_{ao}"},
  {"targets": ["heart/lv/E_A", "heart/rv/E_A"], "min": 1e8, "max": 5e8, "name_for_plotting": "E_A"},
  {"name": "R_scale", "modifies": ["venous_svc/R", "venous_ivc/R"], "modifier": "scale", "min": 0.5, "max": 2.0}
 ]
}

The keys of an entry:

  • targets: the model parameters this calibrated value sets, all to the same value, named as in the [file_prefix]_parameters.json file: <vessel>/<variable> (aortic_root/C), a nested vessel by its path (heart/lv/E_A, a supermodule instance's submodule) and a global constant as global/<variable>.
  • modifies, modifier, inputs (instead of targets): a modifier entry, whose calibrated value acts on the parameters it lists through a modifier function (scale, remainder, or your own, see modifier_funcs_external_path).
  • theta (a modifier entry only): the value the entry starts at in a calibration and is analysed about in a local sensitivity analysis. By default it is the one that leaves the modified parameters at their values in the model (1 for scale).
  • name: the entry's name, unique in the file; by default its first target.
  • min, max: the range of possible values (the uniform prior's bounds, the optimiser's search box).
  • param_type: "state" or "const"; whether the parameter is the initial value of a state or a const.
  • name_for_plotting: the name (latex format) used in plots.
  • prior, prior_params, unbounded, comment: see below.

The file is flat, not nested by instance like the parameters file, because an entry is not one parameter: it groups parameters or modifies them. An optional "defaults" object gives keys every entry takes unless it sets its own.

Note

param_type will be deprecated. All should be "const". Initial values that need to identified should be defined as constants within the cellml module.

A params_for_id CSV (vessel_name,param_name,min,max,..., the older form) is refused. Convert it once with

cuflynx-upgrade params-for-id <params_for_id CSV | directory>...

which writes the .json beside each CSV and removes the CSV: each row becomes one entry, vessel_name "a b" with param_name "C" becomes "targets": ["a/C", "b/C"] (a nested heart__lv as its path, heart/lv/C), and the prior_* columns go under "prior_params". Name the .json wherever the CSV was named (params_for_id_file, a workflow step's params_for_id).

docs.title: Priors
docs.text:
Without further keys every parameter has a uniform prior on [min, max]. An optional prior chooses another, with its settings in prior_params:

prior prior_params Notes uniform (default) — flat on [min, max] normal prior_mean, prior_std default mean: the middle of the range; default std: a sixth of it exponential prior_scale (or prior_lambda), prior_origin decays from prior_origin; scale defaults to max / prior_lambda

Each prior is truncated to [min, max] unless unbounded is true, in which case the range is derived from the prior. Priors shape the log posterior, so they affect MCMC (do_uq) and optimisers run with objective_function: likelihood (the genetic algorithm); a calibration that minimises the cost does not see them. A calibration workflow can also give a step a prior over several parameters at once, from an earlier step's posterior (see Calibration workflows).

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text: Every input file has a JSON Schema shipped in libcuflynx/schemas/ (params_for_id.schema.json, obs_data.schema.json, parameters.schema.json, module_config.schema.json, module_array.schema.json; load one with libcuflynx.schemas.load_schema), describing each key and its default. libcuflynx checks every file against its schema when it reads it, so editors and other tools validating against the schema agree with libcuflynx. An error lists every problem, each with where it is (an item by its name, e.g. data_items[2] ('systolic').value) and what the field is for.

docs.title: Creating param id observables file
docs.text:
This file defines the simulation protocol (protocol_info), and ground truth observables that will be used in the cost function for the parameter id optimisation algorithm. It also defines the measurement standard deviation, and weighting for each observable.

Every obs_data is a JSON object with a protocol_info that has pre_times and sim_times. A bare list of data items, or an object without protocol_info, is refused; convert it once with cuflynx-upgrade obs-data [file] --user-inputs [user_inputs.yaml], which writes a one-experiment protocol_info from that yaml's pre_time and sim_time.

File path of the obs_data.json file should be defined as param_id_obs_path in [CA_dir]/user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml. This path can be absolute or relative to the location of your user_inputs.yaml.

Note

IMPORTANT: For creating obs_data.json files in python (strongly recommended over modifying the json by hand you can use the helper class libcuflynx.utilities.obs_data_helpers.ObsDataCreator. See libcuflynx/scripts/example_format_obs_data_json_file.py (in a checkout, src/libcuflynx/scripts/example_format_obs_data_json_file.py) for an example that you can copy and change for your parameter identification task.

docs.title: protocol info
docs.text:
The protocol info defines the numerical experiments you will be running. Here is an example for a sympathetic neuron calibration where the input current is changed from 0 to 0.15 pA after 1 second then simulated for 2 seconds with that input current. This was performed in two experiments, the first experiment with a M-type potassium conductance of 0.08 uS and the second experiment with an increased M-type potassium channel conductance of 0.12 uS.

For the protocol we define each experiment as each new full simulation that needs to be run. Each subexperiment is a section of an experiment with its own set of parameters. Subexperiments generally relate to different time periods where the inputs in the experiments that are being used for calibration have a change in value (e.g. change in drug concentration, change in stimulatiion frequency, change in applied force). The entries in the protocol info are:

  • pre_times: The amount of simulation that is done before you want to compare to observables or plot (this part of the simulation is thrown away. This is mainly used to simulate for an amout of time to reach steady state or periodic state. shape = (number of experiments)
  • offline_pre_time (optional): A single scalar, in seconds. Before any experiment runs, the solver performs one unlogged warmup integration for this duration, then stores the end state as the default state used when reset_states() is called at the start of each experiment. Use this to separate a long steady-state or periodic warmup from the logged pre_times phase. Calibration runs it once, before the first evaluation, and every evaluation starts from its end state. Supported by the CVODE_myokit, CVODE_libopencor, casadi_python, python (solve_ivp) and aadc_python backends; an emulator ignores it (its training already covered the warmup) and an external_python model raises, because its run() always starts from the initial condition. A traced input (protocol_traces / protocol_shapes) is held at its value at the start of experiment 0 during this warmup. It cannot be combined with a calibration parameter that sets a state's initial value: the frozen state would not move with that parameter, so the run stops with OFFLINE_PRE_TIME_INIT_STATE_ERROR (reformulate in terms of a constant parameter, e.g. total volume rather than initial LV volume). Example: offline_pre_time: 19.0 with pre_times: [1.0] gives 20 s of total warmup before the first logged segment, equivalent to pre_times: [20.0] without offline_pre_time.
  • sim_times: The length in time of each subexperiment. shape=(number of experiments, number of subexperiments) -- Note: the shape isn't completely correct here, the number of subexperiments can be different for each experiment
  • params_to_change: A dictionary where the key is a parameter name and the entry is the assigned value of that parameter in each (experiment_idx, subexperiment_idx).
  • params_to_change_factors (optional, calibration workflow steps only): The same shape as params_to_change, each entry a number that multiplies the value the step's model gives that parameter -- see Protocol factors.
  • experiment_colors: The line color for the plots of each experiment.
  • experiment_labels: The label for each experiment, which is used for plotting and naming plots.
  • protocol_traces (optional): Named {"t": [...], "values": [...]} waveforms. A params_to_change entry may be the name of one instead of a number, and the parameter then follows that waveform over the subexperiment rather than being held constant.
  • protocol_shapes (optional): The same thing written as events rather than as a table of points -- see below. A name is defined in protocol_traces or in protocol_shapes, whichever suits; both are referred to from params_to_change the same way.

docs.title: Time-varying inputs: protocol_shapes
docs.text:
A stimulus is easier to write as "1 unit, 2 ms long, every 1000 ms" than as the forty numbers that describes. protocol_shapes takes the first form, using the same five fields as a Myokit .mmt [[protocol]] table, so a protocol imported from Myokit needs no translation:

# .mmt                                  # obs_data.json
# Level  Start  Length  Period  Mult    "protocol_shapes": {
  1.0    100    2       1000    0           "stim": {"events": [{"level": 1.0, "start": 100,
                                                                "length": 2, "period": 1000,
                                                                "multiplier": 0}]}
                                        },
                                        "params_to_change": {"membrane/stim": [["stim"]]}
