  • level — the value the parameter takes during the event; outside every event it takes baseline (default 0).
  • start, length — when the event begins and how long it lasts. duration is accepted as a synonym for length (it is what Myokit's Python API calls it).
  • period — how often it repeats; 0 means it happens once.
  • multiplier — how many times it repeats; 0 means "for as long as the subexperiment runs", so the number of beats follows sim_times rather than having to be counted out by hand.

A shape is expanded over the subexperiment that refers to it, so its length comes from sim_times. Give the shape its own duration if you want to override that, which is also how a shape shared between subexperiments of different lengths is disambiguated. Overlapping events are rejected, as they are in Myokit, and so is a stimulus that never fires inside the time it is run over.

A step and a single pulse are just pacing events that do not repeat: a step is {"level": v, "start": ts, "length": <rest of the subexperiment>, "period": 0} over a baseline, and a pulse is the same with a shorter length. A linear sweep is not a square event, so it has its own type:

"protocol_shapes": { "load": {"type": "ramp", "from": 0.0, "to": 5.0} }

which runs from from at the start of the subexperiment to to at its end.

The expansion happens when the file is read, so everything downstream -- the solvers, the plots -- sees an ordinary protocol_traces entry and behaves exactly as it would have if you had written the points out.

docs.title: data items
docs.text:
Examples of obs_data.json, data_item entries are shown in below figures for constant, constant with operation_kwargs, series, and frequency data types, respectively.

The entries in the data_item list in the obs_data.json file are:

  • data_item_name: The user defined name of this observable. It does not need to link to a cellml variable name, but it must be unique across every data_item and prediction_item in the file: it is the item's identity, and the name an operation_kwargs reference to another item resolves against. Replaces the old variable entry, which also stood in as the operand — the model variable now always goes in operands.
  • data_type: The format of the data. This can be "constant", "series", or "frequency" as shown above.
  • unit: The unit of the observable.
  • trace_name_for_plotting: The axis label for the trace this item is drawn from, in latex format. May repeat: the mean and the max of one variable are two features of one series, so they share it. Defaults to the first operand.
  • item_name_for_plotting: The label for the item — the scalar feature itself — used in sensitivity tables and error reports. Defaults to "<trace_name_for_plotting> (<operation>)".
  • weight: The weighting to put on this observables entry in the cost function. Default should be 1.0
  • std: The standard deviation which is used in the cost function. The cost function is the relative absolute error (AE) or mean squared error (MRE), each normalised by the std.
  • value: The value of the ground truth, either a scalar for constant data_type, or a list of values for series or frequency data_types.
  • obs_dt: required for series data types and not needed for constant or frequency. It defines the timestep for the observable series values.
  • prob_dist_params: the ground truth when it is a distribution rather than a value — see below. An item that sets this needs no value or std; an item that does not, needs both.
  • data_reference (optional): where the data come from, as a string — a citation key, DOI or table reference, as in the data_reference column of a parameters file. source has been replaced by this key: an item's source is read as its data_reference, which wins if the item has both, with one warning per file giving the number of items. libcuflynx never requires it, and refuses a value that is not a string. It is saved beside the error vectors (error_vec_data_references.npy, in the order of error_vec_names.npy, "" where an item has none), shown as a Data: ... line at the top of the item's reconstruction plot and on any prediction_plots figure that draws its data, and listed under Sources in the methods text, where a word that is a BibTeX key becomes \cite{key} as in a parameter's data_reference. Each item names its own source: there is no file-level default, so items from one paper each carry its key. A module library may require it in its own checks.

Every item is either a scalar or a series, never both. The same rule applies to prediction_items, and the parser checks it, naming the item:

  • data_type: constant: value and std are single numbers.
  • data_type: series: value is a list; std is a number or a list of the same length; obs_dt is required. Sample k is at k * obs_dt from the start of the item's sub-experiment.
  • frequency keeps its own rules.

A series may still have an operation, as long as it returns a series. Examples are addition of two traces, or an operation with series_output.

docs.title: Ground truth as a distribution (prob_dist_params)
docs.text:
Some observables are not known as a single number plus a standard deviation. A measurement repeated across a cohort is a set of points, and it may not even be unimodal. For these, state the ground truth as prob_dist_params and choose a cost_type that scores against a distribution:

cost_type prob_dist_params scores the output against kernel_density_estimation {"data_points": [...]} a smooth density fitted to the measured points, with no assumption about how many modes there are multimodal_gaussian {"means": [...], "stds": [...], "scales": [...]} a named mixture of gaussians (scales must sum to 1) poisson_MLE {"k": <count>} a Poisson likelihood, where the model output is the rate

The observable itself is still an ordinary constant: the model produces one scalar, exactly as for gaussian_MLE. Only what it is compared against differs, and that follows from cost_type.

{
  "data_item_name": "x_steady_state",
  "data_type": "constant",
  "operation": "steady_state_avg",
  "operands": ["benchmark/x"],
  "unit": "dimensionless",
  "weight": 1.0,
  "cost_type": "kernel_density_estimation",
  "prob_dist_params": {"data_points": [1.05, 0.99, 4.08, 3.96, "..."]},
  "cost_kwargs": {"bandwidth": 0.1}
}

Anything that tunes the comparison rather than stating the data goes in cost_kwargs — for kernel_density_estimation that is bandwidth, the KDE smoothing width (a number, "scott" or "silverman"; Scott's rule by default), which you can change without touching the measurements.

docs.title: Series ground truth from .npy files (t_path and value_path)
docs.text:
For large time-series observables you can store arrays in NumPy files instead of embedding long lists in the JSON. On load, Circulatory Autogen reads the files and fills in any missing value and obs_dt fields before calibration runs. You must still set std in the JSON (see below).

  • t_path: Path to a .npy file containing the time vector (seconds).
  • value_path: Path to a .npy file containing the observable values. This is always the quantity that will be compared to the model .

Paths may be absolute or relative to the process working directory when parameter identification is started. If value is already present in the JSON, the file path should not be set;

Example data_item entry:

{
  "data_item_name": "P aortic root",
  "data_type": "series",
  "operands": ["aortic_root/u"],
  "operation": null,
  "unit": "Pa",
  "weight": 1.0,
  "std": 500.0,
  "t_path": "/path/to/pressure_time.npy",
  "value_path": "/path/to/pressure_values.npy",
  "experiment_idx": 0,
  "subexperiment_idx": 0
}

If obs_dt is omitted, it is estimated from the mean step in t_path. For std, provide either one positive number (applied to every sample in the series) or a list with one entry per sample (same length as value after load).

Warning

The dt or sample_rate fields are deprecated for series data. Use obs_dt instead.

Not to be confused with the dt for the model simulation outputs. - operation: This defines the operation that will be done on the operands/variable. The possible operations to be done on model outputs are the built-ins in libcuflynx.param_id.operation_funcs and libcuflynx.funcs.operation_funcs_user, plus any user defined operations in the file named by operation_funcs_external_path in user_inputs.yaml (copy funcs_user/operation_funcs_example.py to start). Since the built-in funcs moved into the package, editing them in place is no longer supported — an upgrade replaces them. - operation_kwargs: An optional dictionary of keyword arguments (kwargs) and their values, passed to the chosen python operation function on top of the operands. Defaults to {}. See operation_kwargs below for the full contract. - operands: The model variables the "operation" is applied to — always required, and always the place the model variable is named. ("operation" may take several.) An item built purely from other items' values, rather than from a trace, states [""]. - experiment_idx and subexperiment_idx: Optional indices to link a data item to a specific experiment/subexperiment in protocol_info.

docs.title: operation_kwargs
docs.text:
operation_kwargs is an optional, per-data_item dictionary of keyword arguments for that item's operation func. It is a supported public field of obs_data.json (it is what the CUFLynx editor writes when you tune an operation's options in the GUI), and it behaves identically in calibration, MCMC/UQ and sensitivity analysis.

At run time Circulatory Autogen calls:

operation(*operands, **operation_kwargs)

so the operands fill the operation func's leading positional arguments and operation_kwargs fills its keyword arguments. For example, with the user operation

@series_to_constant
def mean_in_range(x, start_frac=0.0, end_frac=1.0, series_output=False):
    ...

a data_item can ask for the mean over the last 20% of the sub-experiment:

{
  "data_item_name": "mean late P aortic root",
  "trace_name_for_plotting": "u_{ARlate}",
  "data_type": "constant",
  "operation": "mean_in_range",
  "operands": ["aortic_root/u"],
  "operation_kwargs": { "start_frac": 0.8, "end_frac": 1.0 },
  "unit": "J_per_m3",
  "weight": 1.0,
  "value": 12000,
  "std": 1200
}

The rules are:

  • Optional, default {}. Omitting operation_kwargs (or leaving it empty/null) calls the operation func with its own defaults, exactly as before.
  • Keys must be keyword arguments of the operation func. An unknown or misspelled key is an error, not silently ignored -- otherwise a stale obs_data file would quietly calibrate against a different feature than you asked for. The error names the data item, the operation func, the offending key and the accepted keys, and it is raised as soon as the observation data is set, before any simulation runs. A func that declares **kwargs (like calculate_two_observable_difference) accepts any key.
  • Keys already filled from operands are rejected. If operands supplies the operation's first argument x, you cannot also pass "x" in operation_kwargs.
  • series_output is reserved. Circulatory Autogen sets it itself when it needs the trace for plotting, so a data_item must not set it.
  • String values can reference an earlier observable. A string value that matches the data_item_name of an earlier data_item is replaced, at run time, by that observable's computed value. This is how an observable is built from other observables -- see calculate_two_observable_difference in libcuflynx/funcs/operation_funcs_user.py and resources/3compartment_extra_ops_obs_data.json. A string that matches no earlier observable is passed through unchanged, so plain string options still work. Note that the referenced item must appear earlier in data_items than the item that references it.
  • Type coercion is minimal. JSON has a single number type, so a value written as 20.0 where the func's default is the integer 20 is converted to int, and an integer written where the default is a float is converted to float. Nothing else is coerced: strings, booleans, lists and null reach the operation func as-is.

User-defined operation funcs receive operation_kwargs exactly like the built-ins. This includes the operations libcuflynx ships in libcuflynx/funcs/operation_funcs_user.py, funcs in a file pointed to by operation_funcs_external_path in user_inputs.yaml, and funcs registered from python with add_user_operation_func().

When building obs data in python rather than as a file, pass the same field through ObsDataCreator.add_data_item({... , "operation_kwargs": {...}}).

docs.title: Building an observable from other observables
docs.text:
Sometimes the quantity you want to fit is not something the model reports directly, but a combination of quantities it does. If you have a ground truth for the mean flow and another for the peak flow, what you actually know may be the difference between them -- the pulse amplitude -- and that difference is what you want the cost to see.

An observable can therefore be computed from observables defined earlier in data_items, using the string-reference rule described above: a string in operation_kwargs that matches an earlier item's data_item_name is replaced by that item's computed value.

libcuflynx ships calculate_two_observable_difference for the two-term case. It takes its inputs as pred1 and pred2 and returns pred2 - pred1:

{
  "data_item_name": "mean flow aortic root",
  "trace_name_for_plotting": "v_{AR}",
  "data_type": "constant",
  "operation": "mean",
  "operands": ["aortic_root/v"],
  "unit": "m3_per_s", "weight": 1.0, "value": 0.0001, "std": 1e-05
},
{
  "data_item_name": "max flow aortic root",
  "trace_name_for_plotting": "v_{AR}",
  "data_type": "constant",
  "operation": "max",
  "operands": ["aortic_root/v"],
  "unit": "m3_per_s", "weight": 1.0, "value": 0.0005, "std": 5e-05
},
{
  "data_item_name": "aortic root flow, max minus mean",
  "trace_name_for_plotting": "v_{ARdelta}",
  "data_type": "constant",
  "operation": "calculate_two_observable_difference",
  "operands": [""],
  "operation_kwargs": { "pred1": "mean flow aortic root", "pred2": "max flow aortic root" },
  "unit": "m3_per_s", "weight": 1.0, "value": 0.0004, "std": 5e-05
}

resources/3compartment_extra_ops_obs_data.json is this example as a complete, working file.

Three things to get right:

  • Order matters. An observable can only reference items that appear before it in data_items, because the values are computed in file order and the reference is resolved against the ones already computed. A reference to an item that has not been computed yet is an error naming the item to move, rather than the operation quietly receiving the name as a string.

  • A reference may cross experiments and sub-experiments. The referenced item does not have to be in the same experiment_idx / subexperiment_idx as the item referencing it, so the quantity you actually know — how much a treatment moved a feature, the difference between a baseline run and a forced one — can be written down directly:

    {
  "data_item_name": "peak prey, unforced",
  "operation": "max", "operands": ["Lotka_Volterra_module/x"],
  "experiment_idx": 0, "data_type": "constant", "unit": "dimensionless",
  "value": 23.62, "std": 0.5
},
{
  "data_item_name": "peak prey, forced",
  "operation": "max", "operands": ["Lotka_Volterra_module/x"],
  "experiment_idx": 1, "data_type": "constant", "unit": "dimensionless",
  "value": 21.58, "std": 0.5
},
{
  "data_item_name": "peak prey, forcing response",
  "operation": "calculate_two_observable_difference", "operands": [""],
  "operation_kwargs": { "pred1": "peak prey, unforced", "pred2": "peak prey, forced" },
  "experiment_idx": 1, "data_type": "constant", "unit": "dimensionless",
  "value": -2.04, "std": 0.5
}

    Ordering still applies, and now spans segments: experiments are evaluated in order, and the sub-experiments within each, so an item may reference anything in an earlier segment. tests/test_inputs/Lotka_Volterra_forced_cross_exp_obs_data.json is the worked example.

    One limit: the Myokit CVODES FSA and CasADi AD gradients cannot differentiate a cross-segment reference, because each builds its observables from one sub-experiment's operands. They refuse with a message rather than return a gradient for a different feature than the cost. Use finite differences (do_ad: False) or a gradient-free method, or keep the reference inside one sub-experiment. - operands is empty, written [""]. The item takes its inputs from operation_kwargs rather than from a model variable, so there is no trace to reduce. - data_item_name is what the reference resolves against, and it must be unique. This is now enforced: a repeated data_item_name is rejected when the obs_data is loaded, naming the offenders. Note the two source items above deliberately share a trace_name_for_plotting (v_{AR}) — they are the mean and the max of one trace — and differ only in data_item_name. Before this was split in two, both said v_{AR} for everything, the reference resolved to whichever was computed last, and the example silently computed max - max = 0. A name that matches nothing is still passed through to the operation func as a plain string, so a typo shows up as a strange result rather than a failure.

To combine more than two observables, or to combine them some other way, write your own operation func in a file named by operation_funcs_external_path (see Creating your own operations) and name it in operation. It receives the referenced values as keyword arguments, so it needs to accept them -- either by declaring them explicitly or with **kwargs. @series_to_constant marks it as returning a single number rather than a trace:

@series_to_constant
def combine_three_observables(x=None, series_output=False, **kwargs):
    return kwargs["pred3"] - kwargs["pred2"] - kwargs["pred1"]

and the data_item names it in operation with one operation_kwargs entry per input:

"operation": "combine_three_observables",
"operands": [""],
"operation_kwargs": { "pred1": "v_{ARmean}", "pred2": "v_{ARmax}", "pred3": "v_{ARmin}" }

Note

Older versions could fail with TypeError: operation_funcs.mean() argument after ** must be a mapping, not float when a data_item had no operation_kwargs. This is fixed: every place that forwards operation_kwargs now goes through param_id.operation_funcs.resolve_operation_kwargs, which treats a missing/null/NaN value as "no kwargs" and raises a descriptive ValueError (naming the data item, the operation and the accepted keys) for a key the operation func does not accept.

docs.title: prediction items (optional)
docs.text:
You can include a prediction_items list in obs_data.json to request additional model outputs to plot (not used in the cost function). They take the same vocabulary as a data_item:

  • data_item_name: This item's identity, unique across every data_item and prediction_item in the file.
  • operands: The model variable to record, as a list — e.g. ["heart/u_lv"]. This is what the old variable entry named; it no longer doubles as the item's name.
  • unit: The unit of the recorded variable.
  • experiment_idx (optional; defaults to 0)
  • subexperiment_idx (optional): the sub-experiment of experiment_idx whose run the item is recorded over. Defaults to that experiment's last sub-experiment, and must exist.
  • trace_name_for_plotting (optional): The axis label, in latex format. Defaults to the first operand.
  • item_name_for_plotting (optional): The item's own label. Defaults to "<trace_name_for_plotting> (<operation>)".
  • operation and operation_kwargs (optional): the same operations and the same operation_kwargs checks as a data_item. On a scalar item the operation reduces the operands to one number. On a series item it returns a series, exactly as for a data_item. See Prediction items as scalar features.

docs.title: Validation data in prediction items
docs.text:
A prediction item can also carry held-out data: measurements the calibration does not fit, which the calibrated model is then checked against. Give the item:

  • value: the data, a number (data_type: constant) or a list (data_type: series)
  • data_type: constant or series
  • std (optional): its standard deviation. For a constant this is one number. For a series it is one number for every point, or a list with one per point. Every entry must be greater than 0. Without it, the item is scored by RMSE alone.
  • obs_dt: the spacing of a series' samples. They start at the start of the item's sub-experiment, as a data_item series does. With one sub-experiment, that is the start of the experiment.
  • data_reference (optional): where the held-out data come from, as for a data_item. It is written with the item's scores in validation_results.json.

For example, fit the first 15 years of a series and validate the prediction to year 20, in one file with one experiment that runs to 20:

"prediction_items": [
  {"data_item_name": "x_validation", "operands": ["mod/x"], "unit": "dimensionless",
   "data_type": "series", "value": [30.0, 47.2, "..."], "std": [7.5, 11.8, "..."], "obs_dt": 1.0}
]

After a calibration, saving the prediction data (plot_param_id) also writes validation_results.json in the output directory: for each item with data, the RMSE, the RMSE over the data's range, the mean |model - data|/std and the fraction within 2 std, with the model and data at the observation times. A series is compared at the times the simulation reaches. A constant is compared with the model's value at the end of its sub-experiment. An item with an operation is compared with the operation's result: a scalar for a constant, or the operation's series (series_output for a @series_to_constant operation) for a series. Each result item also names its operation (null for an item without one). The traces are saved as prediction_variable_data_exp_<k>.npy, as before. An item that sets a subexperiment_idx other than its experiment's last is saved in prediction_variable_data_exp_<e>_sub_<s>.npy instead. Its rows are the time from the start of the sub-experiment, then each item's first operand.

docs.title: Experiments used only for validation
docs.text:
An experiment in protocol_info that no data_item belongs to is not part of the cost. The calibration does not simulate it: not in any cost evaluation, nor in the best-fit check and the plots. The run prints one line naming such experiments as prediction/validation only. They are simulated after calibration, for the prediction data and validation_results.json. SA and emulator training simulate them only when include_prediction_items needs a feature measured there. When every experiment has a data_item, nothing changes.

Example: experiment 0 is fitted. Experiment 1 has a different sim_time and a different params_to_change, and holds only held-out prediction items:

{
  "protocol_info": {
    "pre_times": [0.0, 0.0],
    "sim_times": [[8.0], [3.0]],
    "params_to_change": {"benchmark/x_init": [[0.0], [2.0]]}
  },
  "data_items": [
    {"data_item_name": "x_ss", "operands": ["benchmark/x"], "data_type": "constant",
     "operation": "steady_state_avg", "unit": "dimensionless", "value": 1.0, "std": 0.1,
     "experiment_idx": 0}
  ],
  "prediction_items": [
    {"data_item_name": "x_recovery", "operands": ["benchmark/x"], "unit": "dimensionless",
     "experiment_idx": 1, "data_type": "series", "value": [2.0, 1.61, 1.37, 1.22, 1.14, 1.08, 1.05],
     "std": 0.05, "obs_dt": 0.5},
    {"data_item_name": "x_recovery_mean", "operands": ["benchmark/x"], "unit": "dimensionless",
     "experiment_idx": 1, "operation": "mean", "data_type": "constant", "value": 1.3, "std": 0.1}
  ]
}

docs.title: Prediction items as scalar features
docs.text:
A prediction item with an operation is a scalar feature of the prediction, e.g. the maximum of a pressure over an experiment. It is still not part of the cost. It changes three things:

  • Validation. Its held-out value (data_type: constant) is compared with operation(operands) over the recorded run rather than with the value at the end of the experiment. Every operand is recorded, so a two-operand operation works.
  • Sensitivity analysis. With sa_options.include_prediction_items: true it is an extra SA output. See Sensitivity analysis.
  • Emulators. With emulator_settings.include_prediction_items: true the emulator is also trained on it. See Emulators.
"prediction_items": [
  {"data_item_name": "p_max_validation", "operands": ["aortic_root/u"], "unit": "J_per_m3",
   "operation": "max", "data_type": "constant", "value": 16000.0, "std": 800.0}
]

Only a scalar prediction item with an operation becomes a feature. That means data_type: constant, or no data at all and an operation that reduces a trace to a number (max, min, mean and the other @series_to_constant ones). Items without an operation, and series items with or without one, are not features. SA and emulator training skip them, with a warning that names them. If a feature's operation returns more than one number, the run stops with an error naming the item. An item's operation_kwargs may refer to an earlier prediction item by its data_item_name, but not to a data_item. The operation is applied over the item's (experiment_idx, subexperiment_idx) segment, which by default is the experiment's last sub-experiment. That is the same segment the prediction data records and the validation uses.

docs.title: Plots across experiments (prediction_plots)
docs.text:
A family of experiments is often read as one picture: peak current against step potential (I–V), a feature against a dose, a clamp protocol beside the current it drives. The optional top-level prediction_plots list draws one figure per entry. There are four kinds.

Feature kinds: one point per experiment.

"prediction_plots": [
  {"name": "Peak I_Na vs step potential", "kind": "feature_vs_input",
   "x": {"params_to_change": "clamp/V_cmd", "subexperiment_idx": 1}, "y": "I_peak",
   "series": null},
  {"name": "Peak I_Na vs mean step", "kind": "feature_vs_feature", "x": "V_step", "y": "I_peak"}
]
  • A group is the data_items and prediction_items that share an item_name_for_plotting (written, or its default). A group has at most one item per experiment, and each item is a scalar feature.
  • A point is one experiment: y is the y group's item for it; x is the x group's item for the same experiment (feature_vs_feature) or the value params_to_change[key] takes in that sub-experiment (feature_vs_input).
  • series (an input reference, optional) draws one line per value of that input. Points are sorted by x; an item's value/std is drawn as error bars.
  • An input reference is {"params_to_change": <key>, "subexperiment_idx": <i>} with an optional "reduce". A number is used as it is. A trace (a protocol_traces or protocol_shapes name) needs reduce to become one number: "final", "mean", "max", "min", or {"at": <seconds from the start of that sub-experiment>}. These are taken over the trace as the sub-experiment applies it (linear between its points, held past its ends, cut at the end of the sub-experiment). An experiment whose input is a trace with no reduce has no point: it is left out with a warning that names it.
{"name": "Peak I vs ramp end", "kind": "feature_vs_input", "y": "I_peak",
 "x": {"params_to_change": "clamp/V_cmd", "subexperiment_idx": 1, "reduce": "final"}}

Time-course kinds: an input and a model output over time.

"prediction_plots": [
  {"name": "Clamp and current", "kind": "input_and_output",
   "input": {"params_to_change": "clamp/V_cmd"}, "output": "cell/membrane/I_Na",
   "experiments": [0, 2]},
  {"name": "I-V loop", "kind": "output_vs_input",
   "input": {"params_to_change": "clamp/V_cmd"}, "output": "cell/membrane/I_Na"}
]
  • input_and_output draws one figure per experiment, <name>_exp_<idx>.png. The input is on the left y-axis and the model output on the right, against the time since the end of the warm-up. Sub-experiment boundaries are dashed. A data_item that has the output as a series (its first operand, no operation) in that experiment is overlaid.
  • output_vs_input draws the output against the input sampled at the same times, one line per experiment (for example an I–V loop under a voltage ramp), in <name>.png.
  • input is a params_to_change key. Across the experiment, a number is drawn as a step and a trace as its waveform.
  • output is written as an obs_data operand is: <vessel>/<variable>, a nested vessel by its path (SN/soma/membrane/V), or a global's bare name. It is recorded the way prediction items are, in a simulation of those experiments (at the best fit, after a calibration), so any model variable can be drawn. An output the model does not have is refused before anything runs.
  • experiments (optional) lists the experiments to draw. The default is all of them.

The structure is checked when the obs_data is read: a params_to_change key the protocol does not set, a subexperiment_idx or experiment out of range, a malformed reduce, an at after the end of its sub-experiment, and the wrong keys for a kind are refused. A feature group that misses an experiment the other group has is an error, not a gap. save_prediction_data draws the figures in the output directory after a calibration, with a data_item's model value from the cost path. cuflynx-run-predictions draws them without a calibration; a data_item point there shows its data only.

docs.title: Running external cellml models
docs.text:
Running cellml models that weren't generated with Circulatory_Autogen is also just as straightforward:

Simply set the file_prefix in your user_inputs.yaml file to the name of your cellml model <file_prefix>.cellml. Then set generated_models_dir to the path to the dir where your model subdir is and the subdir where the calibrated model will be generated. Make sure your cellml file/files are in a directory of the same name i.e.:

path/to/your/generated_models_dir/<file_prefix>/<file_prefix>.cellml

After calibration, the following directory will be created with your generated model:

path/to/your/generated_models_dir/<file_prefix>_<obs_file_name>/

Note

Currently the generated model needs to be run in newer OpenCOR with the LibOpenCOR backend because a CellML 2.0 model is generated.

docs.title: Creating your own operations
docs.text:
To enable flexibility we allow you to create your own user-defined operation functions in python to extract features from your model outputs and compare to data in the calibration. The operation functions libcuflynx ships can be found in src/libcuflynx/param_id/operation_funcs.py and src/libcuflynx/funcs/operation_funcs_user.py. Those are library files -- do not edit them, since an upgrade replaces them. Write your own in a file of your own and name it with operation_funcs_external_path in user_inputs.yaml; funcs_user/operation_funcs_example.py is a template to copy. Here is an example of an operation function for calculating the ratio of the two peaks (used for mitral valve flow).

Note:

  • kwargs can be used and defined for each entry in your obs_data.json with operation_kwargs, see above.
  • if series_output is needed to return the variable trace for plotting.
  • A more elegant method of returning a high cost if the observable can't be calculated is being discussed.

docs.title: Creating your own cost functions
docs.text:
To allow even more flexibility, we also allow users to define their own cost functions (or likelihood functions). The ones libcuflynx ships are at src/libcuflynx/funcs/cost_funcs_user.py -- a library file, so do not edit it. Write your own in a file of your own and name it with cost_funcs_external_path in user_inputs.yaml; funcs_user/cost_funcs_example.py is a template to copy. An example for the maximum likelihood estimator for gaussian noise (equivalent to weighted mean squared error) is:

Note:

  • Currently there are no kwargs for user defined cost functions. But there will be: see issue

docs.title: Solver
docs.text:
Before doing calibration, a solver for the model needs to be chosen

  • model_type defaults to cellml. A config that names a solver but no model_type takes that solver's model_type, so solver: casadi_integrator alone is a casadi_python run.
  • solver defines the solver family. Options depend on model_type:
    • CellML (model_type: cellml): CVODE_myokit (Myokit, the default) or CVODE_libopencor (libOpenCOR: the libopencor extra, Python 3.12 or later; no protocol traces or FSA gradients). CVODE is read as CVODE_myokit. The batched solvers BE_batched_c and CVODES_batched_c also take CellML models; see Choosing a batched solver below.
    • Python (model_type: python): solve_ivp with solver_info.method set to RK45, BDF, etc.
    • CasADi Python (model_type: casadi_python): casadi_integrator with solver_info.method set to cvodes (the default), idas, collocation, rk, semi_implicit_euler, or bdf. cvodes and idas integrate each run as one solve over the output times, pass the model the true time, and can drive a constant from a protocol_traces trace as CVODE_myokit does. jit (on by default) compiles the model to C (see below).
    • C++ (model_type: cpp): CVODE, or the fixed-step RK4, Heun, midpoint or explEul.
  • solver_info defines settings for the chosen solver:
    • dt_solver: the step of the fixed-step and C++ solvers; sets max_step_size for casadi_integrator and max_step for solve_ivp when those are not given. The CellML (variable-step) solvers do not read it: giving it with a different MaximumStep is an error, and giving it without MaximumStep warns that the step is unbounded
    • MaximumStep: maximum step size (CVODE_myokit, CVODE_libopencor)
    • MaximumNumberOfSteps: maximum number of substeps before stepping (CVODE_libopencor and the C++ solvers)
    • method: any method for solve_ivp or casadi_integrator, e.g. RK45, BDF, cvodes, etc.
    • jit (casadi_integrator, default true): generate C for the model's right-hand side and its derivatives and compile it, once per process per model, timeline and options. Needs a C compiler (gcc by default): with jit unset and no compiler, the run continues without jit and warns; jit: true with no compiler is an error; jit: false turns it off. compiler (shell or clang) and jit_options (e.g. {compiler: clang, flags: ['-O3']}) choose the compiler. It speeds up forward runs; the AD gradient's symbolic graph uses the interpreted integrator, since CasADi 3.7 does not differentiate through a jit-compiled CVODES integrator.

Choosing a batched solver (BE_batched_c, CVODES_batched_c)

CVODE_myokit is the more general-purpose solver, and the one to start with. BE_batched_c and CVODES_batched_c are good when you have many perturbations through time: inputs that change at many points in a run (a protocol trace with many breakpoints, or a game that changes an input every macro step). CVODE has to stop and restart its adaptive time steps at each of those changes, while the batched solvers integrate the model as independent blocks of states in generated C (one block per unconnected part, such as each cell of a module array) and restart only the blocks whose inputs changed. They are opt-in: they run only when you name them in the config, e.g.

solver_info:
  solver: BE_batched_c      # or CVODES_batched_c
  method: trbdf2            # BE_batched_c: backward_euler (default) or trbdf2

They have no sensitivities (no do_ad gradient), and do not take models with algebraic loops or external variables. BE_batched_c suits moderate tolerances (default rtol 1e-4); CVODES_batched_c uses CVODE_myokit's tolerances and needs SUNDIALS 6 or later (SUNDIALS_DIR). The settings of each are listed in src/libcuflynx/solver_wrappers/batched_c_helper.py, and timings are in benchmarks/README.md (Batched CellML solvers).

Automatic differentiation supports constant and series observables only

With do_ad: true the cost is built symbolically. constant and series data items are both supported, and dt does not have to equal a series item's obs_dt: the simulated series is linearly interpolated onto the observation times, which is a multiply by a matrix of weights fixed by the two time grids, so it stays differentiable. Frequency (amp / phase) observables cannot be differentiated yet, and raise rather than silently contributing nothing to the cost.

Gradients: do_ad, Myokit FSA and CasADi AD

With do_ad: true the gradient-based methods take the model's analytic gradient: Myokit CVODES forward sensitivities (FSA) for cellml on CVODE_myokit, CasADi AD for casadi_python. On cvodes or idas CasADi AD is computed by CVODES forward sensitivities (one per calibrated parameter), which match finite differences on the stiff 3compartment model, warm-up included. (The CVODES adjoint, CasADi's reverse mode, fails there with CV_TOO_MUCH_WORK, so it is not used.) do_ad: false, the default, uses finite differences. gradient_sources(model_type, solver) lists the choices for a model and marks the one to pre-select; default_gradient_source(model_type, solver) returns it.

CasADi semi_implicit_euler — a fixed-step AD method (verify with a convergence study)

semi_implicit_euler differentiates by reverse mode through a fixed-step graph rather than by CVODES sensitivities. To use it set solver_info.method: semi_implicit_euler. This is a fixed-step, linearly-implicit (semi-implicit) Euler scheme with diagonal-Jacobian damping:

x_{n+1} = x_n + dt * f(x_n) / (1 - dt * d f_i / d x_i)

The damping term stabilises the stiff modes at the model dt, and because the whole integrator is built as a single symbolic graph, CasADi differentiates the cost by ordinary reverse-mode AD, with no ODE solver in the gradient.

model_type: casadi_python
solver_info:
  solver: casadi_integrator
  method: semi_implicit_euler
  max_step_size: 0.001

Less accurate than cvodes — do a convergence study

semi_implicit_euler is a first-order, fixed-step scheme that damps using only the diagonal of the Jacobian, so it is less accurate than the adaptive cvodes integrator and, on a stiff model, can noticeably differ from the true (CVODE) trajectory at a practical dt. It is not the accurate choice.

Do not trust the results at a single dt. Perform a convergence study: rerun with progressively smaller dt (e.g. halve it) and confirm the trajectories and the identified parameters stop changing meaningfully before relying on them. cvodes remains the more accurate default.

CasADi bdf — a fixed-step AD method for stiff models

bdf is a fixed-step, symbolic implicit BDF2 scheme (a rootfinder per step, differentiated through the implicit-function theorem). Like semi_implicit_euler it is built as a single symbolic graph, so CasADi produces exact gradients by reverse-mode AD — but it is second order and full-Jacobian implicit, so it tracks a stiff trajectory far more accurately than the first-order, diagonally-damped semi_implicit_euler at the same dt. Prefer bdf over semi_implicit_euler; still do a convergence study in dt.

model_type: casadi_python
solver: casadi_integrator
do_ad: true
solver_info:
  method: bdf
  max_step_size: 0.001

Myokit CVODES forward sensitivity — AD gradients for cellml models

A cellml model run through the Myokit backend can produce an exact gradient without converting to casadi_python, using Myokit's native CVODES forward-sensitivity analysis (FSA). Set model_type: cellml, solver: CVODE_myokit, do_ad: true, and a gradient-based param_id_method (sp_minimize or multi_start_sp_minimize). FSA integrates the state and sensitivity equations together with the adaptive stiff CVODES solver, so it handles stiff dynamics and a long pre_time warmup natively while staying as accurate as the forward simulation itself.

model_type: cellml
solver: CVODE_myokit
do_ad: true
param_id_method: multi_start_sp_minimize
solver_info:
  rtol: 1e-9
  atol: 1e-9        # tight tolerances keep the sensitivities out of the integrator noise floor

A parameter that only sets a state's initial value cannot be a CVODES sensitivity independent; such parameters automatically fall back to finite differences (a one-line warning reports how many and which). Tighten rtol/atol when using FSA so the sensitivities are well resolved.

our AADC wrapper is not yet suitable for stiff models or general observables

The AADC tape backend (model_type: aadc_python) records a fixed-step integrator, which is inaccurate or unstable on stiff models — on the 3compartment cardiovascular model its fixed-step implicit solve deviates from CVODE by orders of magnitude. Every AADC run now probes the first second of dynamics and prints a loud warning if the model is stiff, pointing you at CasADi bdf or Myokit CVODES FSA instead.

AADC puts only some observables on the tape. The operand may be a state or an algebraic variable (a pressure or flow computed from the states, which the tape recomputes from them at each step), and the observable must be one of:

  • a constant with operation mean, max, min or max_minus_min (or no operation, which takes the final value) — on the tape-consistent methods (rk4, semi_implicit, implicit_euler_ift, implicit_newton);
  • a series on a state or algebraic variable — on the tape-consistent methods only;
  • a constant with operation mean, max, min or max_minus_min — on semi_implicit_signed with gradient_strategy: kernel (aadc-ode). A series is not supported there.

Any other observable — a user operation such as steady_state_avg, another data type, or an operand that names neither a state nor a variable — makes the gradient raise an error on those paths, naming the observables it cannot tape, rather than silently minimising a reduced cost. The bdf_newton method and the semi_implicit_signed tape strategy do not check yet: they leave such an observable out of the cost, or cost it wrongly, so keep to the observables above there. For other observables use casadi_python (method: bdf) or a Myokit CVODES FSA run.

Multiple sub-experiments / experiments are not yet supported by the AADC wrapper. The tape records one straight-line integration, so a protocol with more than one sub-experiment (or more than one experiment) raises rather than silently differentiating the wrong thing. The Myokit CVODES FSA gradient (model_type: cellml + solver: CVODE_myokit) does support multi-sub protocols; the AADC equivalent is tracked as future work.

docs.title: Parameter Identification Settings
docs.text:
To run the parameter identification we need to set a few entries in the [CA_dir]/user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml file:

  • param_id_method: this defines the optimisation method we use. Currently supported methods are:
    • CMA-ES: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy using Nevergrad (the default when param_id_method is not set; supports parallel execution)
    • genetic_algorithm: Genetic algorithm optimizer (well-tested; its default population is 744 per generation, so it needs a budget of at least that many evaluations)
    • bayesian: Bayesian optimization using scikit-optimize (deprecated, untested)
    • sp_minimize: Gradient-based optimizer (L-BFGS-B, local only)
    • multi_start_sp_minimize: Multi-start L-BFGS-B — a gradient-based descent from many scattered starting points, so it exploits the gradient but still escapes local minima
  • pre_time: the unlogged time a plain simulation (no obs_data) runs to reach steady state. A calibration is timed by the pre_times and sim_times in the obs_data's protocol_info, which every obs_data must have (see the next section).
  • sim_time: the logged duration of a plain simulation (no obs_data). A calibration takes its durations from the obs_data's sim_times.
  • dt: The output (sample) time step for model outputs
  • solver_info.MaximumStep: The CVODE maximum step size (CVODE_myokit, CVODE_libopencor)
  • solver_info.dt_solver: The step of the fixed-step and C++ solvers. A CellML solver does not read it, and refuses a dt_solver that differs from MaximumStep
  • param_id_obs_path: the path to the obs_data.json file described above (absolute or relative to your user_inputs.yaml).

  • optimiser_options: Dictionary for optimizer-specific options. Common options shared across optimisers:

    • num_calls_to_function: Maximum number of function evaluations (default: 10000)
    • cost_convergence: Convergence tolerance for cost (default: 0.0001)
    • max_patience: Stop after this many generations without an improvement in cost (default: 10). For CMA-ES a generation is one population of candidates (4 for two bounded parameters, and at least the MPI rank count + 1), on any number of ranks
    • cost_type: Cost function type (e.g., 'MSE')

    CMA-ES specific options:

    • The initial step is not an option: Nevergrad's CMA-ES picks it itself, in a space scaled per parameter to (max - min) / 6. sigma0 was removed; a config that names it is refused
    • Note:
      • The number of parallel workers is automatically determined from the number of MPI processes
      • Initial parameter values are automatically loaded from {file_prefix}_parameters.json
      • The start value is evaluated first, as one of num_calls_to_function, so a run never ends with a worse cost than its start (a warm start or a profile likelihood point stays at least as good)

    sp_minimize specific options:

    • do_ad: Boolean value to determine whether to use automatic differentiation for gradient calculation. If it's set to False, gradients will be estimated using finite difference approximation.

    multi_start_sp_minimize specific options:

    • num_starts: Number of L-BFGS-B descents to run (default: 10, or 4 when DEBUG is true). The starts are spread round-robin over the MPI ranks; make num_starts several times the rank count so the work balances (see the note under "Multi-start Gradient-based Optimizer" below).
    • start_sampling: How the starting points are scattered over the parameter bounds: sobol (default), latin_hypercube or random.
    • include_init_point: If true (default), the first start is the initial parameter values from {file_prefix}_parameters.json, so this method can never do worse than a single-start sp_minimize run.
    • seed: Seed for the start sampler (default: 0), so a run is repeatable.
    • fd_step: Finite-difference step used when an automatic-differentiation gradient isn't available — i.e. any configuration without an AD backend (see the gradient-backend note below), or when do_ad: false (default: 1e-4).
    • cost_convergence: Once any start reaches this cost, every MPI rank stops launching new starts (signalled between ranks with a non-blocking message), so no rank keeps working after a good-enough solution has been found. (Set no_new_starts_on_convergence: false to disable this.)
    • no_new_starts_on_convergence: true (default) is the behaviour above — stop launching starts once one converges. Set to false to run every start regardless, then report how many converged and how many landed in each distinct minimum. That maps the basin structure of a multi-modal problem (which minima exist, and how the starts split between them); the counts are written to multi_start_convergence_clusters.csv and printed at the end of the run.
    • convergence_cluster_tol_frac: When counting how many starts reached each minimum, two converged starts are treated as the same solution if every parameter agrees to within this fraction of that parameter's range (default: 0.02, i.e. 2%).

    Automatic-differentiation gradient backends

    Gradient-based calibration (do_ad: true) is provided by two open-source backends: CasADi (model_type: casadi_python, LGPL — symbolic differentiation) and Myokit CVODES forward sensitivity (model_type: cellml + solver: CVODE_myokit). Both require no proprietary licence and both handle stiff models; see the Solver section for which method to pick.

    Circulatory Autogen also ships an optional adapter for AADC (Matlogica), which is third-party proprietary software, not part of Circulatory Autogen, not bundled with it, and restricted to academic/non-commercial use under Matlogica's own licence. It is not required. It can drive sp_minimize / multi_start_sp_minimize only for non-stiff, state-observable, single-experiment problems (its tape records a fixed-step integrator); it is unsuitable for stiff models such as the full cardiovascular model. See Optional third-party backends if you already hold a Matlogica licence.

docs.title: Genetic Algorithm (genetic_algorithm)
docs.text:
• Pros: Well-tested, robust, handles non-smooth cost functions well
  • Cons: Can be slower, requires more function evaluations
  • Best for: Complex, multi-modal optimization problems, when you have many function evaluations available

docs.title: CMA-ES (CMA-ES)
docs.text:
• Pros: Efficient gradient-free optimization, supports parallel execution, good convergence properties
  • Cons: Requires Nevergrad package (pip install nevergrad)
  • Best for: Smooth optimization landscapes, when you want faster convergence with parallel execution
  • One parameter: Nevergrad runs a different search (OnePlusOne) in one dimension, which can stall on a parameter's bounds, so a one-parameter calibration searches a second, unused variable beside it and runs CMA-ES (benchmarks/cmaes_one_parameter.py). For a single parameter of a smooth cost, sp_minimize is usually faster.

Example configuration for CMA-ES: 

param_id_method: CMA-ES
optimiser_options:
  num_calls_to_function: 10000  # shared option
  cost_convergence: 0.001         # shared option
  # Note: Initial parameter values are automatically loaded from {file_prefix}_parameters.json

docs.title: Gradient-based Optimizer (sp_minimize)
docs.text:
• Pros: Efficient gradient-based optimization, fast convergence
  • Cons: Can get stuck in local minima
  • Best for: Smooth optimization landscapes, when you want faster convergence

For an AD gradient use model_type: casadi_python (CasADi symbolic differentiation) or a cellml model run through solver: CVODE_myokit with do_ad: true (Myokit CVODES forward sensitivity — see the Solver section). Any other configuration falls back to a finite-difference gradient.

docs.title: Multi-start Gradient-based Optimizer (multi_start_sp_minimize)
docs.text:
L-BFGS-B only ever finds the minimum of the basin it starts in, so on a multi-modal cost surface sp_minimize is at the mercy of the initial parameter values. This method scatters num_starts starting points over the parameter bounds and runs a bounded L-BFGS-B descent from each one, keeping the best minimum found. It explores globally, like the population-based optimisers, while still using the gradient to descend each basin quickly and accurately.

  • Pros: Escapes local minima while still exploiting the gradient; the starts are independent so they are distributed over the MPI ranks with no communication; typically reaches a far lower cost than a gradient-free global search for the same wall-clock time.
  • Cons: Cost scales with num_starts; a very rugged surface may need many starts.
  • Best for: Multi-modal cost surfaces — the common case when calibrating oscillatory models, where a wrong rate constant puts the simulation out of phase with the data.

Parallel multi-start pays off only for many starts

The starts are distributed statically round-robin over the MPI ranks (run_param_id.sh with num_processors > 1). Because individual L-BFGS-B descents vary a lot in length — some converge in a handful of iterations, some take many — the per-rank workloads only even out when each rank runs many starts, i.e. when num_starts is much larger than the number of ranks. With num_starts ≤ num_processors each rank runs a single descent and the wall-clock is bounded by the slowest one, so extra ranks buy little. As a rule of thumb, run with several times as many starts as ranks. Measured on a 20-core host with 100 starts: ~3.8× on 4 ranks, ~4× on 8. Once any start reaches cost_convergence, every rank stops launching new starts, so a converged run doesn't keep the other ranks busy needlessly. run() reports the achieved speedup in its final log line.

This works for any model_type. The gradient comes from get_gradient(), which has an AD backend for casadi_python (symbolic jacobian), cellml run through CVODE_myokit with do_ad: true (Myokit CVODES forward sensitivity), and aadc_python (tape reverse pass — non-stiff, single-experiment problems with the observables listed in the AADC caveat in the Solver section). For every other configuration there is no AD gradient, so the cost is evaluated with the usual simulation cost and the gradient falls back to finite differences.

Example configuration: 

param_id_method: multi_start_sp_minimize
model_type: casadi_python     # for AD gradients; other model types use finite differences
solver: casadi_integrator
do_ad: true
optimiser_options:
  cost_convergence: 0.0001
  num_starts: 10              # number of L-BFGS-B descents
  start_sampling: sobol       # sobol | latin_hypercube | random
  include_init_point: true    # first start is the x0 from {file_prefix}_parameters.json
  seed: 0

Alongside the usual best_cost_history.csv / best_param_vals_history.csv (written as a running-best curve over the concatenated starts), this optimiser writes a multi_start_summary.csv with one row per start — its initial cost, final cost, iteration count and final parameter values. That tells you how many distinct basins your starts fell into, which is the quickest way to see whether num_starts is high enough.

It also streams three live per-start histories during the run, appended one row per L-BFGS-B iteration (iteration 0 is the start point), independent of DEBUG: multi_start_cost_history.csv (start_idx, iteration, cost), multi_start_param_vals_history.csv (start_idx, iteration, then one named column per parameter, holding the actual parameter values — same columns as multi_start_summary.csv) and multi_start_gradient_history.csv (start_idx, iteration, then one named column per parameter, holding the cost gradient dJ/dp in real parameter space at that iterate). Group by start_idx and order by iteration to plot a cost-, parameter- and gradient-vs-iteration line per start while the run is still going. The three files share the same (start_idx, iteration) keys, and start_idx is a stable global index, so rows from starts running concurrently on different MPI ranks demux cleanly regardless of interleaving.

docs.title: Benchmark: FitzHugh-Nagumo
docs.text:
resources/FitzHugh_Nagumo_* is a deliberately multi-modal benchmark. The FitzHugh-Nagumo excitable-cell model

$$\dot V = c\left(V - \tfrac{V^3}{3} + R\right), \qquad \dot R = -\tfrac{1}{c}\left(V - a + bR\right)$$

is a standard hard case for parameter estimation: its least-squares surface has many local minima, because a wrong recovery rate c puts the simulated spike train out of phase with the data (Ramsay et al. 2007, J. R. Statist. Soc. B 69(5), "Parameter estimation for differential equations: a generalized smoothing approach"). The supplied FitzHugh_Nagumo_parameters.json starts at (a, b, c) = (0.8, 0.9, 2.0), which sits inside a local basin; the true values are (0.2, 0.2, 3.0).

sp_minimize never leaves the basin it starts in. The genetic algorithm escapes it but, being gradient-free, converges slowly. The multi-start finds the global basin and refines it with the gradient — whatever gradient backend drives it (finite differences, CasADi AD, or Myokit CVODES FSA). The table below is regenerated by the benchmark runner (python benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py --update-docs) and by the Benchmarks GitHub Actions workflow, so the published numbers stay current; they depend on the hardware and MPI rank count used.

Generated by benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py; numbers depend on the hardware and MPI rank count used.

docs.title: FitzHugh-Nagumo (non-stiff, multi-modal)
docs.text:
Gradient-free global searches (genetic algorithm, CMA-ES) vs multi-start L-BFGS-B driven by four gradient sources. Holding the optimiser fixed and varying only the gradient isolates what the gradient buys.

1 MPI rank(s); 30000 cost evaluations for the population methods; 16 starts for multi-start.

method best cost time (s) max param err genetic_algorithm 1.9049e-03 257.9 0.0125 CMA-ES 1.4413e+02 286.2 4.0000 multi_start (FD) 2.4545e-03 40.0 0.0359 multi_start (CasADi AD) 9.6440e-06 66.0 0.0019 multi_start (Myokit FSA) 2.0599e-06 86.8 0.0021 multi_start (AADC AD) skipped — no Matlogica licence in this environment

True parameters: a=0.2, b=0.2, c=3.

docs.title: Goodwin oscillator (external PMR CellML, non-stiff, multimodal)
docs.text:
Gradient-free global searches (genetic algorithm, CMA-ES) vs multi-start L-BFGS-B (finite differences and Myokit CVODES FSA) recovering rate constants of the Goodwin 1965 oscillator, taken directly from the Physiome Model Repository as external CellML. Oscillatory dynamics make the least-squares surface multimodal.

1 MPI rank(s); 30000 cost evaluations for the population methods; 16 starts for multi-start.

method best cost time (s) max param err genetic_algorithm 2.0251e-04 83.6 0.0046 CMA-ES 2.7517e-06 112.0 0.0017 multi_start (FD) 9.1452e-15 26.7 0.0000 multi_start (Myokit FSA) 1.3269e-13 117.6 0.0000 multi_start (CasADi AD) 1.3147e-12 69.7 0.0000

True parameters: a_i=72, b_i=2, A_i=36.

docs.title: Teusink 2000 yeast glycolysis (external PMR CellML, 14 states, stiff regions)
docs.text:
The realistic, many-parameter case: recover four enzyme v_max values from metabolite time courses of the Teusink 2000 glycolysis model, taken from the Physiome Model Repository as external CellML (originally a BioModels SBML export). 14 coupled metabolite states and 90 constants, with stiff regions in the search box -- a much harder calibration than the small oscillator benchmarks. Multi-start finite differences also run on the batched C solvers (CVODES_batched_c, BE_batched_c).

1 MPI rank(s); 5000 cost evaluations for the population methods; 16 starts for multi-start.

method best cost time (s) max param err genetic_algorithm 8.9298e-04 29.0 0.0799 CMA-ES 7.1010e-09 3.6 0.0003 multi_start (FD) 3.2838e-15 35.2 0.0000 multi_start (Myokit FSA) 3.8772e-15 2500.2 0.0000 multi_start (FD, CVODES_batched_c) 3.9399e-15 23.5 0.0000 multi_start (FD, BE_batched_c) 8.5629e-07 24.2 0.0001

True parameters: Vmax_GLK=226.452, Vmax_PGI=339.677, Vmax_PYK=1088.71, Vmax_GAPDH_f=1184.52.

The stiff 3compartment cardiovascular benchmark (long warmup, Myokit/CasADi) runs in the same set; it is slower, so the workflow schedule is weekly. See benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Running parameter identification
docs.text:
After creating the params_for_id file and the param id observables file, and configuring the above settings, run the parameter identification using the below command.

./run_param_id.sh <NUM_CORES>

Following a successful parameter id process, the model with updated parameters can be generated with:

./run_autogeneration_with_id_params.sh

Note

IMPORTANT: After running the calibration, you should plot the simulation outputs vs the ground truth to analyse the fits!! This can be done with:

./plot_param_id.sh

The generated models will be saved in generated_models/ and plots will be saved in param_id_output/.

Full model time-series dumps (all states and variables) are written as NumPy archives in the param_id output directory:

  • all_outputs_with_best_param_vals_exp_{i}.npz — written when calibration completes successfully.
  • all_outputs_with_best_param_vals_exp_{i}_plot.npz — written at the start of every plot_outputs() call. Use these to recover trajectories after an interrupted run as long as best_param_vals.npy exists in the same output folder.

docs.title: The study working dir
docs.text:
param_id_output_dir is the study's working dir: every calibration, MCMC, sensitivity analysis and emulator run from one config records itself in the study manifest <param_id_output_dir>/<study_name>_cuflynx_study.json, and every input it was run from is copied into the same folder. So the one folder holds the whole study: zip it, send it, unzip it anywhere and open the manifest (or the folder, as the working dir) in CUFLynx.

<param_id_output_dir>/
    <study_name>_cuflynx_study.json   the manifest: inputs, solver settings, runs, sensitivity, emulator
    inputs/
        index.json                    every version stored below: its kind, file, folder,
                                      content hash, when it was first used and the runs that used it
        <kind>/<yyyy-mm-dd_HHMMSS>/   one version of one input, in a folder named for the local
                                      date-time it was first used. The kinds:
          model/                      the model, with the CellML files it imports
          obs_data/, params_for_id/   the obs_data and params_for_id files
          user_inputs/                the user_inputs.yaml given
          funcs/                      the *_funcs_external_path files
          system/                     a generated model's module array and parameters file, with
                                      modules/ (each module library version it uses) and
                                      external_modules/ (its external_modules_dir)
          emulator/                   an emulator trained elsewhere
          workflows/<workflow_name>/  a calibration workflow, packed (see Calibration workflows)
        user_inputs/user_inputs_<yymmdd>.yaml  each day's resolved config
    <prefix>_calibrated.cellml        the model with the best fit written in, from
                                      CVS0DParamID.write_calibrated_model (a pipeline bundle's
                                      run_pipeline.py writes it after its calibration)
    <method>_<prefix>_<obs_data>/     each calibration, <method> its param_id_method
    mcmc_<prefix>_<obs_data>/         the MCMC run (mcmc_chain.npy, its statistics and plots),
                                      a directory of its own beside the calibration it follows
    sensitivity/                      Sobol and local sensitivity output
    emulators/                        trained emulators

A calibration and the MCMC run that follows it each have a directory and an entry in the manifest's runs. The obs_data and params_for_id a run used are the copies in inputs/ that its manifest entry names; a run with no working dir (write_cuflynx_study: false or cuflynx_study_copy_inputs: false) copies them into its run directory instead, with a _<yymmdd>_<HHMMSS> suffix.

A pipeline bundle written by cuflynx-generate-pipeline is a working dir too: its run_pipeline.py writes the manifest, the run directories, sensitivity/ and inputs/ into the bundle folder.

An input is copied when the manifest is written, once per content, into a folder named for the date-time (local time) it was first used, for example inputs/obs_data/2026-10-31_091502/obs.json. Every copy is in such a folder, so no file under inputs/ looks like the current version when it is an older run's: each run's entry in the manifest names the copies it ran with, and inputs/index.json lists every version with the runs that used it. A second run from the same files copies nothing (copies are matched by content hash), and a changed file goes into a new dated folder beside the first (_2, _3... when two contents are first used in the same second). Every path in the manifest is relative to the manifest's folder.

An output written outside the working dir, such as an sa_options output_dir set to an absolute path elsewhere, is allowed but does not travel with the working dir: a zip of the working dir does not hold it. The run prints a warning naming the directory, and its entry in the manifest keeps the absolute path with "outside": true. cuflynx_study.outside_outputs(read_study('<W>')) lists those entries. Opening the study elsewhere never writes into that path: nothing re-runs a study from its manifest (read_study resolves output directories only to read their results, and generation_inputs names none).

To share a working dir, export it:

from libcuflynx.utilities.cuflynx_study import export_working_dir

left_behind = export_working_dir('<W>', 'my_study.zip')

Your working dir is not changed; these changes are only in the zip, so that a yaml run from it reads and writes only in the recipient's working dir, with no edits:

  • Each archived user_inputs yaml names its output directories relative to where it is unzipped: param_id_output_dir is the unzipped working dir, and an outside sa_options output_dir such as /scratch/sa_runs becomes sensitivity/sa_runs in the working dir (output_dir: sa_runs in the yaml). An outside generated_models_dir becomes generated_models, and an outside emulator_dir the default under emulators/.
  • Each archived user_inputs yaml names its inputs by their copies under inputs/, the versions that yaml's own run used (the manifest's yaml_inputs records them), not simply the latest: resources_dir is the inputs/system/<date>/ folder (module array and parameters file), module_library_dirs and external_modules_dir are the folders in it, and param_id_obs_path, params_for_id_file, the *_funcs_external_path keys and, with use_emulator, emulator_dir name their own copies. The model the run used goes in generated_model_path (external_model_path for external_python).
  • The manifests and inputs/index.json drop the outside entries and every absolute path.

Each outside path gets a warning naming it and its new relative path, and the results there are not in the zip. Each input rewritten gets a warning naming its copy. left_behind lists the same paths, the inputs marked 'input': True.

An input with no copy in the working dir, such as an external_modules_dir added by hand or a yaml whose run the manifest does not record, keeps the path it had, with a warning: the run then stops at that path on another machine rather than silently using a default in its place. left_behind lists it with relative None. Paths the yaml derives (model_path, vessels_csv_abs_path and so on) are left out, since the parser works them out again.

To run an unzipped yaml, point user_inputs_path_override at it in your user_inputs.yaml: that is what makes its relative paths resolve from its own folder. --user-inputs does not: it takes relative paths from the current directory. Nothing else is needed, and the originals need not exist. generated_model_path makes the run use the model the study ran; to run a model generated again from inputs/system/, delete that key from the yaml first. A calibration workflow's step yamls (in its step folders) and a packed calibration_workflow.json are not rewritten: rerun a workflow from its packed copy.

A generated model's inputs/system/ holds everything generating it again needs, so the model can be regenerated from the working dir alone. Built-in modules are not copied: they come with libcuflynx, so the manifest records use_builtin_modules and libcuflynx_version instead.

from libcuflynx.scripts.script_generate_with_new_architecture import generate_with_new_architecture
from libcuflynx.utilities.cuflynx_study import generation_inputs, read_study

inp = generation_inputs(read_study('unzipped_study/'))   # resources_dir, file_prefix, module sources
generate_with_new_architecture(False, dict(inp, model_type='cellml',
                                           generated_models_dir='regenerated'))
user_inputs setting default what it does study_name file_prefix names the manifest; two studies can share one working dir write_cuflynx_study true false writes no manifest and copies nothing; sensitivity output and the dated user_inputs go where cuflynx_study_copy_inputs: false puts them cuflynx_study_copy_inputs true false copies nothing: the manifest names each input outside the working dir by its absolute path and records the working dir as study_dir; sensitivity output defaults to sensitivity_outputs/<file_prefix>_SA_results and the dated user_inputs_<yymmdd>.yaml goes in resources_dir

docs.title: The calibrated model
docs.text:
libcuflynx.param_id.calibrated_model writes values into a CellML file. It is the one writer of a calibrated CellML: CVS0DParamID.write_calibrated_model, a calibration workflow's CellML steps and CUFLynx all use it, so one best fit gives one file.

from libcuflynx.param_id.calibrated_model import (substitute_parameter_values,
                                                  write_calibrated_model, write_cellml_values)

report = write_cellml_values('model.cellml', {'aortic_root/C': 2e-8, 'global/E_lv_A': 4e8},
                             'model_calibrated.cellml', flatten=None)
# {'updated': ['aortic_root/C', 'global/E_lv_A'], 'unresolved': [],
#  'resolved': {'aortic_root/C': 'parameters/C_aortic_root',
#               'global/E_lv_A': 'parameters_global/E_lv_A'},
#  'path': 'model_calibrated.cellml', 'flattened': True}
new_text, report = substitute_parameter_values(cellml_text, values)   # the same, on text
write_calibrated_model(cellml_path, param_id_info, best_param_vals, output_path,
                       flatten=None, return_report=True)               # from a best fit

A value is named vessel/param (resolved by model_qname_candidates, so aortic_root/C is parameters/C_aortic_root and global/E_lv_A is parameters_global/E_lv_A in a generated model) or component/variable. Only a variable with a numeric initial value in a component the file defines is written. The report lists the names written (updated), those with no such variable (unresolved, which write_calibrated_model also names in a warning) and where each went (resolved, component/variable; PhLynx reads back only the values in parameters and parameters_global).

flatten=None (the default) flattens a file that has imports: a generated model imports its parameters from <prefix>_parameters.cellml, so the calibrated model is one flattened file that runs by itself. A file with no imports is written as it is, with only the initial values changed. flatten=False writes the file itself whatever it imports (its imported constants are then unresolved); flatten=True always flattens.

docs.title: Calibration workflows
docs.text:
Some parameters can only be calibrated in a larger model, after its parts have been calibrated alone: a neuron soma's leak conductances once every channel has its own values, or a whole circulation once an isolated aorta has been fitted. A calibration workflow records that order in one JSON file and repeats it with one command:

cuflynx-calibration-workflow workflow.json
mpiexec -n 4 cuflynx-calibration-workflow workflow.json    # every step on 4 ranks

or from Python:

from libcuflynx.calibration_workflow import run_calibration_workflow
result = run_calibration_workflow('workflow.json', output_dir='wf_out')
result['merged_parameters']    # [{'parameterisation_name': 'aortic_root/C', 'value': ..., 'from_step': ...}]

Each step is an ordinary calibration, named by its three inputs: a model, an obs_data file and a params_for_id file, the same three that cuflynx-param-id takes. A step can instead be one of the analyses around a calibration -- a sensitivity analysis, an emulator, an identifiability analysis, or a reduction that picks which parameters a later calibration fits (see Step kinds) -- so the file records the whole order of a study. The results of every calibration are merged into the workflow's target model. To redo a calibration, edit its obs_data and run the workflow again: every step that used its values is redone too.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
libcuflynx ships small example models for trying workflows. They are algebraic, so a run takes seconds, and every answer is known. Write them anywhere:

python -c "from libcuflynx.external_testing.workflow_library import build_workflow_library as b; b('wf_example')"
WF=wf_example/arrays/chain_array.json
cuflynx-calibration-workflow $WF --dry-run              # the plan: where each parameter lands
cuflynx-calibration-workflow $WF --output-dir wf_run    # A/p = 2, C/q = 3
cuflynx-methods-latex --workflow $WF --run-dir wf_run -o methods.tex --pdf

chain_module_array.json is a model of two vessels: A (lin_a, y = 2 p^2) feeding C (lin_c, z = y + k q^2). Step a-alone calibrates p on a model of A alone; step chain then calibrates q in the whole chain, with p fixed. Read $WF and the files next to it for a layout to copy. The same chain written with library modules is wf_example/modules/chain/versions/v1/parameterisations/rest/calibration_workflow.json, and .../screened/calibration_workflow.json adds a Sobol screen, a reduction and an identifiability analysis to it (see Step kinds).

docs.title: Building a workflow in Python
docs.text: WorkflowBuilder makes the same file with API calls, so a script or a notebook needs no hand-written JSON. The obs_data and params_for_id can be dicts, as CVS0DParamID takes them (or an ObsDataCreator). Every method is in the API reference.

docs.title: One calibration
docs.text:
With the example models of Try it in wf_example, fit p of the vessel A (y = 2 p^2) to y = 8:

from libcuflynx.calibration_workflow import WorkflowBuilder

settings = {'param_id_method': 'CMA-ES', 'dt': 0.1,
            'optimiser_options': {'num_calls_to_function': 400, 'cost_convergence': 1e-14,
                                  'max_patience': 60, 'seed': 1, 'cost_type': 'gaussian_MLE'}}
wf = WorkflowBuilder('one_fit', target='wf_example/arrays/a_only_module_array.json',
                     directory='wf_one', module_library_dirs=['wf_example/modules'],
                     settings=settings)
wf.add_calibration(
    'fit',
    obs_data={'protocol_info': {'pre_times': [0.0], 'sim_times': [[1.0]],
                                'params_to_change': {}},
              'data_items': [{'data_item_name': 'y_a', 'data_type': 'constant',
                              'unit': 'dimensionless', 'operands': ['A/y'],
                              'operation': 'mean', 'value': 8.0, 'std': 0.08}]},
    params_for_id=[{'vessel_name': 'A', 'param_name': 'p', 'min': 0.1, 'max': 5}])
wf.run()
wf.result('fit')['values']      # {'A/p': 2.0}
  • target is the model the calibrated values are merged into, and the model of every step that names none: a module array path (or module_array(path, parameters=...)), or library_module(type, version, parameterisation).
  • directory is where the workflow file and its data are written; the run goes to <directory>/workflow_output/<name> (wf.output_dir).
  • module_library_dirs is needed whenever a model names modules of a module library, as these arrays do ("parameterisation": "default" of lin_a).
  • settings are user_inputs.yaml keys. A calibration needs its param_id_method and that method's optimiser_options (genetic_algorithm, the method when none is named, requires num_calls_to_function). wf.check() names what is missing, without running anything; wf.update_settings(...) changes settings later.

wf.run() checks the workflow, writes it and runs it. It prints one [workflow] line per step; everything else a step writes (the optimiser's iterations, compiler output, warnings) goes to <output_dir>/<step>/log.txt, and what is written outside the steps to <output_dir>/workflow_log.txt. wf.run(verbose=True) prints all of it as well.

print(wf) lists the steps and whether each has run. wf.show_status() prints a table with each step's state (done, stale, not run), best cost and finish time, and wf.show_plan() one with each step's model, the steps it takes from and the parameters it gives; wf.status() and wf.plan() return the same as dicts.

docs.title: A chain of steps
docs.text:
The chain of Try it: a-alone calibrates p on a model of A alone, then chain calibrates q in the whole chain (z = y + q^2) with p fixed.

from libcuflynx.calibration_workflow import WorkflowBuilder, module_array

def obs(item, operand, value, std, operation='mean'):
    return {'protocol_info': {'pre_times': [0.0], 'sim_times': [[1.0]], 'params_to_change': {}},
            'data_items': [{'data_item_name': item, 'data_type': 'constant',
                            'unit': 'dimensionless', 'operands': [operand],
                            'operation': operation, 'value': value, 'std': std}]}

arrays = 'wf_example/arrays'
wf = WorkflowBuilder('chain_from_python', target=module_array(f'{arrays}/chain_module_array.json'),
                     directory='wf_python', module_library_dirs=['wf_example/modules'],
                     settings=settings)
wf.add_calibration('a-alone', model=module_array(f'{arrays}/a_only_module_array.json'),
                   obs_data=obs('y_a', 'A/y', 8.0, 0.08),
                   params_for_id=[{'vessel_name': 'A', 'param_name': 'p', 'min': 0.1, 'max': 5}])
wf.add_calibration('chain', obs_data=obs('z_c', 'C/z', 17.0, 0.17),
                   params_for_id=[{'vessel_name': 'C', 'param_name': 'q', 'min': 0.1, 'max': 10}],
                   fixed_from=['a-alone'])
wf.plan()                       # the order, and where each parameter lands; runs nothing
wf.run()                        # A/p = 2, then C/q = 3
wf.result('chain')['values']    # {'C/q': 3.0}

add_calibration, add_sensitivity, add_reduction, add_emulation, add_identifiability, add_uq, add_set, add_combine and add_sweep make the step kinds. Their keyword arguments are the step's keys from The file; the options a kind takes in its settings are an argument of their own (sa_options=, ia_options=, uq_options=, emulator_settings=, and for a reduction method=, n_params=, ...). add_step(id, kind=..., **keys) takes any step as its raw keys. In all of them model defaults to the target. library_module(type, version, parameterisation), module_array(path, parameters=None), external_model(path), cellml_model(path, parameters=None), selection(*instances), fixed(step, parameters=), prior(step, kind=, inflate=, parameters=), set_value(parameter, value, reason=), scale_value(parameter, scale, of=, reason=) and set_theta(entry, theta, reason=) give a step's model, fixed values, priors and set entries. A step is checked against the schema when it is added.

Values set by hand go in a set step (add_set), not in a parameters dict: each carries its reason into the provenance.

docs.title: Your own operations
docs.text:
An obs_data item's operation can be a function defined in the script or in a notebook cell:

import numpy as np
from libcuflynx.param_id.operation_funcs import series_to_constant

@series_to_constant
def double_mean(x, series_output=False):
    if series_output:
        return 2 * x
    return 2 * np.mean(x)

wf.add_operation(double_mean)
wf.add_calibration('a-alone', model=module_array(f'{arrays}/a_only_module_array.json'),
                   obs_data=obs('y_a', 'A/y', 16.0, 0.16, operation='double_mean'),
                   params_for_id=[{'vessel_name': 'A', 'param_name': 'p', 'min': 0.1, 'max': 5}])
wf.run()                        # A/p = 2 still (2 * mean(2 p^2) = 16), and chain again after it

add_operation (and add_cost_func, add_modifier_func) copies the function's source into <name>_operation_funcs.py beside the workflow, with an import for each module it uses and a marker set on it after its def (f.series_to_constant = True) as its decorator. The workflow's operation_funcs_external_path names the file, so every rank, the command line and CUFLynx load it; it has the layout of CUFLynx's "Custom funcs" dialog (libcuflynx.utilities.user_funcs_file). wf.functions() lists what was added and wf.remove_operation(name) takes one out.

  • The file is imported on its own, so a function must carry what it needs. A lambda, a function using a variable of the function it is defined in, and one using a value or a function defined only in the session (in its body, a default value or an annotation) are refused: pass helper functions to add_operation too (a name starting with _ is not registered as an operation), and put values into the function.
