With do_param_reduction: true, run_sensitivity_analysis.sh follows the Sobol run with a reduction and writes the kept entries of your params_for_id file as reduced_params_for_id.json, ready to calibrate:

do_param_reduction: true
param_reduction_options:
  method: pca            # or sobol
  # n_params: 3          # pca: at most this many; sobol: needed
  # index_type: ST       # ST or S1
  # min_mode_std: 1.0    # pca; measured over the whole prior box (global, not local to the fit)
  # variance_fraction: 1.0  # pca; 1 = no relative cut
  # min_index: 0.05      # pca
  # redundancy_check: true  # pca
  # criterion: max       # sobol
  # threshold: 0.01      # sobol
  # sensitivity_dir: ... # default sa_options.output_dir
  # output_dir: ...      # default <sensitivity_dir>/param_reduction

method: pca (the default) asks in how many independent ways the parameters move the data by more than its noise, and keeps one parameter for each:

  1. Each output over the Sobol samples is centred and divided by its obs_data std over the square root of its weight, the scale the gaussian_MLE cost measures it on. A change of 1 is then one noise std.
  2. Principal component analysis of these scaled outputs gives modes: independent directions in which the parameters move the data, largest variance first. A mode whose std is at least min_mode_std (default 1, the noise) is informative; the others move the data by less than the noise and cannot be fitted. Only the leading modes that together explain variance_fraction of the variance are considered. The default, 1, is no relative cut. A smaller value ignores the noise: a mode that moves the data by several noise stds but has a small share of the variance can be dropped.
  3. Sobol indices are computed for each mode's score, from the same samples. A parameter whose largest index over the informative modes is below min_index is not a candidate.
  4. With redundancy_check: true (the default), the reduction asks which candidates move the data in different ways, using local derivatives (see "How the redundancy check works" below). Of the candidates whose effect is at least min_mode_std noise stds, it keeps the one with the highest Sobol index over the informative modes, removes that direction from the others' effects, and repeats, stopping when no effect left reaches min_mode_std: what such a parameter would add to the fit is inside the noise. Parameters that move the data the same way (only their product or ratio matters, or a scaling symmetry) have the same effect, so only one of them is kept, however many modes they drive: the one the Sobol indices rank highest. The local derivatives decide which parameters are redundant; the Sobol indices, which cover the whole prior box, decide which of them is kept.
  5. With redundancy_check: false it goes through the informative modes, largest first, and keeps the parameter, not kept already, with the largest index for that mode, skipping a mode that no free parameter reaches min_index for. This keeps at most one parameter per mode, so it reduces only when there are fewer informative modes than parameters. Outputs that are a time course (series binned into features, an oscillation) have many more modes than parameters, and it keeps them all.

Both stop after n_params. A parameter that drives an output strongly, but by less than that output's noise, is not kept.

docs.title: How the redundancy check works
docs.text:
Sobol indices say how much of a mode's variance each parameter drives, but not in which direction, so they cannot tell that two parameters are interchangeable: when only a * b matters, a and b get the same large index on the same modes. The check needs, for each parameter, the direction it moves the data in, and compares those.

The derivatives. Every Sobol run also takes local derivatives, set by sa_options:

key default what it sets jacobian_points 8 how many points; 0 skips the derivatives jacobian_location base_points base_points: the first jacobian_points Saltelli base points, the rows starting each block of 2M + 2 samples, which come from a Sobol sequence and so spread over the box; centre: one point at the centre of the box jacobian_scheme central central (2 runs per parameter and point) or forward (1, reusing the base point's own run) jacobian_step 0.01 the step in ln(parameter), or as a fraction of the range for bounds that straddle 0 jacobian_check_steps true also take them with half the step (twice the runs), for redundancy_converged_only

With the defaults a run costs 4 x jacobian_points x M extra simulations (central differences at two steps), about 2 x jacobian_points / num_samples of the Sobol run: 384 next to 6656 (5.8%) for 12 parameters and num_samples: 256. jacobian_check_steps: false halves that, and then a reduction needs redundancy_converged_only: false. Central differences are the default because a forward step's error is first order: in an oscillator a step shifts the phase, the error grows along the time course, and in the Goodwin benchmark it hid an exact symmetry. Each derivative is multiplied by the parameter's prior range (ln(max/min), or max - min for bounds that straddle 0), so it reads as how far the data would move if that slope held across the whole range. They are saved in all_outputs_n<N>_Sobol_local_jacobian.csv, one row per step, point and parameter.

The effects. At each point, each derivative is scaled to noise stds like the outputs in step 1 and projected onto the informative modes: a parameter's effect at that point, a vector with one entry per informative mode.

The choice. Pivoted Gram-Schmidt, done at each point separately and chosen jointly. For every parameter, take what is left of its effect at each point once the kept parameters' effects at that point are removed, and its root mean square length over the points. Keep the parameter with the largest, remove its direction at every point, and repeat until the largest is below min_mode_std. Because each point is explained by the kept parameters at that same point, the combination that reproduces a redundant parameter may change across the box, as it does for a scaling symmetry or for parameters entering as a sum. The report lists each parameter's effects (the statistic before anything is removed) and the unexplained_effects of those not kept (what was left).

Two param_reduction_options set how the points are combined:

  • redundancy_statistic: median (the default) keeps a parameter only if it is unexplained at most points, which ignores a minority of points where the derivatives are poor, and also a parameter that matters in less than half the box; rms keeps a parameter that is unexplained at any point, however few.
  • redundancy_converged_only (default true): leave out the points where the derivatives at jacobian_step and at half of it differ by more than redundancy_convergence_tol (default 0.1) of the effect. It needs the Sobol run's derivatives at both steps (jacobian_check_steps, on by default); a run without them is refused, naming redundancy_converged_only: false, which uses every point. The report lists the unconverged_points, and a warning says how many were left out.

The defaults (central differences of 0.01 and 0.005 at 8 base points, the median over the points whose derivatives agree at the two steps) come from benchmarks/param_reduction/compare_redundancy.py, which runs every setting on the FitzHugh-Nagumo, Goodwin and Teusink benchmarks and compares the kept count with the Fisher information at the truth (redundancy_comparison_results.md; the defaults are its K8_central_1e-2_checked rows, median_converged column). FitzHugh-Nagumo and Teusink give the same count under every setting: 5 for both, which is Teusink's Fisher count of 6 less one. On Goodwin the defaults keep 4 parameters, its Fisher count, leaving out 3 of the 8 points (the ai of the bullet below). The median over every point at this step keeps 5 (redundancy_converged_only: false), and so does rms at every step. The median at jacobian_step: 0.001 also keeps 4, but on a stiff model such as the 3-compartment test model solver noise (which grows as 1/step) leaves no point converged at that step; at 0.01 all 8 of its points converge. The centre point alone also gives 4 on Goodwin, but it misses a parameter that is flat at the centre. The cost of median is a parameter that matters in less than half the box: set redundancy_statistic: rms to keep such parameters.

Why local derivatives, at several points.

  • Products and ratios stay exact. If only a * b matters, a 1% step in a and a 1% step in b change the data identically at every point, so once a is kept nothing of b is left. Differences between Saltelli samples cannot do this: each pair of samples jumps by a different random amount, and on a curved response even jumps of the same size in ln(a) and ln(b) leave a remainder (about 20% of the effect, many noise stds, in a test of a * b).

  • A flat spot at one point is not mistaken for no effect. p^2 on [-1, 1] has slope 0 at the centre of its range, and a derivative there alone would drop it. Across 8 points its effect is many noise stds, and it is kept.

  • Points where the outputs are not smooth. In the Goodwin benchmark ai, Ai and ki form an exact scaling symmetry, so ai is explained by the other two at every point in exact arithmetic. At a step of 0.001 the derivatives show it at six of eight points (under 1 noise std left), but at the two where ai is small next to Ai they do not settle as the step shrinks, and leave tens of noise stds. The median outvotes those points and drops ai; rms over every point keeps it. At the default step of 0.01 the median over every point keeps ai too; leaving out the points that have not converged (redundancy_converged_only, the default) drops it.

Limits. The derivatives are local: a parameter whose effect lies wholly between the points, such as a sharp switch, can still be missed, and more jacobian_points make that less likely. A point where a run fails is left out, with a warning. jacobian_points: 0 skips the derivatives, and then a reduction needs redundancy_check: false.

method: sobol keeps the n_params parameters with the highest Sobol index over the outputs (the max or mean by criterion), dropping any below threshold. It ignores the noise and counts correlated outputs separately.

method: manual keeps the parameters named in parameters, a choice made by hand for the reason given (both required). It reads nothing of the Sobol run; it records the choice where the other methods record theirs. A parameter is named as its params_for_id entry is labelled (heart/E_lv_A; a grouped entry's names joined by +; a modifier's name).

Each writes param_reduction.json: the options and the kept parameters with their scores. For pca each kept parameter also has its mode, and the report lists every mode's std and variance share. pca_modes.csv holds each mode's loadings on the outputs, pca_mode_sobol_indices.csv the indices per mode (in the layout of the Sobol indices CSV), and pca_mode_sobol_ST.png a heatmap of them; with the redundancy check the report also has each parameter's effects and the unexplained_effects of those not kept. A pca reduction reads all_outputs_n<N>_Sobol_samples.csv, ..._outputs.csv, ..._local_jacobian.csv and sobol_problem.json, which every Sobol run writes.

A sample whose simulation fails cannot be left out (Saltelli's estimators need every row), so each output it lacks is filled with that output's mean over the samples that ran. The count is failed_samples in sobol_problem.json, with a warning: it shrinks the indices toward zero by about the failed fraction, so narrow the bounds if it is large. In a calibration workflow, a reduction step does the same (see calibration workflows).

docs.title: Deriving an observable from other observables
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis uses the same data_items as calibration, so a feature built from other features -- the difference between two observables, say -- is available here too, and is defined the same way. See Building an observable from other observables.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text: You should have Sobol index plots saved to sa_options.output_dir.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• If you see errors about params_for_id_path, confirm your params_for_id.json filename and resources_dir.
  • If MPI errors occur, ensure mpiexec is available and mpi4py is installed in the environment you are running from — it is the [mpi] extra, not part of a plain pip install libcuflynx.

docs.title: Following a run: progress files
docs.text:
A Sobol analysis, an emulator training and a profile likelihood each write progress.json into the directory their results go to (the sa_options output_dir, the emulator's directory, profile_likelihood/; in a calibration workflow, the step's own folders). MPI rank 0 rewrites it while the run goes, at most about once a second, through a rename, so a reader never sees half a file. CUFLynx reads the same file; nothing in it depends on how the run was started.

{"schema_version": 1, "kind": "sobol", "state": "running",
 "started": "2026-11-23T02:10:00+00:00", "updated": "2026-11-23T02:10:41+00:00",
 "phases": [{"name": "sampling", "state": "running", "done": 1200, "total": 4608, "failed": 3}]}
  • kind is sobol, emulation or profile_likelihood.
  • state is running, then done once the result files are written, or failed if the run raised an error. A run that was killed stays running: compare updated with the clock.
  • Each phase counts done of total items, with those that failed among the done, and has its own state (queued, running, done, failed). A phase is added when its size is known, so later phases can be missing while an earlier one runs.
Kind Phases sobol sampling (the model runs of the design), local_jacobian (the runs for a PCA reduction's redundancy check, when there are any), analysis emulation one sampling phase per design stage, with stage and method (the training simulations), then training, whose models list each emulator compared: name, state, score (its held-out value of the phase's metric) and duration_s profile_likelihood one phase per calibrated entry, named by its label, with param_index: the points evaluated of num_points; a failed point is one whose re-calibration gave no finite cost

The file's definition is libcuflynx/schemas/progress.schema.json (libcuflynx.schemas.PROGRESS_SCHEMA); the writer is libcuflynx.utilities.progress. A phase may gain keys: ignore those you do not know.

A Sobol run also writes, in the same directory:

  • sobol_design.npy: the design (samples by parameters) in run order, before the first simulation, and sobol_design_params.json with its columns (names, bounds, num_samples, sample_type, rows).
  • sobol_sample_status.npy: one int8 per design row, 0 not run, 1 ran, 2 failed (an output that is not finite), rewritten as the ranks report and kept after the run. Failed samples are filled with each output's mean before the indices are computed, so the outputs CSV does not show which they were; this file does.
  • sobol_convergence.json, at the end: S1 and ST with their confidence half-widths at num_samples / 8, / 4, / 2 and num_samples base samples (from 4 up), each the analysis the run would have given had it stopped there: {"n": [32, 64, 128, 256], "outputs": {output: {"S1": {parameter: [[value, conf], ...]}, "ST": {...}}}}, one [value, conf] per entry of n; a value that is not finite is null.

docs.title: Surrogates
docs.text:
A surrogate is a cheaper stand-in for a model, built from runs of that model. Use one when an analysis needs many more model evaluations than you can afford: a Sobol design, MCMC, or a calibration of a slow solver.

Circulatory Autogen has two kinds. They differ in what they stand in for.

Emulator Reduced-order model (ROM) Stands in for the map from the calibrated parameters to the scalar features of the obs_data the model: it is integrated in time and returns traces Gives one number per data item, after its operation the outputs over time, for any protocol the ROM covers Built by do_emulation, cuflynx-train-emulator, or a workflow emulation step you, outside CA Used by use_emulator, or a workflow step's emulator_from / emulator_dir running it as the model: model_type: external_python Series data, prediction traces, plots refused available, as for any model
  • Emulators: training, the settings, when CA refuses one, and gradients.
  • Reduced-order models (ROMs): how a ROM runs as a model.

The settings keep the name of the kind they configure: do_emulation, use_emulator, emulator_settings, emulator_from and emulator_dir are an emulator's. A ROM has no settings of its own, because CA runs it as a model.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
This section documents the Python API for driving Circulatory Autogen programmatically, and by external tools such as the CUFLynx GUI. The interactive tutorials use it: generation_and_calibration.ipynb generates and simulates a model with these calls, then calibrates it as a calibration workflow built with WorkflowBuilder (libcuflynx.calibration_workflow), and workflow_quickstart.ipynb shows every WorkflowBuilder call on a small model. A workflow is a file, so the notebooks, the cuflynx-calibration-workflow command and CUFLynx's Workflow tab run the same study; see Building a workflow in Python.

The reference pages are generated automatically from the docstrings in src/libcuflynx/, so they stay in sync with the code.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The repository is circulatory_autogen; the installable package is libcuflynx. Install it and import from the libcuflynx namespace — there is no import path to set up, and no checkout is required.

pip install libcuflynx

from libcuflynx.utilities.utility_funcs import get_default_inp_data_dict

The old flat imports were removed in 0.6.0

from param_id.paramID import CVS0DParamID (no libcuflynx. prefix) resolved in 0.4.0 and 0.5.x as a shim that warned. In 0.6.0 it raises ModuleNotFoundError; prefix the import with libcuflynx.. See CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Public API at a glance
docs.text:
The entry points below cover the full generate → simulate → calibrate → analyse pipeline. Each links to its detailed reference page.

Task Entry point Page Build the config dict get_default_inp_data_dict Utilities Generate a model generate_with_new_architecture Model generation Run a simulation get_simulation_helper / get_simulation_helper_from_inp_data_dict Simulation Build observation data ObsDataCreator Observation data & utilities Calibrate parameters CVS0DParamID Parameter identification Build and run a calibration workflow WorkflowBuilder / run_calibration_workflow Calibration workflows Sensitivity analysis SensitivityAnalysis Sensitivity analysis Identifiability analysis IdentifiabilityAnalysis Identifiability analysis Run protocols standalone ProtocolRunner Protocols

docs.title: Typical call sequence
docs.text:
from libcuflynx.utilities.utility_funcs import get_default_inp_data_dict
from libcuflynx.scripts.script_generate_with_new_architecture import generate_with_new_architecture
from libcuflynx.solver_wrappers import get_simulation_helper_from_inp_data_dict
from libcuflynx.utilities.obs_data_helpers import ObsDataCreator
from libcuflynx.param_id.paramID import CVS0DParamID

# 1. Configuration (the library's defaults, then mutate in code)
inp = get_default_inp_data_dict(file_prefix, input_param_file, resources_dir)
inp["sim_time"], inp["pre_time"] = 2, 20.0

# 2. Generate the model
generate_with_new_architecture(inp_data_dict=inp)

# 3. Simulate
sim = get_simulation_helper_from_inp_data_dict(inp)
sim.run()
t, y = sim.get_time(), sim.get_results(variables_to_plot, flatten=True)

# 4. Build observation data
obs = ObsDataCreator()
obs.add_protocol_info(pre_times, sim_times, params_to_change)
obs.add_data_item(entry)
obs_data_dict = obs.get_obs_data_dict()

# 5. Calibrate
pid = CVS0DParamID.init_from_dict(inp)
pid.set_ground_truth_data(obs_data_dict)
pid.set_params_for_id(params_for_id_dict)
pid.run()
pid.simulate_with_best_param_vals()
pid.plot_outputs()

resources_dir is a directory of your own holding the model's inputs: {file_prefix}_module_array.csv (or .json) and the parameters file input_param_file ({file_prefix}_parameters.json). The package installs no example models: copy one from the repository's resources/ directory (for example 3compartment_module_array.csv, 3compartment_parameters.json, 3compartment_obs_data.json and 3compartment_params_for_id.json), or write your own (see Designing a model). Generated models and results go under the current directory unless generated_models_dir and param_id_output_dir say otherwise. get_default_inp_data_dict fills in the library's defaults, which are not the values of the repository's user_run_files/user_inputs.yaml (for example solver_info.MaximumStep and optimiser_options).

params_for_id_dict is the content of a {prefix}_params_for_id.json file: the whole {"version": 1, "params": [...]} document, or its list of entries ({"targets": ["aortic_root/C"], "min": ..., "max": ..., "name_for_plotting": ...}). A list of {vessel_name, param_name, min, max, name_for_plotting} entries is read too; there vessel_name may be a single name or a list to share one calibrated parameter across many vessels.

docs.title: Calibration workflows
docs.text: A calibration workflow is an ordered set of steps (calibrations, and the analyses around them) whose results are merged into one target model; see Calibration workflows for the how-to. WorkflowBuilder makes a workflow with API calls and runs it; the functions below it run, plan and read a workflow file however it was written.

add_calibration(
    id,
    *,
    obs_data,
    params_for_id=None,
    params_for_id_from=None,
    model=None,
    fixed_from=(),
    priors_from=(),
    store_distribution=False,
    start_from=None,
    emulator_from=None,
    emulator_dir=None,
    module=None,
    submodule=None,
    module_map=None,
    settings=None,
    description=None,
    comment=None
)

Add a calibration: fit parameters of a model to an obs_data.

Nothing is written or run by this call; the step is checked against the schema, and the dicts given are copied. A step with this id already is replaced in place, so to change a step, change what you pass and call this again.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default id

the step's name: other steps refer to it and its results go to <output_dir>/<id>/. No / or \; at most 80 characters; unlike every other id whatever the case.

required obs_data

what to fit: a path to an obs_data JSON file, an obs_data dict, or an ObsDataCreator. A dict is written to data/<id>_obs_data.json by :meth:write.

required params_for_id

what to calibrate: a path to a params_for_id JSON file, a list of {vessel_name, param_name, min, max} entries (as CVS0DParamID takes), a list of {targets, min, max} entries, or a {"version", "params"} document. Not a path: written to data/<id>_params_for_id.json.

None params_for_id_from

instead of params_for_id, the reduction step (:meth:add_reduction) whose chosen parameters are calibrated.

None model

the model the step runs on: a module array path, :func:module_array, :func:library_module or :func:selection. Default: the target.

None fixed_from

calibration or set step ids, or :func:fixed entries for only some of a step's values (one, or a list), whose values are fixed in this step's model; this step runs after them.

() priors_from

step ids or :func:prior entries whose stored distributions become this step's priors (those steps set store_distribution).

() store_distribution

after the fit, sample the posterior by MCMC (needs the UQ_options setting) and store it for later steps.

False start_from

a calibration or set step at whose values this step's own parameters start.

None emulator_from

an emulation step (:meth:add_emulation) whose emulator this step is evaluated on; give the same model, obs_data and params_for_id. With params_for_id_from a reduction of that emulator's params_for_id, the step calibrates the parameters the reduction kept and holds the emulator's others at their values in the emulation step's model.

None emulator_dir

instead of emulator_from, the directory of an emulator trained outside the workflow.

None module

for a library module in a module-array target, the module it is (inferred when the module occurs once).

None submodule

for a library module in a library supermodule target, where it sits (inferred when the module occurs once).

None module_map

for a module-array model, {its module name: the target's}.

None settings

this step's settings, merged over the workflow's one dict level deep.

None description

free text, shown in reports.

None comment

free text, kept in the file.

None

Returns:

Type Description

id.

Raises:

Type Description WorkflowError

the step does not fit the schema (the message names the key).

docs.text:
add_reduction(
    id,
    *,
    sensitivity_from=None,
    param_reduction_options=None,
    params_for_id=None,
    method=None,
    n_params=None,
    parameters=None,
    reason=None,
    index_type=None,
    criterion=None,
    threshold=None,
    min_mode_std=None,
    variance_fraction=None,
    min_index=None,
    redundancy_check=None,
    redundancy_statistic=None,
    redundancy_converged_only=None,
    redundancy_convergence_tol=None,
    description=None,
    comment=None
)

Add a reduction: choose the parameters a later step calibrates (its params_for_id_from) from the Sobol indices of a sensitivity step, or by hand (method='manual').

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default id

the step's name (see :meth:add_calibration).

required sensitivity_from

the sensitivity step whose results are reduced (not for 'manual').

None param_reduction_options

the reduction's options (the schema's param_reduction_options), written as the step's settings.param_reduction_options; a key left out takes the schema's default, and method is 'pca' unless given:

  • method: 'pca' (one parameter per informative mode of the Sobol outputs), 'sobol' (the n_params parameters with the highest index) or 'manual' (the parameters named, chosen by hand);
  • parameters: manual: the parameters to keep, each named as its params_for_id entry is labelled ('heart/E_lv_A');
  • reason: manual: why these parameters were chosen;
  • n_params: how many parameters to keep (pca: at most; sobol: required);
  • index_type: 'ST' (total, the default) or 'S1' (first-order);
  • criterion: sobol: a parameter's score, the 'max' or 'mean' of its index;
  • threshold: sobol: drop parameters scoring below this;
  • min_mode_std: pca: a mode is informative when its std over the samples is at least this many obs_data stds (default 1);
  • variance_fraction: pca: only the leading modes explaining this fraction of the variance (default 1, no cut);
  • min_index: pca: skip a mode whose largest index is below this (default 0.05);
  • redundancy_check: the check for parameters with the same effect on the outputs;
  • redundancy_statistic: pca with redundancy_check: 'median' (default) or 'rms' of a parameter's unexplained effect over the local Jacobian points;
  • redundancy_converged_only: pca with redundancy_check: leave out the points whose derivatives change with the step (needs sa_options.jacobian_check_steps);
  • redundancy_convergence_tol: the largest relative change between the two steps (default 0.1).
None params_for_id

manual: the params_for_id whose entries, with their ranges, are kept (what :meth:add_calibration takes).

None description, comment

free text.

required

Returns id.

Raises:

Type Description WorkflowError

an option is given both ways with different values, or the step does not fit the schema.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run(
    *,
    only=None,
    from_step=None,
    force=False,
    output_dir=None,
    dry_run=False,
    write_calibrated=False,
    ranks=1,
    progress=None,
    verbose=False
)

Check and write the workflow (:meth:check, :meth:write), then run it.

Without only and from_step, the steps that are done and current are kept (one line is printed for each) and only those that have not run, or are stale, are run: running the same cell or script again repeats no calibration. A step is stale when its obs_data, params_for_id, parameters, settings or functions file changed since it ran, or a step it takes values from is stale or ran again (:meth:status).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default only

run just this step, reusing the results it depends on (which must be current).

None from_step

run this step and every step after it, whether or not they are current.

None force

run every step again, current or not.

False output_dir

where the run goes. Default :attr:output_dir.

None dry_run

run nothing; return the plan (as :meth:plan).

False write_calibrated

also write the merged values beside the target's parameters file, as <name>_calibrated_parameters.json (complete runs only).

False ranks

the number of MPI ranks. More than one runs mpiexec -n <ranks> python -m libcuflynx.scripts.calibration_workflow_run_script on the written file.

1 progress

callable(event) called for each step event (one rank only). Default: print one [workflow] line per event. False: print no such line.

None verbose

also print everything the steps write (the optimiser's iterations, compiler output, warnings) as it comes. By default only the [workflow] lines are printed; the rest is in the log files either way.

False

Returns:

Type Description

the workflow result, also written as <output_dir>/workflow_result.json:

{'workflow_name', 'complete', 'order', 'steps', 'merged_parameters', ...}.

With dry_run, the plan.

The run writes <output_dir>/<step id>/ for each step (step_result.json, the generated model, the calibration's outputs), workflow_result.json, the provenance graph and _target/, the target generated with every merged value.

Everything the run writes to the terminal is kept: a step's output in <output_dir>/<step id>/log.txt (<output_dir>/step_log.<step id>.txt while the step runs), and what is written outside the steps, with every [workflow] line, in <output_dir>/workflow_log.txt. Each run replaces the logs of the steps it runs.

Raises:

Type Description WorkflowError

the workflow cannot run (see :meth:check), a result only needs is missing or stale, or the launched command failed.

workflow_model(
    source,
    view,
    *,
    output_dir,
    work_dir,
    module_library_dirs=None,
    with_own_results=True,
    validate=True
)

Generate the model one tab of a workflow shows, from whatever results exist so far.

view is a step id, or 'target' for the workflow's target. A step's model gets the values its fixed_from and result_from steps calibrated (those that have run into output_dir) and, with with_own_results, its own calibrated values once it has run. The target gets every calibrated value there is, mapped into its naming. Nothing is calibrated, and nothing in output_dir is written but the model, under work_dir (which may be <output_dir>/models, :data:MODELS_DIR, a folder no step's output can have).

validate=False skips the trial run generation ends with (a Myokit compile, about half the time of a view), for a caller that compiles or runs the model itself straight after. A model with parameters left unset is still refused.

Returns {view, kind ('step' or 'target'), target, submodule_path, model_path, flat_model_path (one self-contained CellML file), parameters_path, obs_data_path, params_for_id_path, fixed, calibrated, waiting_for, stale, result, param_id_output_dir}. fixed lists the values given by earlier steps, but not result_from's values of the parameters the step analyses; calibrated the view's own (for the target, the merged set: each value from the last step that set it, with origin and reason when it was set by hand); waiting_for the steps whose results it should have but that have not run; stale those whose inputs changed since they ran. obs_data / params_for_id are None when the parameterisation has none (a target with no step of its own). For the target, step_id, its obs_data, params_for_id, result and param_id_output_dir are those of the last calibration on the target that has run, or of the last one when none has.

docs.title: libcuflynx.utilities.user_funcs_file
docs.text:
The files of user functions -- operations, cost functions, modifiers -- that the operation_funcs_external_path, cost_funcs_external_path and modifier_funcs_external_path settings name.

One layout for every writer (CUFLynx's "Custom funcs" dialog, and calibration_workflow.WorkflowBuilder.add_operation), so either can read and rewrite what the other wrote::

"""<the kind's header docstring>"""
import numpy as np
from libcuflynx... import <the kind's decorators>
mb = make_math_backend("numpy")         (operations and cost functions)
# libcuflynx-generated sha256: <hex>     (the checksum of the rest of the file)

import scipy.signal as signal           (the imports the functions use, if any)

CUFLYNX_OPERATIONS = ["peak_count", "half_mean"]     (the functions, in order)


@series_to_constant
def half_mean(x, series_output=False):
    ...

The decorators are imported, never defined, so libcuflynx registers only the functions below them (param_id.external_funcs.register_funcs_from_file keeps the callables whose module is the file). :func:read_funcs_file reads such a file back: its functions (each with its decorators) in order, and the imports beyond the header's.

The checksum line is a comment, so Python and any reader of the functions ignore it. It is the sha256 of the file without that line: while it matches (:func:is_unedited), the file is exactly what a writer generated and can be generated again without losing anything. A file holds only the header, imports and functions: :func:unkept_statements lists what a rewrite would drop (constants, classes), so a writer can refuse instead.

docs.title: Emulators
docs.text:
EmulatorTrainer fits a surrogate of the model's scalar observable features, and EmulatorBundle is the saved artefact plus the checks that decide whether it may be used. See Emulators for the workflow, and Surrogates for the other kind of surrogate, a reduced-order model.

The emulator is used through the ordinary simulation-helper interface, so every analysis reaches it the same way it reaches a solver.

docs.title: libcuflynx.emulators.emulator_trainer.EmulatorTrainer
docs.text:
EmulatorTrainer(param_id, emulator_settings, comm=None)

Design -> simulate -> fit -> validate -> persist, for one param-id engine.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default param_id

an ParamID built against the truth solver. Passing one whose sim helper is itself an emulator is rejected: it would fit a surrogate of a surrogate.

required emulator_settings

the emulator_settings block (see ANALYSIS_OPTIONS).

required comm

an MPI communicator; None means "discover one, or run serially".

None

There is deliberately no DEBUG shrinking here, unlike the optimiser and MCMC options. num_train_samples is the one setting that decides whether the emulator is any good, and quietly cutting it would produce an emulator that answers everything and is wrong -- the failure mode this whole feature is built to prevent. A cheap run asks for it by name.

Build the truth-solver engine this config describes, then a trainer over it.

docs.title: design
docs.text:
design(n_samples=None, sample_type=None, seed_offset=0)

Training points over the params_for_id box, shape (n_samples, num_params).

Deterministic given the seed, so every rank builds the identical design and no broadcast is needed to agree on who evaluates which sample. seed_offset separates one stage from the next: two stages of the same method on the same seed would otherwise draw the same points twice.

docs.title: evaluate
docs.text:
evaluate(design, phase=None)

Run the truth model at every design point; returns (x, y) on rank 0.

Contiguous block split across ranks then a gather, the same shape as the Sobol sampler's parallel loop. A sample whose simulation fails is dropped rather than imputed: an imputed training target is a fabricated observation, and the emulator would learn it as fact. phase is the key of the progress phase the points count towards (in a train()); None reports nothing.

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(x, y, space_filling=None)

Fit and compare emulators; returns (model, r2, rmse, name, x_scale, y_scale).

Both x and y are mapped onto a well-conditioned range first. CA parameters routinely span a compliance near 1e-9 and a resistance near 1e8, and autoemulate works in float32 torch, where that spread alone is enough to ruin a kernel fit.

A test split is held out here, before fitting, and the reported R2/RMSE are scored on it. Scoring on the training points instead would report a number that says how well the emulator memorised the design, which is precisely the reassurance a bad emulator would give.

docs.title: train
docs.text:
train()

The whole pipeline. Returns the bundle on rank 0, None elsewhere.

With reuse_samples set, the design and the simulations are skipped entirely and the samples a previous run saved are fitted instead -- see :meth:load_previous_samples. The rest of the path (fit, metadata, bundle, save) is the same one a fresh run takes, so the artefact is not a lesser kind of emulator.

Rank 0 writes the run's progress.json (libcuflynx.utilities.progress, kind emulation) into the emulator's directory: a sampling phase per design stage (stage, method; the training simulations done, and failed among them) and a training phase listing the models compared (ModelProgress).

docs.title: check_quality
docs.text:
check_quality(min_r2, labels=None)

Refuse an emulator whose worst held-out R2 is below min_r2.

Named per feature, because "the emulator is bad" is not actionable while "max of aortic_root/u has R2 0.42" tells the user which observable to add samples for.

labels limits the check to the features a run actually reads; by default the data_item features. A calibration reads only those, so a poorly emulated prediction feature does not stop it; a sensitivity analysis that includes prediction features checks them by passing their labels.

docs.text:
make_scale(values)

Shift/span for an affine map onto a well-conditioned range.

A span of zero (a constant column -- a parameter pinned to one value, or a feature the model does not respond to) would divide by zero, so it becomes 1: the column maps to a constant, which is exactly what it is.

docs.title: libcuflynx.emulators.emulator_bundle.fingerprint
docs.text:
fingerprint(
    param_id_info,
    obs_info,
    protocol_info,
    model_path=None,
    prediction_info=None,
    prediction_indices=None,
)

A stable digest of everything an emulator was trained against.

Changing a parameter's bounds, adding a data_item, editing an operation, moving a sub-experiment or regenerating the model all change what theta -> features means. None of those changes make the old emulator raise on its own -- it would keep answering, about a different model. Comparing this digest is what turns that into an error.

model_path is hashed by content when it exists, so a regenerated CellML invalidates the emulator even if the inputs that produced it are unchanged. model_content_sha256 (:func:model_content_digest) is the hash check_matches compares; model_sha256, the model file's bytes alone, is what it compares for a bundle stored without the other.

prediction_info with prediction_indices (the prediction items an emulator trained with include_prediction_items predicts) adds a separate prediction_sha256. Separate so inputs_sha256 is unchanged by it: a calibration, which uses the data_item features only, computes no prediction_sha256 and so is not refused for an edited prediction item (check_matches compares the keys the live fingerprint has).

docs.title: set_theta
docs.text:
set_theta(theta)

Set the calibration vector directly, in params_for_id entry order.

This, not set_param_vals, is the emulator's real input. A modifier entry occupies one slot in theta but names several model parameters, and by the time the executor calls set_param_vals those slots have already been expanded to per-parameter values -- which is the wrong thing to feed a surrogate trained on theta. CA's call sites set theta here before the protocol runs, so no inversion is ever needed.

docs.title: set_param_vals
docs.text:
set_param_vals(param_names, param_vals, change_states=True)

Accept the executor's per-parameter values.

With no modifiers in play these are theta itself, entry for entry, so they are recorded as such and the helper works for a caller that only knows the ordinary interface. With modifiers they are the expanded per-target values, which theta cannot be recovered from here -- set_theta must have been called, and this is then a consistency check.

Each operand slot holds a length-1 array carrying its data_item's predicted feature. The consumers that know about emulates_features read the value and skip the operation; anything else applying mean/max/min to it gets the same number back, which is the least surprising thing an unaware caller could receive.

The emulator's outputs are ordered by obs_info['const_idx_to_obs_idx'] while the consumers index by data_item. The protocol executor concatenates each sub-experiment's tSim onto a cumulative time vector and drops the duplicated first sample, so a missing or single-point axis would break the caller rather than the emulator. Mirrors the libOpenCOR backend.

docs.title: run_laplace_approximation
docs.text:
run_laplace_approximation(ia_options)

Run the Laplace approximation around the best fit.

Forms the precision (negative log-likelihood Hessian) via ia_options['gradient_source'] -- 'AD'/'FSA' build the Fisher information matrix from the analytic observable sensitivities, 'FD' (default) uses the finite-difference sub_method -- and inverts it (in Jacobi-normalised space, see _invert_precision_normalised) to the parameter covariance, saving {prefix}_laplace_mean.npy and {prefix}_laplace_covariance.npy.

The normalisation makes wide-magnitude models (e.g. 3compartment, params ~1e-9..1e8) succeed with a real covariance where the raw inverse used to give meaningless, massively inflated uncertainties. Raises RuntimeError only when the normalised precision is still ill-conditioned (jointly non-identifiable parameters) or a parameter has literally zero curvature (no information). A mildly indefinite finite-difference Hessian -- a small negative curvature from FD/optimiser noise at a rough optimum -- still yields a finite covariance (with a logged warning), as the plain inverse always did (issue #293).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ia_options

Options dict; gradient_source ('FD'|'AD'|'FSA', default 'FD') and, for 'FD', sub_method (default 'parabola_fit').

required

ProtocolExecutor(sim_helper)

docs.title: run_protocol
docs.text:
run_protocol(
    protocol_info,
    id_param_names=None,
    id_param_vals=None,
    result_variables=None,
    extra_result_variables=None,
    exp_indices=None,
    continue_on_failure=False,
    reset_after_experiment=True,
)

Run the multi-experiment / multi-subexperiment protocol loop.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: protocol_info : dict Must contain: - 'sim_times' list[list[float]] — sim duration per (exp, sub) - 'pre_times' list[float] — pre-simulation time per exp - 'params_to_change' dict — {param_name: [[val_exp0_sub0, ...], ...]} May also contain pre-computed keys added by process_protocol_and_weights: - 'num_experiments' int - 'num_sub_per_exp' list[int] Both are derived from sim_times when absent. id_param_names : list, optional Parameter names set once before each experiment (e.g. ID candidates). id_param_vals : list, optional Values matching id_param_names. result_variables : list, optional Variables to retrieve per sub-experiment via get_results(). None → collect all variables via get_all_results(flatten=True). extra_result_variables : list, optional A second variable set collected in the same pass (e.g. pred_names). exp_indices : iterable, optional Only run these experiment indices. Other slots in the output will be absent from results_by_sub / extra_by_sub, and None in t_by_exp. continue_on_failure : bool, default False If True, record None for failed sub-experiments and continue rather than returning early. If False (default), return immediately on the first simulation failure. reset_after_experiment : bool, default True If True (default), call sim_helper.reset_and_clear() after the final sub-experiment of each experiment. Pass False for AD (automatic differentiation) mode where the solver state must be preserved across experiments.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: success : bool False only when a simulation failed AND continue_on_failure is False. results_by_sub : dict Mapping (exp_idx, sub_idx) → result of get_results() or get_all_results(flatten=True). None for failed sub-experiments when continue_on_failure is True. extra_by_sub : dict Same structure for extra_result_variables. Empty dict when extra_result_variables is None. t_by_exp : list[np.ndarray | None] Concatenated, pre_time-shifted time vector per experiment index. None for skipped or failed experiments.

docs.title: set_joint_priors
docs.text:
set_joint_priors(joint_priors)

Add log densities over several parameters to the log prior.

joint_priors is a list of (names, logpdf): names are generated-model parameter names (param_names_for_gen, e.g. g_leak_mod_i_leak_Na), one per calibrated parameter the density is over, and logpdf(values) takes those parameters' values, in that order, and returns a log density (-inf outside its support). It is added to the per-parameter priors, whose bounds checks still apply -- so a parameter with a joint prior is usually given a uniform row in params_for_id.

Used by calibration workflows to make an earlier step's stored posterior the prior of a later one (libcuflynx.calibration_workflow). Like every prior, it only affects the log posterior: MCMC, and optimisers run with objective_function 'likelihood'.

docs.title: get_lnlikelihood_lnprior_from_ensemble
docs.text:
get_lnlikelihood_lnprior_from_ensemble(ensemble)

Log-posterior for a whole ensemble, predicting the surrogate once for all of it.

The saving is entirely in the emulator call. Evaluating a fitted regressor at sixty-four points costs barely more than at one -- 84.8 ms against 355 ms on the study this was written for, 15x less per point -- because the per-call overhead dominates the arithmetic. An ensemble sampler asks for its whole population at every step, so it is exactly the caller that can pay that overhead once.

Everything after the prediction is unchanged and still per-walker: the protocol loop, the cost reduction, the priors. Only the surrogate is batched, which is the part that was expensive.

Walkers whose prior is not finite are dropped before the prediction rather than after. They contribute nothing but would still cost a row in the batch, and an out-of-bounds row is exactly what out_of_bounds='error' refuses -- so predicting them would turn a walker that is merely being rejected into a failed run.

docs.title: accumulating_temp_results
docs.text:
accumulating_temp_results()

One temp_results table across every segment of a single cost evaluation (#466).

Only the cost loop wants that. Every other caller evaluates one segment on its own -- CUFLynx's obs_cost, plot_outputs, the gradient backends, a test double -- and must not resolve a reference against values left behind by whatever ran before it. evaluating_segment gives those callers a fresh table, and this is how it knows not to.

docs.title: obs_output_dicts_per_segment
docs.text:
obs_output_dicts_per_segment(
    operands_outputs_list, get_all_series=False
)

get_obs_output_dict for every segment, in order, with one temp_results table.

operands_outputs_list is indexed like get_cost_and_obs_from_params's operands (flat over experiments, then sub-experiments). Each item's value is right in its own segment's dict, including an item that references an item in an earlier segment, as in the cost. Returns a list of dicts (with get_all_series, a list of (dict, all_series)); a segment with no operands gives None ((None, None)).

docs.title: evaluating_segment
docs.text:
evaluating_segment(exp_idx, sub_idx)

Mark which (experiment, sub-experiment)'s operands the next evaluations receive.

Carried as state rather than passed to get_obs_output_dict, so that method keeps the signature every other caller already uses -- the gradient backends, plot_outputs, CUFLynx, and any test double that stands in for it. Adding parameters to it broke all of those for no gain.

Inside the block an item is only evaluated and recorded when the segment is its own, and temp_results is left alone so the caller can accumulate one table across the whole protocol. Outside it -- the default -- every item is evaluated against whatever operands are handed over and the table is cleared per call, which is the pre-#466 behaviour.

docs.title: get_obs_output_dict
docs.text:
get_obs_output_dict(
    operands_outputs,
    get_all_series=False,
    is_symbolic=False,
)

Evaluate every data_item's operation against one sub-experiment's operands.

    ``temp_results`` is the table an ``operation_kwargs`` reference to another item resolves
    against. It used to be cleared on every call, i.e. once per (experiment, sub-experiment),
    which is why a reference could only ever see the segment being evaluated (#466, #127).
    Two arguments change that:

A caller that steps through the segments in order does so inside evaluating_segment, which says which segment these operands belong to and leaves the table alone so it accumulates across all of them.

    Knowing the segment matters because every data_item is evaluated against every one of
    them -- which item *counts* is decided afterwards by the zeroed weight vectors. Without
    it an item would be recorded under its name from some other experiment's trace, and a
    cross-segment reference would silently read that.

docs.title: get_observable_sensitivities
docs.text:
get_observable_sensitivities(
    param_vals, gradient_method=None, fd_rel_step=None
)

d(observable feature)/d(param) for the scalar observables -- the backend-agnostic local-sensitivity accessor, parallel to get_gradient.

Returns {observable_label: {param_name: d(feature)/d(param)}}, dispatching by model_type to the same analytic machinery the cost gradient uses: the CasADi jacobian of the observable vector, or the Myokit CVODES sensitivities with a directional derivative of the feature. Every arm reports the identical quantity, so a local sensitivity analysis is comparable across backends whichever computed it.

gradient_method selects how, in the same FD/AD/FSA vocabulary as gradient_sources() and the Laplace gradient_source -- the arm's own name, so a front-end can offer it, disable it, and report back which one ran:

  • None / 'auto' (default) -- the analytic arm for this backend, raising when there is none. Deliberately still not a silent fall back to FD: a result quietly computed a different way, at a different cost and accuracy, is not the same result.
  • 'AD' -- the exact CasADi jacobian; requires model_type='casadi_python' (aadc_python names its arm AD too, but its local SA is not implemented yet and says so). Any other backend raises naming the mismatch rather than silently reinterpreting.
  • 'FSA' -- Myokit CVODES forward sensitivities; requires cellml + CVODE_myokit + do_ad. Raises naming exactly what is missing otherwise.
  • 'FD' -- central finite differences (param_id.fd_backend). Works on any backend that runs a forward simulation, which is how AADC and the plain scipy backend get a local SA at all (issue #338). Costs 2M simulations for M parameters.

fd_rel_step is the FD step, relative to each parameter, and is ignored by the analytic arms. It matters more than it looks: on Lotka-Volterra, moving it from 1e-3 to 1e-2 changes a sensitivity coefficient by up to 48%, because max of an oscillating trace is a rough functional. So it is the caller's to choose, not a constant buried in the backend -- the same reason the prior hyper-parameters stopped being hardcoded.

docs.title: get_cost_and_gradient
docs.text:
get_cost_and_gradient(param_vals)

Return (cost, gradient) in one evaluation.

L-BFGS-B needs both J(p) and ∇J(p) at every point it visits. For the Myokit CVODES FSA path a single augmented solve yields both, so this avoids the separate cost solve the optimiser would otherwise do. Other backends fall back to separate calls (CasADi's reverse pass and the AADC tape are cheap, so there is little to merge there).

docs.title: get_cost_aadc
docs.text:
get_cost_aadc(param_vals)

J(p) evaluated on the AADC tape.

This must be the cost an AADC-gradient optimiser minimises. The forward solver and the tape do not integrate the same way -- the tape has to replay a fixed sequence of operations, so it uses a fixed-step scheme, while sim_helper.run() may use an adaptive one -- and the tape's cost is a separate implementation of the cost function. Taking J(p) from get_cost_from_params and dJ/dp from the tape therefore hands L-BFGS-B the gradient of a different function than the one it is minimising, which breaks the line search. Measured on Lotka-Volterra, that mismatch gave AD/FD ratios of [1.79, 1.96, 1.32, -0.067] -- the last one has the wrong sign.

docs.title: TODO check the parallelisation for this mcmc
from_param_id classmethod
docs.text:
from_param_id(engine, UQ_options=None)

Adopt an already-built ParamID instead of constructing a second one.

Building an engine compiles the model. Because mcmc_instead selects the inner class at construction time, a UQ run following a calibration had to build a second CVS0DParamID and pay that compile again (CUFLynx #217) -- for the same model, the same obs_info and the same parameters.

MCMC only adds to ParamID, so the built engine's state is exactly what it needs: adopt its __dict__ (simulation helper, parsed infos, output_dir, and the best_param_vals of the calibration that just ran, which is what seeds the walkers) and then run only the MCMC-specific tail.

The result shares the engine's simulation helper rather than copying it -- that is the point -- which is safe because UQ follows a calibration rather than running beside it. Do not use the engine concurrently afterwards.

docs.title: calibration_weighting
docs.text:
calibration_weighting()

Evaluate costs inside this block with the obs_data weights, not the flat ones.

The flattening exists for the likelihood being sampled: a weighted likelihood is not a posterior (#193). It must not follow the cost out into the artifacts, because best_cost is a calibration artifact -- plot_param_id and simulate_once re-derive it and compare against the saved value, and the calibration itself optimised the weighted cost. A best_cost written on the flat scale is simply a different quantity under the same name, and the two disagree by whatever the weights were (measured on 3compartment: 0.0377 saved against 0.1058 recomputed, which tripped simulate_once's consistency check).

docs.title: can_vectorise_the_ensemble
docs.text:
can_vectorise_the_ensemble()

Whether the whole walker population can be evaluated in one call.

Two conditions, and both are about what the likelihood is:

  • The forward model has to be a surrogate. Batching wins because a fitted regressor costs almost the same at sixty-four points as at one; a solver integrates sixty-four times either way and gains nothing, while losing the worker pool that was genuinely parallelising it.
  • The sampler has to advance a whole ensemble at once and accept a vectorised log-probability. emcee and zeus both do; pyMC has no such hook and parallelises in the opposite direction, by giving each rank chains of its own.

docs.title: sampler_needs_a_worker_pool
docs.text:
sampler_needs_a_worker_pool()

Whether this backend parallelises across ranks by farming out the likelihood.

The two backends parallelise in opposite directions, and running one arrangement under the other hangs:

  • emcee and zeus advance one ensemble in one process. The parallelism is the likelihood: the sampler is handed a schwimmbad.MPIPool, and every other rank sits in pool.wait() serving evaluations until the master closes the pool.
  • pyMC has no such hook. PyMCSampler instead gives each rank chains_for_rank(...) chains of its own and gathers them along the walker axis at the end -- which means every rank must reach run_mcmc, and its comm.Barrier() and comm.gather are collectives over COMM_WORLD.

Opening a pool for pyMC therefore deadlocked every mpiexec -n >1 UQ run with library: pymc: the workers were parked inside pool.wait(), blocked in a receive that only the master's pool.close() ends, so they could never join the master's barrier -- and the master waits on that barrier forever, holding the pool open. Neither side can move, and the run hangs after sampling with no error and no chain written. It was never seen because nothing exercised it: the pyMC tests run on one rank, where this branch is not taken at all.

docs.title: mcmc_chain_path
docs.text:
mcmc_chain_path()

Where the chain is written -- the same path during the run as at the end of it.

Deliberately one file rather than a partial one that is renamed at the end: everything that reads a chain (load_mcmc_chain, the plotters, a front-end) then needs no notion of "the run has finished", and a run that is cancelled or killed leaves its chain exactly where the tooling already looks for it.

docs.title: burn_in_index
docs.text:
burn_in_index(num_steps)

The first step to keep, from UQ_options['burn_in'].

A value below 1 is a fraction of the chain; 1 or above is a number of steps. Defaults to half the chain, which is what this used to hardcode. Always leaves at least one step, so a burn_in longer than the run degrades to "keep the last sample" rather than producing an empty array and a stack of nan statistics.

docs.title: flat_param_names
docs.text:
flat_param_names()

One name per calibrated parameter, for labelling the statistics.

A grouped row calibrates one value shared across several model variables, so it is one parameter with several names; the first stands for the group, as it does elsewhere.

docs.title: posterior_statistics
docs.text:
posterior_statistics(flat_samples)

Per-parameter summary of the posterior, plus the cost at its point summaries.

A posterior is a distribution, and the honest summary of one is a spread rather than a single number -- so mean and median and the quartiles and the 95% interval, not a winner. The costs are reported for comparison with the calibration's best, deliberately without acting on that comparison: see save_mcmc_statistics.

docs.title: calibration_best_cost
docs.text:
calibration_best_cost()

The calibration's best cost as a finite float, or None if there isn't one.

Prefers the value on disk: a UQ run is often handed the calibration's parameters (set_best_param_vals) without its cost, leaving the in-memory best_cost at inf. Reporting inf would put a JSON Infinity in the file -- which strict JSON parsers reject -- and make every posterior median look like it had beaten the calibration.

docs.title: save_mcmc_statistics
docs.text:
save_mcmc_statistics(flat_samples)

Write mcmc_statistics.json, and leave the calibration's best fit alone.

This used to overwrite best_param_vals.npy and best_cost.npy with the posterior median whenever that median scored a lower cost. Two different estimators were being conflated: a posterior median summarises a distribution, a calibration best is an argmin, and they answer different questions. Silently replacing one with the other meant a UQ run mutated the calibration's answer -- and the file gave no clue which estimator it held.

The comparison is still reported, because it is genuinely informative (a median that beats the optimum usually means the calibration stopped early, or that the posterior is skewed), but nothing is decided on it. Choosing between the two is the user's call, and both are now on disk to choose from.

The one exception is a UQ run with no calibration behind it at all: nothing else has written a best fit, so the median is the only estimate there is, and the rest of the pipeline (plotting, predictions) needs one. That is recorded in the file's source.

docs.title: save_posterior_point_estimates
docs.text:
save_posterior_point_estimates(medians, means)

Write the posterior median and mean as loadable parameter sets.

mcmc_statistics.json already records both, but keyed by display name (g_{Na}) and buried in a per-parameter summary alongside quartiles. That is a report, not a parameter set: nothing can feed it back into a model, because the display names are not the model's and the file's shape is not one any parameter loader reads.

The consequence is that save_mcmc_statistics promises "both are now on disk to choose from" while only one of the two -- best_param_vals.npy -- is actually in a form anything can load. Choosing the median meant reading the JSON and retyping fourteen numbers, and that matters, because a calibration best is an argmin found by whatever surrogate drove it and can sit somewhere the model behaves quite differently. One SN_full cpvt run put its "best fit" at a resting potential of -19 mV against data at -75; the posterior median from the same chain sat at -80.

So, beside the JSON:

  • posterior_median_params.csv -- vessel_name,param_name,value, the format CUFLynx's parameter loader reads. Self-describing, so it does not depend on column order matching the model that loads it.
  • posterior_median_param_vals.npy -- the bare array in optimiser order, the same shape as best_param_vals.npy, for anything that reads that.

And the same pair for the mean, because the two costs are reported side by side and a reader invited to compare them should be able to load either.

A modifier slot names several model parameters and holds one value, so every member is written with that value -- matching how best_param_vals.npy is read back.

docs.text:
CVS0DParamID(
    model_path,
    model_type,
    param_id_method,
    mcmc_instead=False,
    file_name_prefix="no_name",
    params_for_id_path=None,
    param_id_obs_path=None,
    sim_time=2.0,
    pre_time=20.0,
    dt=0.01,
    solver_info=None,
    UQ_options=None,
    optimiser_options=None,
    do_ad=False,
    DEBUG=False,
    param_id_output_dir=None,
    resources_dir=None,
    one_rank=False,
    operation_funcs_external_path=None,
    cost_funcs_external_path=None,
    modifier_funcs_external_path=None,
    use_emulator=False,
    emulator_dir=None,
    emulator_settings=None,
    study_name=None,
    write_cuflynx_study=True,
    user_inputs_path=None,
    study_settings=None,
)

Parameter identification (calibration) for a 0D CVS model.

This is the main user-facing entry point for calibration. It wraps an inner optimisation engine ([ParamID][param_id.paramID.ParamID], or [MCMC][param_id.paramID.MCMC] when mcmc_instead=True) and coordinates loading observation data, selecting parameters, running the optimiser, and writing/plotting results. It is MPI-aware: rank 0 handles all file I/O and output directory creation.

Construct it either directly, or from a config dict with [init_from_dict][param_id.paramID.CVS0DParamID.init_from_dict]. A typical flow is::

pid = CVS0DParamID.init_from_dict(inp)
pid.set_ground_truth_data(obs_data_dict)
pid.set_params_for_id(params_for_id_dict)
pid.set_param_id_method("genetic_algorithm")
pid.run()
pid.simulate_with_best_param_vals()
pid.plot_outputs()

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model_path

Path to the generated model file (CellML/Python/CasADi).

required model_type

One of 'cellml', 'python', 'casadi_python'.

required param_id_method

Optimiser to use, e.g. 'genetic_algorithm', 'CMA-ES', 'bayesian', 'sp_minimize'.

required mcmc_instead

If True, build an MCMC sampler instead of an optimiser.

False file_name_prefix

Model name prefix; ties together the resource files and names the output case directory.

'no_name' params_for_id_path

Optional path to a {prefix}_params_for_id.json. Alternatively call [set_params_for_id][param_id.paramID.CVS0DParamID.set_params_for_id].

None param_id_obs_path

Optional path to an obs_data.json. Alternatively call [set_ground_truth_data][param_id.paramID.CVS0DParamID.set_ground_truth_data].

None sim_time

Logged simulation duration (s).

2.0 pre_time

Unlogged steady-state spin-up duration (s).

20.0 dt

Output sampling step (s); must be <= every dt in the obs data.

0.01 solver_info

Solver config dict (defaults to {"solver": "CVODE_myokit"}).

None UQ_options

Options dict for uncertainty quantification (used when mcmc_instead=True): method (only 'mcmc' so far), library, num_steps, num_walkers, burn_in.

Options dict for the optimiser (e.g. cost_convergence, max_patience, num_calls_to_function, cost_type). Sensible defaults are used if omitted.

Enable automatic differentiation (CasADi backend).

Enable debug behaviour and the debug optimiser options.

docs.text:
get_simulation_helper(
    model_path=None,
    solver=None,
    model_type=None,
    dt=None,
    sim_time=None,
    solver_info=None,
    pre_time=0.0,
    use_emulator=False,
    emulator_dir=None,
    emulator_bundle=None,
    out_of_bounds="error",
)

Create a SimulationHelper for the requested solver.

Returns the appropriate backend (Myokit, libOpenCOR, SciPy, CasADi, ...) based on solver and model_type. All backends share the common [SimulationHelper][solver_wrappers.python_solver_helper.SimulationHelper] method surface.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model_path str

Path to the generated model file.

None solver str

Solver identifier. One of:

  • 'CVODE_myokit': Myokit CVODE for CellML models (the default).
  • 'CVODE_libopencor': libOpenCOR CVODE for CellML models. Needs the libopencor extra (Python 3.12 or later); raises LibOpenCORUnavailableError without it.
  • 'BE_batched_c': generated C for CellML models, each block of independent states integrated on its own by adaptive backward Euler, on solver_info threads threads (needs a C compiler and CMake).
  • 'CVODES_batched_c': as 'BE_batched_c', each block integrated by its own CVODES (also needs SUNDIALS 6 or later).
  • 'solve_ivp': Python/SciPy solver for model_type='python' (method set via solver_info, e.g. RK45, BDF).
  • 'casadi_integrator': CasADi integrator for model_type='casadi_python' (cvodes, idas, collocation, rk).
  • 'external': a user-supplied solver class that does its own time stepping, for model_type='external_python'.
None model_type str

'cellml', 'python', 'casadi_python' or 'external_python'.

None dt float

Output sampling step (s).

None sim_time float

Logged simulation duration (s).

None solver_info dict

Solver config dict (e.g. MaximumStep, method).

None pre_time float

Unlogged steady-state spin-up duration (s).

0.0 use_emulator bool

Answer from a trained emulator instead of integrating (issue #333). solver keeps naming the truth solver -- the one an emulator was trained against, and the one to compare its answers with -- so this is a separate flag rather than another solver name.

False emulator_dir str

Directory holding the trained emulator, when use_emulator.

None emulator_bundle

An already-loaded EmulatorBundle, used instead of reading emulator_dir.

None out_of_bounds str

What the emulator does off its training box: 'error', 'warn' or 'clip'.

'error'

Returns:

Name Type Description SimulationHelper

The backend instance for the requested solver.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the solver is unknown or incompatible with model_type.

RuntimeError

If the requested backend is not installed.

docs.title: libcuflynx.utilities.utility_funcs.latin_hypercube_sample_and_evaluate
docs.text:
latin_hypercube_sample_and_evaluate(
    fun,
    center,
    radius,
    n_samples,
    param_norm_obj=None,
    half_width=None,
)

Generate Latin Hypercube samples around a center point, run the function, and return samples and results. The range for each parameter is set as: scan_min = center[i] - radius * center[i] scan_max = center[i] + radius * center[i] unless half_width is given, in which case an absolute per-parameter half-width is used: scan_min = center[i] - half_width[i] scan_max = center[i] + half_width[i] (used to sample a fixed fraction of each parameter's range rather than of its value, so a wide magnitude range does not make the box collapse for the large-magnitude parameters). Args: fun: Callable that takes a parameter vector and returns a scalar result. center (np.ndarray): Center point for sampling. radius (float): Fractional range for each parameter (param_range_factor). n_samples (int): Number of samples. param_norm_obj (optional): If provided, used to clip samples to parameter bounds. half_width (optional): Absolute per-parameter half-width; overrides radius. Returns: samples (np.ndarray), results (np.ndarray)

docs.title: Coupling to external models
docs.text:
A model generated as C++ (model_type: cpp) can run alongside another model, such as a PDE solver, a 1D blood-flow solver, or any code of your own. The two exchange values every coupling step. The 0D side stays generated C++, so it runs fast, and the other model keeps its own solver, mesh and time stepping.

To CA, the other model is a module: a row of the module array, connected to CellML modules through ports like any other. What makes it external is its module config entry:

  • "module_format": "external_api": it has no CellML;
  • an api block saying how the generated code talks to it.

docs.title: Choosing a path
docs.text:
Your other model is… api How it runs Example a Python class (FEniCS, numpy, a wrapped library…) role: provider, transport: python cuflynx-couple steps the generated C++ (loaded as a shared library) and your class in one process Couple your own Python model, tissue O2 with FEniCS, NE around a varicosity with FEniCS the FV 1D blood-flow solver shipped with CA role: consumer, transport: named_pipe, process: FV1D_solver the coupler launches main0d and the 1D solver, which talk over named pipes 1D finite-volume coupling a C++ program that drives the 0D model step by step role: provider, transport: cpp_class your program links the generated library and calls a generated class (set_…, get_…, solve_time_step) the provider section of src/libcuflynx/generators/cpp/templates/README.md

Not the same as model_type: external_python

External Python Solvers is for calibrating, sweeping or emulating a model CA does not generate at all: CA runs it whole and reads its outputs. On this page, CA generates the 0D model and runs it together with your model.

docs.title: What crosses the coupling
docs.text:
The variables exchanged are the external module's own port variables. Ports connect by port_type, and variables pair up by position, exactly as between CellML modules. For a Python model, the direction of each variable is worked out from the CellML side, so you never list functions:

  • connected to a variable the 0D model computes (a state, or the result of an equation): the external model receives it each step;
  • connected to a boundary condition (or constant) of the 0D model: the external model sets it.

For example, GE_capillary's ub_O2_t (tissue O2) is a boundary condition, so a tissue model sets it, and flux_O2_c is computed, so the tissue model receives it. A variable that is set becomes a libCellML external variable of the generated C. Its parameter value is the starting value until the external model sets it.

cuflynx-couple --check <model folder> prints this table for a generated model.

A port connected to several 0D modules (several capillaries feeding one tissue model, say) exchanges one value per module, as an array ordered as the module array lists them.

Values are in the CellML units of the 0D variables (mol/s, mM, Pa, …). Add api_units or a factor per variable in api.variables if your model works in other units.

docs.title: Coupling step and accuracy
docs.text:
Each coupling step from t to t + dt is explicit and staggered:

  1. the external model receives the 0D values at t, advances to t + dt, and returns what it sets;
  2. those values are held in the 0D model while it steps to t + dt.

This is first order in dt: halving the step halves the coupling error. For stiff exchanges, or when the step can't be small, set "subiterations": n in the api block. Each step is then iterated from snapshots of both models until the exchanged values change by less than tol: each side holds the average of the other's start and end values, which is second order. tests/test_external_coupling.py checks both orders against the all-CellML model.

docs.title: The api block
docs.text:
"api": {
  "name": "my_tissue",
  "role": "provider",
  "transport": "python",
  "python": {"file": "my_tissue.py", "class": "MyTissue"},
  "coupling_dt": 0.01,
  "subiterations": 0,
  "variables": {"C_t": {"api_units": "mM"}}
}
Key Meaning python.file, python.class the model; the file path is relative to the module config's folder coupling_dt the coupling step [s] (default: the model's dt). A module constant coupling_dt (set per instance in the parameters file) overrides it subiterations, tol, relaxation fixed-point iteration of each step (default 0: explicit) variables optional per-variable direction (to_external / from_external), api_units or factor

The block is checked when the module configs load. An unknown key, a missing model file or a bad value is reported with the module's name.

The other transports are described on their pages: named_pipe and process in 1D coupling, and cpp_class in src/libcuflynx/generators/cpp/templates/README.md.
